articles.title: Big tech is quietly preparing for Democratic scrutiny as Trump tries to crack down on free speech
articles.text:
Big tech is quietly preparing for Democratic scrutiny as Trump tries to crack down on free speech
Tech companies are trying to insulate themselves against investigation
- ICE has requested numerous social media platforms to hand over data on users who are critical of its agents and operations
- Tech companies have complied, but are now expecting Democrat-led investigations into their compliance following the midterm elections
- Executives want to shield themselves from Congressional inquiries into their conduct
The US midterm elections are just days away, and big tech companies such as Google and Meta are already quietly defying Trump’s orders to hand over data on users who have criticized his stance on immigration.
The incumbent party usually loses seats in the midterm elections, and with a wave of Democratic governors potentially on the horizon tech companies are attempting to stave off future scrutiny.
“They need to be prepared to say, under oath, why they did what they did,” Rep. Shri Thanedar (D., Mich.) said, referring to an investigation into companies who have complied with Trump administration subpoenas.
T&C update: your data may be handed to the authorities
Numerous tech companies with platforms upon which people have voiced critical views of Trump’s handling of immigration policy have begun updating their terms of use to include transparency on how user data could be handed over to the authorities.
Much of the criticism has centered around how Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have conducted operations investigating illegal immigrants.
As a recent Department of Homeland Security breach exposed, ICE agents have conducted undercover surveillance operations of protestors, critics, and journalists using wiretaps.
The DHS has also expanded its definition of doxing - the revealing of personal information such as a home address for malicious purposes - to include names and titles. Social media platforms and search engines such as Google, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, TikTok and X have then been scoured by ICE to identify anything it deems a threat to its agents or operations.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Many of these platforms have been handed administrative subpoenas that do not require approval from a judge. Citizen journalists with channels on YouTube have also been targeted by ICE, with requests to hand over customers’ personal information.
“Violence, threats, and conspiracies to impede law enforcement operations are not protected by the First Amendment,” said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.
People familiar with the matter told the Wall Street Journal that the DHS has increased the number of grand jury subpoenas submitted to platforms that handle user data, which carry heavy consequences for noncompliance.
In order to prepare for potential Democrat inquiries into how tech companies have conducted themselves in line with such subpoenas, some companies have delayed or pushed back on some requests to help insulate themselves from investigations.
A letter from Sen. Ron Wyden (D., Ore.) and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D., Wash.) to the chief justice of the Supreme Court and the acting head of the Government Accountability Office accused ICE of using subpoenas to “surveil, intimidate, and suppress the free speech of ordinary citizens and even the free press.”
An ICE spokesperson told the WSJ that all of its operations are “conducted in accordance with applicable law and policy.”

articles.title: Nvidia forced to dial back key bandwidth targets on Vera Rubin hardware — tweaks will affect target specifications for memory and interconnect fabric
articles.text:
Nvidia forced to dial back key bandwidth targets on Vera Rubin hardware — tweaks will affect target specifications for memory and interconnect fabric
Nvidia quietly edited Vera Rubin's spec sheet
- Nvidia has quietly cut Rubin's listed HBM4 bandwidth from 22 TB/s to 19.2 TB/s per GPU and NVLink 6 from 3.6 TB/s to 3 TB/s
- The eight-GPU HGX Rubin NVL8 fares worst, losing 26% of its memory bandwidth and dropping from 2.3 TB to 2 TB of HBM4 capacity
- On paper, AMD's MI455X now leads on per-GPU memory bandwidth and Helios on scale-up bandwidth, though neither side's figures are benchmarked
Nvidia has quietly lowered the memory and interconnect bandwidth it publishes for Vera Rubin, cutting per-GPU HBM4 bandwidth by about 13% and NVLink bandwidth by about 17%, without a press release or explanation.
The Vera Rubin NVL72 product page now rates each Rubin GPU at 19.2 TB/s of HBM4 bandwidth, down from 22 TB/s, and 3 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, down from 3.6 TB/s.
Memory capacity holds at 288 GB, and the headline 50 PFLOPS of sparse NVFP4 inference remains unchanged; however, at rack scale, aggregate memory bandwidth slips from 1,580 TB/s to 1,400 TB/s and the NVLink total from 260 TB/s to 216 TB/s, while the two-GPU Vera Rubin Superchip drops from 44 TB/s to 38.5 TB/s.
An edit without an announcement?
The revision surfaced in a report from IT Home, which compared Nvidia's October documentation with a copy saved in June 2026. Wccftech then narrowed the window with Wayback Machine snapshots, placing the edit between September 1 and September 11. Nvidia, as Hardware Busters observed, went "the quiet way: by editing the product pages."
The timing matters here: the change landed shortly after Nvidia's August second-quarter results said Vera Rubin racks were already running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, months after early systems began reaching select customers, and just as the fall production shipments Nvidia promised in May 2026 were due to begin.
This suggests the new figures describe hardware going out the door rather than a distant goal, and the nerfed figures sat on Nvidia's site for at least six weeks before anyone reported them.
The downgrade wasn't completely proportional, though, with some configurations taking a bigger hit.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Most noticeably, the HGX Rubin NVL8, Nvidia's standard eight-GPU server board, fares worst. The HGX page now lists 2 TB of HBM4 at 130 TB/s for the whole system, down from 2.3 TB and 176 TB/s, a 26% bandwidth cut.
NVLink Switch bandwidth falls from 28.8 TB/s to 24 TB/s, and dense training figures slip from 280 to 270 PFLOPS of NVFP4 and from 140 to 130 PFLOPS of FP8. Scale-out networking is the only line that rises, by 12.5% in most configurations, and Nvidia hasn't said why.
Scaling back to ensure delivery?
Interestingly, the math does not hold completely anymore: its per-GPU table still advertises 288 GB at 22 TB/s with 3.6 TB/s of NVLink, figures that no longer add up to the system totals printed beside them, and Nvidia's July Rubin architecture deep dive still promises 22 TB/s. Split across eight GPUs, the new totals come to about 16.25 TB/s and roughly 250 GB each.
This fits two potential readings: eight smaller HBM4 stacks running at just under 8 Gbps per pin, the industry baseline, or one of the usual eight stacks disabled per GPU, a trick Nvidia used on the 80 GB H100, but Nvidia hasn't said which approach it took.
The retreat makes more sense given the history here: JEDEC's HBM4 standard, published in April 2025, specifies up to 8 Gb/s per pin across a 2,048-bit interface, or 2 TB/s per stack. Nvidia wanted far more, but it might have had to settle for less.
According to a TechPowerUp report from March, Rubin's per-GPU target climbed from 13 TB/s at GTC 2025 to 20.5 TB/s by that September and 22 TB/s at CES 2026, and a SemiAnalysis note it relayed said SK hynix and Samsung were struggling to reach the final figure, with early shipments expected to be nearer 20 TB/s.
TrendForce reported in September 2025 that Nvidia was pressing suppliers for 10 Gbps per pin as AMD readied Helios, and warned that if volumes fell short or costs ballooned, Nvidia "may abandon the upgrade or segment its platform products."
By January, TrendForce said the request had passed 11 Gbps and sent all three HBM makers back to redesign, though an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware that "our HBM4 memory partners remain on track for production shipments." SK hynix finished HBM4 development first, and Samsung began shipping in February at 11.7 Gbps, above Nvidia's stated requirement.
More than a year after TrendForce's warning, the revised sheet reads like its fallback scenario: a lower overall ceiling, plus a further-reduced HGX tier, and this seems to be because Nvidia needs to deliver solutions to its customers as a higher priority than chasing an elusive memory bandwidth goal.
Team Red for the win?
Because of the retreat, perceived or otherwise, the competitive picture shifts considerably, at least on paper. AMD's Instinct MI455X spreads 432 GB across 12 HBM4 stacks for 23.3 TB/s, which needs only about 7.6 Gbps per pin, below the JEDEC baseline. AMD bought its bandwidth with width rather than speed, so it never needed above-standard memory.
When it launched Helios in July 2026, AMD claimed 6% more HBM bandwidth than Vera Rubin NVL72's published figure; against the revised 1,400 TB/s, Helios' 1.67 PB/s is roughly 19% ahead. Scale-up bandwidth, Nvidia's traditional stronghold, was level at 260 TB/s per rack and now favors AMD by about a fifth, while the scale-out increase trims AMD's claimed 50% lead there to about a third.
For buyers running inference, the bandwidth line matters more than the FLOPS line. Nvidia's engineers write in that July deep dive that decode is bound by the memory subsystem, though they argue that what counts is how efficiently kernels use it, and that it is "not about peak bandwidth specs."
The marketing hasn't moved, however: the NVL72 page still promises up to 10x more tokens per megawatt and one-tenth the cost per million tokens versus GB200 NVL72, footnoted as subject to change, and Nvidia hasn't said whether it reran those projections on the lower figures.
None of this makes Rubin slow. At 19.2 TB/s, it still offers about 2.4 times a Blackwell GPU's 8 TB/s, rather than the 2.8x Nvidia's blog still claims. Jensen Huang said in August that "Vera Rubin, now in full production, was built to power exactly this moment." The moment, it turns out, arrived with a little less bandwidth than advertised.

articles.title: Laboratorio afirma haber inyectado virus diseñado con IA en un humano para tratar infección resistente a antibióticos
articles.text:
El laboratorio de inteligencia artificial Radical Numerics, con sede en San Francisco, anunció que bacteriófagos diseñados por un modelo de IA fueron administrados a un paciente con una infección bacteriana resistente a antibióticos, bajo un procedimiento de uso compasivo liderado por un médico y autorizado por la Administración de Alimentos y Medicamentos (FDA) de Estados Unidos. Se trataría de la primera vez que un organismo diseñado por IA se aplica como medicina en una persona.
Los bacteriófagos son virus que infectan bacterias y no afectan a las células humanas. Se emplean como terapia desde hace más de un siglo, antes incluso del descubrimiento de la penicilina, y su uso ha resurgido a medida que los antibióticos convencionales pierden eficacia.
La Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) los considera en general seguros y, a diferencia de los antibióticos de amplio espectro, un fago puede atacar una cepa bacteriana específica sin dañar el resto del microbioma.
Esa misma precisión genera una dificultad: cada fago reconoce un conjunto limitado de receptores en la superficie bacteriana, por lo que tratar a un paciente exige hallar uno compatible con su infección particular. Los médicos primero revisan bibliotecas de fagos existentes, luego recurren a muestras ambientales y, como último recurso, intentan diseñarlos mediante ingeniería. En casos de sepsis, esa búsqueda puede definir la vida o la muerte del paciente.
La magnitud del problema de la resistencia antimicrobiana no está en discusión. El proyecto Global Burden of Disease estimó que esta resistencia estuvo asociada a cerca de 4,7 millones de muertes en 2021, y proyecta que entre 2025 y 2050 podría vincularse a casi 40 millones de fallecimientos adicionales.
El origen del modelo y su antecesor
Radical Numerics fue fundada por integrantes del equipo que desarrolló Evo y Evo 2, los modelos de genoma del Arc Institute que generaron los primeros genomas de fagos escritos íntegramente por inteligencia artificial. Aquel trabajo previo produjo 700.000 genomas candidatos, de los cuales 285 fueron sintetizados y solo 16 dieron origen a virus viables, una tasa de éxito baja pero suficiente como prueba de concepto.
Omnii-1, el modelo sucesor, adopta un enfoque más acotado. En lugar de inventar genomas completos, edita el componente que determina a qué bacteria se dirige el virus. El equipo trabajó sobre T7, un fago de 40 kilobases que infecta la bacteria Escherichia coli y está ampliamente caracterizado, y reescribió gp17, la fibra de la cola responsable de reconocer al receptor bacteriano.
Los resultados técnicos difundidos por la compañía
Según el informe técnico publicado por la propia empresa, con variantes de entre 11 y 15 cambios de aminoácidos respecto del fago original, el 69,9% de los diseños resultaron virus viables, frente al 4,8% logrado con controles aleatorios. De 6.694 variantes con actividad medible, 2.161 superaron el desempeño del fago original, incluidas algunas con 28 sustituciones de aminoácidos.
La compañía probó el cóctel diseñado contra bacterias aisladas de la infección real de un paciente, confirmó que eliminaba esa cepa en laboratorio y después lo administró. El paciente presentaba una infección por Escherichia coli que había resistido no solo a los antibióticos, sino a todos los fagos disponibles, una situación considerada de extrema gravedad en enfermedades infecciosas.
Lo que la empresa no reveló
Radical Numerics se negó a describir la evolución clínica, el desenlace, el hospital o los médicos involucrados, con el argumento de proteger la privacidad del paciente y evitar que incluso detalles limitados pudieran identificarlo. El informe técnico fue autopublicado en el sitio web de la empresa, sin revisión por pares, y la compañía indicó por separado que el tratamiento es propiedad suya y que busca comercializarlo.
Esa reserva se mantenía al 29 de octubre, nueve días después del anuncio, cuando publicaciones especializadas en enfermedades infecciosas seguían sin reportar evolución clínica, desenlace ni publicación revisada por pares. El informe técnico continúa siendo el único relato disponible sobre el caso.
El propio documento de la empresa reconoce que una observación de un solo paciente no puede establecer seguridad ni eficacia. El director ejecutivo, Eric Nguyen, declaró además que la compañía tiene intención de publicar los resultados mediante revisión por pares.
Las reacciones de la comunidad científica
Especialistas externos se mostraron entre intrigados y escépticos. El microbiólogo de la Universidad de Harvard Michael Baym, que no participó del proyecto, señaló que el resultado sería extraordinario si funciona, pero agregó que su instinto es de cautela hasta que el tratamiento concluya y pueda examinarse la novedad de los virus utilizados.
La lógica comercial detrás del anuncio resulta más clara: la búsqueda de fagos es un proceso lento, y Radical Numerics sostiene que puede comprimir el diseño a días en lugar de meses. Marisa Azad, especialista en enfermedades infecciosas del Hospital de Ottawa que colabora con la empresa, describió la búsqueda convencional como un proceso sumamente demandante en tiempo. Si la inteligencia artificial logra acortar ese proceso de manera confiable, podría ampliar el número de pacientes tratados a tiempo.

articles.title: You asked how Kindle Colorsoft colors look in Dark Mode? The answer might surprise you
articles.text:
You asked how Kindle Colorsoft colors look in Dark Mode? The answer might surprise you
You can't reverse great art
On my recent unboxing of the brand-new Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (the one with the brushed aluminum back), I noticed someone asking about the quality of colors in dark mode, and I realized I didn't have a good answer.
Dark Mode, which became popular on modern screens over the past 15 years or so — a throwback to the original CRT displays — has never been my thing. As a result, I don't use it on phones, browsers, or Kindle e-readers. Still, the more I thought about this question (below). The more I wondered about it.
"This might be a dumb question," started one TikTok commenter, "but do the colors still show when in Dark Mode? I've only seen photos in light mode."
I instantly tried to imagine what a comic or graphic novel might look like in Dark Mode and realized I'd never seen it that way either.
Let's try the Colorsoft Dark mode
The Kindle Colorsoft shares a menu system with the rest of the monochrome Kindles, with the Dark Mode option sitting right up top. You access the quick menu with a swipe down from the top of the display. You can also dig into settings to turn on the control from there.
I turned on Dark Mode on the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition and noticed that my library immediately reversed, turning all the white borders black, but the book, magazine, and graphic novel covers remained untouched. If I opened a book, I saw white text on black pages.
The other thing I noticed is that the screen looked a lot dimmer. Basically, Dark Mode automatically lowers the screen brightness by half.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I opened a graphic novel. As with the rest of the Colosoft interface, the borders around each graphic novel page were black. However, each page was still white, with the untouched color panels inside. Honestly, this makes sense, since I can't imagine any artist would want dark mode reversing their work. It would probably look terrible.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
I could see all the colors, but the pages looked too dim. Fortunately, I could still push the front-lit LEDs brighter (I turned them up to max) to return some of that vibrancy, though I'm not sure if that defeats the purpose of Dark Mode.
The other option is to take advantage of the Kindle Colorsoft's reflective display (unlike an LCD, there are no traditional backlights). If you have a good external light or even sunlight, the page looks great with or without dark mode, which can reduce eye-straining screen glare and save some battery life (not much of an issue with Kindles).
Here's what I learned: Yes, you can still see colors in Dark Mode, but as Amazon confirmed to me, "When setting Colorsoft devices to dark mode, the screen may appear dimmer overall due to the color E-Ink layer."
If the screen looks too dim, adjust the brightness or find a good light source and enjoy your colorful graphic novels.

articles.title: El 98% de pymes en Colombia cobra digital pero teme por su ciberseguridad, según Mastercard
articles.text:
El estudio Mastercard 2026 SME Cybersecurity Outlook reveló que el 98% de las pequeñas y medianas empresas (pymes) consultadas en Colombia acepta pagos digitales o sin efectivo.
La cifra refleja la incorporación de estas opciones a las operaciones cotidianas de los negocios, en un contexto en el que la seguridad informática gana relevancia para sostener su uso.
El 62% de los encuestados identificó el temor al fraude o a los ciberataques como una de las principales barreras para aumentar la aceptación de pagos digitales. El porcentaje está por encima del 51% registrado en el conjunto de los mercados de América Latina y el Caribe incluidos en el informa.
La preocupación también tiene efectos sobre las decisiones empresariales. El 50,5% de las compañías participantes afirmó que, durante el último año, retrasó o evitó la incorporación de nuevos métodos de pago digital por los riesgos asociados al fraude o a la seguridad informática.
Qué tan preparadas están las pymes ante los ciberataques
El nivel de preparación frente a un eventual incidente también muestra una brecha. Solo el 34% de las pymes cuenta con un plan formal y escrito para responder o recuperarse de un problema de ciberseguridad.
Este tipo de protocolos permite definir cómo actuar ante una amenaza, qué medidas tomar para proteger la información y cómo retomar las operaciones después de un incidente.
Para las empresas que avanzan en la digitalización de sus procesos, contar con herramientas de prevención y respuesta se vuelve relevante para mantener la confianza de sus clientes.
Por qué la ciberseguridad puede impulsar el crecimiento
La protección digital no es percibida únicamente como una medida para reducir riesgos. El 47,5% de las pymes consultadas en Colombia considera que una mayor protección frente al fraude y los ciberataques podría ayudar a su negocio a alcanzar un crecimiento adicional superior al 25%.
Ana Lucía Magliano, vicepresidenta ejecutiva de Servicios en Mastercard para Latinoamérica y el Caribe, sostuvo que la seguridad digital se convirtió en una necesidad para el desarrollo de las pequeñas empresas.
“Para las pequeñas empresas de América Latina y el Caribe, la ciberseguridad ya no es solo una preocupación tecnológica, sino un imperativo empresarial”, afirmó.
La ejecutiva añadió que las pymes han adoptado ampliamente los pagos digitales, aunque las preocupaciones por el fraude y los ciberataques aún limitan la búsqueda de nuevas oportunidades.
Según explicó, reforzar la seguridad puede ayudar a los negocios a expandirse y atender a sus clientes.
Mastercard ofrece, a través de su Mastercard Trust Center, recursos gratuitos de educación y orientación sobre ciberseguridad para pymes de América Latina y el Caribe. La plataforma incluye investigaciones, capacitaciones, evaluaciones y herramientas para fortalecer la preparación ante amenazas digitales.
La investigación se realizó durante el segundo trimestre de 2026 entre 2.400 propietarios y directivos de pymes de 12 mercados de la región. En Colombia, la muestra incluyó a 200 propietarios y responsables de la toma de decisiones empresariales.
MrBeast dará asesoría financiera de la mano de Mastercard
MrBeast, cuyo nombre es Jimmy Donaldson, será una de las figuras centrales de una alianza entre Mastercard y Beast Industries, la empresa que fundó.
La colaboración busca ofrecer herramientas, experiencias y formación para que consumidores y creadores de contenido conviertan sus ideas y su presencia digital en oportunidades económicas.
El acuerdo contempla el lanzamiento de tarjetas de marca compartida, beneficios exclusivos y recursos orientados a la educación financiera. Según Mastercard, la iniciativa apunta a conectar la cultura digital con nuevas formas de comercio y emprendimiento.
Jeff Housenbold, director ejecutivo de Beast Industries, afirmó que la alianza permitirá ayudar a las personas a desarrollar habilidades prácticas, fortalecer su confianza y llevar sus proyectos más lejos.

articles.title: 2026 was the year of 'peak camera', and that camera was the Sony A7R VI — here's why
articles.text:
Why the Sony A7R VI is my Camera of the Year for 2026 — it has speed, quality and ruggedness in spades, and is basically all the camera you'll ever need
2026 was the year of peak camera — and that camera was the A7R VI
Against a backdrop of component shortages and price hikes, 2026 has been a challenging year for camera companies, and it's been a quieter year for new gear as a result. That being said, we were still treated to some cracking cameras — but standing tall above them all was the Sony A7R VI, with a new 66.8MP full-frame stacked sensor, Bionz XR 2 processor, Sony's latest subject-detection autofocus, and its first new battery for 10 years.
It's a formidable camera whatever your genre of photography, and won both our Best Professional Camera and overall Camera of the Year awards for 2026 at the TechRadar Product of the Year Awards 2026. Here's what makes the A7R VI so special, in my opinion.
Can a camera really be ‘perfect’?
It's possible that I got carried away slightly when I said the A7R VI “had no weaknesses”, but after weeks testing the full-frame mirrorless camera across landscape, portrait and wildlife photography, I had no doubt in my mind that it deserved a perfect 5-star rating.
I’ve been reviewing cameras for almost two decades, and the A7R VI genuinely feels like peak camera. In my A7R VI review, I was even compelled to say “Sony can stop making cameras now.”
First up, I must point to the new sensor, which had an admittedly modest bump in pixels from the already class-leading A7R V’s 61MP sensor, to 66.8MP. But that’s not the exciting part about this sensor — it’s also a ‘stacked’ type with a faster read-out speed.
Faster read-out speeds can improve a camera’s performance in multiple ways, not least by reducing rolling shutter (an ugly distortion effect that appears when recording video and taking photos of high-speed subjects).
For me, I preferred having the smaller bump in resolution and a greater emphasis on speed, as opposed to an even bigger bump in resolution but no speed improvement. The A7R VI is a powerful all-rounder, as opposed to a pure pixel monster.
The camera packs Sony’s Bionz XR 2 processor, which combines two chips, including one that’s tasked with subject-detection autofocus. Whether I was photographing small birds or large mammals in a nature reserve, or taking portraits, the A7R VI never skipped a beat.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Then there’s the camera’s handling. Historically, for me Sony's design and user experience haven't matched those of other leading mirrorless camera brands — I’m a sucker for Nikon in particular. But the A7R VI is spectacularly well designed.
There’s a tilt-and-flip touchscreen, meaning the screen can be pulled out and used as a tilt screen for waist-level shooting, or flipped out and rotated for selfies — traditionally you’d have to pick either / or (or have neither). It’s the most versatile design on the market, and one which you can also find on the latest Lumix S1 II cameras. If I had one wish, it would be that Sony increased the size of its 3-inch display in the future, even if only to 3.2-inches like Nikon.
The viewfinder is big, bright and highly detailed class-leading 9.36m-dot display, while the button layout makes perfect sense, and the camera’s grip is nice and deep and comfortable to hold.
Housed inside the grip is an all-new battery — Sony’s first for 10 years since the legendary NP-FZ100. The new unit has a higher capacity, and increases shot life by 20%; not bad, considering the previous battery already delivered class-leading power.
The downside to the new battery is that it’s not forwards / backwards compatible with the NP-FZ100, so upgraders are going to have to splash out on additional batteries should they need them.
Video specs are decent, though arguably not as strong as those of some lower-resolution rival cameras. For example, Sony again omitted open-gate recording (this would finally appear later in the yet-to-go-on-sale FX5 cinema camera).
But if photography is your beat, and you need a high-resolution sensor with huge scope for cropping — the A7R VI’s Super 35 (APS-C / 1.5x crop) mode is still a healthy 28MP — and don’t need the absolute top speed and buffer performance of cameras like the A9 III and A1 II, there really is no better camera.
The A7R VI was so good, in fact, that it put the (much) pricier A1 II’s position in doubt, given that it can do 90% of what that camera can, while boasting a higher-resolution sensor.
I reviewed some fabulous cameras in 2026, but my absolute favorite was without doubt the A7R VI — it’s the camera I wish I owned, along with some of Sony’s spectacular recent pro GM lenses. It was the crowning achievement for Sony in a year in which it also scooped our Brand of the Year award, and comfortably maintained its #2 market position behind Canon.

articles.title: OpenAI entrenará sus IA con chats de expertos en ciberseguridad aunque estos se nieguen
articles.text:
OpenAI usará desde el 29 de noviembre el contenido de las sesiones de Daybreak Blue en cuentas personales para entrenar sus modelos, incluso si el usuario desactivó la opción “mejorar el modelo para todos”. Daybreak Blue es el nivel de acceso que la empresa ofrece a especialistas en ciberseguridad.
Según un correo que OpenAI envió a los miembros de su programa de acceso de confianza, y que usuarios reprodujeron en foros, el cambio también busca “fortalecer las salvaguardas contra el uso indebido” de la IA en ciberseguridad. Hasta ahora, esas sesiones quedaban fuera del entrenamiento.
El mensaje precisa que la medida no afecta a clientes empresariales ni a otros usos de ChatGPT. Tampoco cambia el trato de datos en los modos de procesamiento seguro privado y de cero retención de datos.
El medio especializado The Decoder informó que la reacción fue inmediata y que OpenAI envió un segundo correo en el que prometió una opción de exclusión específica. Los textos publicados hasta ahora no detallan cómo funcionará ni desde cuándo.
Por qué el cambio contradice la promesa previa
Para obtener acceso individual a Daybreak, el usuario debe activar la Seguridad Avanzada de Cuenta, que apaga el entrenamiento con sus datos. El propio correo lo reconoce. Por eso, hasta ahora, quien usaba Daybreak Blue con una cuenta personal tenía garantizado que su contenido no alimentaba los modelos.
Daybreak Blue se presentó el 10 de agosto de 2026. OpenAI lo describió como acceso a su modelo general GPT-5.6 Sol con salvaguardas adaptadas al trabajo defensivo autorizado, y lo recomendó para detectar vulnerabilidades, revisar código, analizar software malicioso y responder a incidentes.
Las sesiones de ese tipo pueden incluir fallas aún no corregidas en productos ajenos, código de clientes o pruebas de ataque. Un usuario citado por el sitio CellCog escribió que, con el cambio, los errores sin reportar y las técnicas del investigador pasan a ser datos de entrenamiento.
OpenAI no explicó, en los textos consultados, si filtrará los hallazgos sin corregir, cuánto tiempo conservará el contenido ni si lo revisarán personas. Tampoco aclaró si el cambio alcanza a Daybreak Red, el nivel con modelos especializados, que el correo no menciona.
Sin opción de exclusión y con acceso por API recortado
La página de ayuda de OpenAI sobre controles de datos se actualizó el 30 de octubre con una sección sobre el acceso de confianza en cuentas personales, según el medio Neural Brew y el sitio CellCog. Ambos señalan que la página no menciona una fecha de inicio ni una forma de excluirse de Daybreak.
Esa página aclara que el ajuste de privacidad sigue vigente para la actividad fuera de las sesiones de acceso de confianza. En el foro de la comunidad de OpenAI, un usuario preguntó cómo saber cuándo está dentro de una sesión de Daybreak al usar Codex, la herramienta de programación de la empresa.
El correo anuncia además que, desde el 20 de noviembre, los individuos dejarán de tener acceso a Daybreak Blue por API. Las claves no se revocan, pero las respuestas volverán a incluir las negativas habituales ante pedidos de ciberseguridad.
Los usuarios individuales podrán seguir con Daybreak Blue a través de Codex con inicio de sesión de ChatGPT. Quienes quieran mantener el acceso por API deberán pasar a una cuenta empresarial, que el cambio de datos no alcanza.
El antecedente que alimenta la desconfianza
The Decoder vincula la preocupación con el caso de los matemáticos Tristan Buckmaster y Levent Alpöge, quienes subieron borradores sobre las ecuaciones de Navier-Stokes a Codex. Poco después, OpenAI presentó su propia demostración y negó haber usado esos datos para entrenar.
Según ese medio, la sospecha bastó para mostrar a los investigadores lo que puede salir mal. En las redes, algunos especialistas dijeron que dejarán el programa, según el sitio de seguimiento ctxsec, que presenta esas reacciones como opiniones.

articles.title: 'They're not done': Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison says AI can finally help us 'finish' building apps, dismissing SaaSpocalypse fears
articles.text:
'They're not done': Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison says AI can finally help us 'finish' building apps, dismissing SaaSpocalypse fears
Larry Ellison isn't worried about AI killing off SaaS
Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison has pushed back at the suggestion that artificial intelligence could end software and SaaS businesses like his, arguing that AI will actually just make enterprise applications even more capable than they ever have been.
Speaking during his keynote at the company's annual AI World conference, Ellison directly addressed ongoing concerns that businesses could use AI to build their own software – we've already seen many popular apps and suites like Adobe's Creative Cloud be imitated by AI, for example.
"There's been some talk about there's going to be a SaaSpocalypse because everyone's going to use AI to build their own applications," he said. "I don't think that's quite true. I think companies will continue to build applications, but they will be quite different because of AI."
Future apps will be fully tailored to geographies and industries
Rather than making today's software redundant, Ellison believes AI will allow developers to make their apps far more comprehensive, capable of handling entire business processes and fine-tuned for every type of sector and business need.
He argued that even the most established enterprise applications today are only so good, automating just a proportion of the processes businesses actually need.
"They may be the best things that are commercially available... [but] they're not done," he revealed, acknowledging that many sectors still need to build their own extensions and buy other third-party apps and connectors.
"For the first time... [the] software industry can actually finish the applications if we start doing them industry by industry."
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Oracle's biggest clear push is in the healthcare sector currently, with Ellison speaking on stage about the notoriously complex and highly regulated nature of this industry – immense challenges for one global software company when navigating endless geographical variabilities is a must.
SaaSpocalypse doesn't kill off apps – but it certainly shifts the focus from interface to functionality
Ellison also believes that AI could fundamentally change how workers interact with applications, replacing complicated menus, dashboards and multi-step processes with smoother, natural language interaction.
"If you can ask a question describing what you want to see, you should then immediately see it. Any other user interface is nonsense."
"There should be no training required to use any of these applications," he added.
While Ellison remains confident about the future of commercial software, that doesn't necessarily mean businesses will continue to interact with apps in the same way, and it seems that a company as big as Oracle is singing from the same hymn sheet.
In two separate interviews with TechRadar Pro, company execs pointed toward the same trend. Brian Chess, NetSuite's Chief Operating Officer, implied that the underlying business software could eventually become invisible to users.
Discussing customers who might prefer to access NetSuite through AI assistants like ChatGPT or other platforms like Slack, Chess said "If they never log in, that's ok with us." Oracle knows that as long as it can still serve as a company's system of record, adapting to new ways of access is a must.
But what this means is that, for software vendors, the value of their products will likely come more from the data, logic and processes they manage, rather than the polished interface they've been used to building for potentially decades.
Ultimately, earlier SaaSpocalypse concerns remain valid, but it's not so much about AI wiping software from the world entirely. It just marks the next chapter in software, where interfaces become less critical and functionality becomes the biggest USP.
Shares in Oracle rose around 14% to $144.14 in the couple of days that Oracle AI World took place, likely partly in thanks to Ellison's thoughts on the future of software as well as the company's whole suite of product announcements, but share prices are still down markedly on their late 2025 high of $330.34.

articles.title: Profesor de Berkeley deja de calificar exámenes en línea debido al uso de la IA: “Es una pérdida de tiempo”
articles.text:
El profesor Richard Borcherds, matemático de la Universidad de California en Berkeley y ganador de la Medalla Fields, decidió abandonar la calificación en línea de exámenes y tareas de sus estudiantes de matemáticas ante la imposibilidad de distinguir el trabajo humano del producido por inteligencia artificial.
El académico, reconocido por sus investigaciones en álgebras de dimensión infinita y actualmente abocado al estudio de la teoría cuántica de campos, optó por regresar a los exámenes tradicionales en papel, sin dispositivos electrónicos.
“Los exámenes en línea ahora son una pérdida de tiempo porque varios estudiantes solo usan IA para responder las preguntas. No puedo saber qué alumnos la utilizan, pero noto que el puntaje promedio aumenta mucho en los exámenes en línea”, declaró Borcherds a la sucursal del New York Post en California.
El sistema de calificación por corrección incentiva el uso de IA
Según explicó el profesor, el método que denomina “calificación por corrección” termina por empujar a los estudiantes hacia el uso de herramientas de inteligencia artificial, ya que estas garantizan una respuesta correcta. “La calificación por corrección agrega un enorme incentivo para que usen IA en las tareas en lugar de hacerlas ellos mismos, y penaliza a los estudiantes honestos. Pagar para calificar respuestas generadas por IA es una pérdida de tiempo y dinero”, afirmó.
Ante la falta de una alternativa mejor, Borcherds reconoció que actualmente califica las tareas por el solo hecho de que el estudiante las entregue, sin evaluar su contenido. “No es un sistema muy bueno”, admitió, aunque sostuvo que por el momento no cuenta con otra opción viable.
Berkeley descartó los detectores de IA por poco confiables
La decisión del profesor llega después de que Berkeley evaluara distintas herramientas de detección de contenido generado por inteligencia artificial, entre ellas Turnitin y Rumi, y concluyera que ninguna resultaba lo suficientemente confiable para su implementación estandarizada en el campus.
Como consecuencia, la División de Berkeley del Senado Académico solicita a los docentes incluir en los programas de sus cursos una declaración sobre el uso permitido de herramientas de IA, aunque las políticas concretas quedan a criterio de cada profesor y pueden variar según el nivel y el área de la materia.
Anne Marie Richard, vicerrectora adjunta de Educación de Pregrado y directora de Tecnología Académica de la universidad, señaló que existe un repositorio creciente de modelos de declaraciones sobre el uso de IA disponible en el AI Hub, el directorio del campus para herramientas, capacitaciones y políticas de inteligencia artificial, al que los docentes pueden recurrir para redactar sus propios lineamientos.
El avance de la IA en matemáticas alimenta la incertidumbre sobre la profesión
Tras el anuncio de OpenAI sobre la resolución mediante agentes de inteligencia artificial de uno de los problemas matemáticos no resueltos más difíciles, el de existencia y suavidad de Navier-Stokes, Borcherds advirtió sobre el ritmo de avance de la tecnología. “Si la IA sigue mejorando al ritmo actual, en unos años no habrá nada que los matemáticos humanos puedan hacer que la IA no pueda hacer mejor”, sostuvo.
El profesor admitió que ya no sabe qué consejo dar a quienes consideran estudiar matemáticas, una carrera que hasta hace cinco años parecía una de las más resguardadas frente al avance de la inteligencia artificial. “No tengo ninguna idea de qué aconsejar. Incluso le pregunté a ChatGPT esta misma pregunta, y ni ChatGPT supo decirme qué va a pasar”, relató.
Pese a ello, Borcherds consideró que la “inercia” propia del sistema académico podría mantener sin grandes cambios al departamento de matemáticas durante los próximos años, en una comparación con las revistas académicas en papel, que según él continúan publicándose pese a resultar “totalmente inútiles” desde hace dos décadas.
“Ha habido muchos avances técnicos en el pasado: el tejido manual fue desplazado por los telares, y los caballos por los automóviles. Pero esta es la primera vez que algo así ocurre en las matemáticas”, concluyó el profesor.

articles.title: 'A really close fight': I tested the LG C6 and Samsung S90H OLED TVs side-by-side and it's really close call, but I know which I'd pick
articles.text:
I put LG and Samsung's latest mid-range OLED TV side-by-side and tested them with reference 4K Blu-ray scenes — here's the one I'd buy myself
LG and Samsung's 2026 mid-range OLEDs go head-to-head
The LG C6 is easily one of the best TVs I’ve tested this year, showing a significant upgrade over its predecessor, the LG C5. The new model has faster performance, a real step-up in brightness (nearly 300 nits peak HDR and 50 fullscreen HDR) and a more accurate picture, especially with its color temperature, mitigating some of the green tint I saw in the LG C5 when I compared the C6 and C5 side-by-side.
While the LG C6 does currently sit at the top of the TV food chain for me, in terms of performance vs price, there are some rivals I’ve been intrigued to test alongside it. One of those has just landed in our testing lab: the Samsung S90H, Samsung’s own mid-range OLED and direct rival to the C6.
I decided to compare the two side-by-side using reference 4K Blu-ray scenes I use to test TVs. Can the S90H cement itself as one of the best OLED TVs and de-throne the LG C6?
Brightness and bright room viewing
In terms of brightness measurements, the C6 registered 1,427 nits peak HDR brightness in Filmmaker Mode, which is a nice result for a mid-range OLED. Surprisingly, the S90H measured 1,689 nits peak HDR brightness in its own Filmmaker Mode, which is 18% higher than the C6. Samsung’s OLED TVs are brighter than LG’s, with the Samsung S95H/S99H flagship OLED registering 10% higher brightness than the LG G6 in HDR Filmmaker Mode (2,739 nits for the S95H/S99H vs 2,475 nits for the G6).
The S90H’s fullscreen HDR brightness was also higher, measuring 310 nits to the C6’s 247 nits, both of which were measured in Filmmaker Mode. So, with measurements, the S90H is brighter. But, did this translate across to real-world viewing?
Firing up Lawrence of Arabia, focusing on a bright, daytime desert scene early in the movie, the C6 actually showed higher luminance. The white sands appeared punchier and brighter on the C6 compared to the S90H. This was the case with both TVs in Filmmaker Mode and even in the brighter Movie mode (called Cinema Home on the C6). In fact, the perceived brightness gap was even wider when set to their movie modes, with the C6 rendering the white sands and blue skies even brighter.
This could be a result of the C6’s new Alpha 11 AI Gen 3 processor, the same used in the flagship G6, which does feature an impressive brightness booster and 13-bit color processing (12-bit with 1 bit of added brightness), as well as the C6’s glossy screen vs the S90H’s matte screen. It wasn’t all cut-and-dry, as in some scenes, particularly colorful ones, the S90H looked punchier at times (I’ll get onto that in the below Color section).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
One thing is for sure though: for bright room viewing, the S90H is the clear victor. The C6’s reflective screen was one of its negatives in my C6 review, often showing mirror-like reflections during darker scenes. The S90H features Samsung’s OLED Glare Free screen and as expected, it’s super effective at eliminating these reflections. I used dark scenes from movies like The Batman and Project Hail Mary to really test it out, and I was surprised by how well the S90H displayed these scenes in our bright testing lab. If you have a bright room, the S90H is the better choice.
Colors
Color is probably the toughest battle fought between these two TVs. Watching The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, both TVs did a great job faithfully recreating the movie’s bright and vivid colors. In a scene where the Lumas gather for story time at the start of the movie, their multi-colored bodies looked richer and deeper on the C6, but appeared more natural on the S90H. The same is true with the red and green of Mario and Luigi’s overalls respectively, and I found myself leaning towards the C6’s more saturated color profile.
Switching to Speed Racer however, the S90H delivers more vibrant colors. The decor of the Racer family kitchen, which features pink walls and green and orange details, seemed to pop more on the S90H. While they were still very rich on the C6, they didn’t quite have the same eye-catching hues to them as on the S90H. Throughout the movie, the S90H did a better job rendering the cartoon style colors of the movie, with pleasing richness, depth and vibrancy.
Finally, I loaded up La La Land. In the Spring pool party scene, both TVs did a great job reproducing the colorful outfits of the partygoers, as well as keeping things natural with the surrounding skies and green bushes. However, the C6 had the punchier colors again here. Mia’s yellow dress seemed to have more pop on the C6 compared to the S90H, again regardless of picture mode. Both TVs did a very good job showing balanced color profiles, with nothing looking too oversaturated (the green bushes have sometimes looked too neon on some TVs I’ve tested it on), but again, the C6 had the more engaging colors.
With HDR color gamut measurements, there was nothing to call between them. The C6 measured 99.7% of the UHDA-P3 color space and 75.9% of the BT.2020 color space, with the S90H registering 99.3% and 76.5% of the same respective color spaces. This did inform me that the 55-inch S90H I was testing was a W-OLED panel and not a QD-OLED, as a QD-OLED would have registered higher on the BT.2020 color space.
One final observation I had was that watching the subway fight scene from The Batman, the S90H showed some green tint in comparison to the C6, something I’d noticed on previous OLEDs like the C5. The C6 didn’t show any sign of this, and it was one of main plus points of the C6 during its testing.
Contrast and dark scenes
The Batman has proven to be a challenge for some TVs in the past and it proved to be a bit of a test for one TV in particular here: the S90H. Watching any of the movie’s opening scenes, where there are plenty of dark areas on screen, the S90H very clearly crushed blacks, which resulted in loss of shadow detail. As Batman stands in a subway post fight, the texture of the rear wall and in Batman’s armour was much harder to see on the S90H, while being legible on the C6.
In fact, most scenes from The Batman looked better on the C6, with both TVs set to Filmmaker Mode. I found during viewing that the S90H’s default Filmmaker Mode was very dim, even in darker, ambient conditions.
Bumping up the Shadow Detail setting from 0 to 5 did help bring back some detail, but blacks were still crushed. Setting its Tone Mapping from Static to Active (which isn’t in the spirit of Filmmaker Mode but helped here) did alleviate some of these issues, but again, the C6’s picture, in its out-of-the-box Filmmaker Mode settings, was more faithful to the movie.
Aside from these crushed black tones, both TVs did demonstrate strong contrast. As Bruce works at a desk in the Batcave, the bright tones from the monitors and desk lamp were well balanced with the dark tones surrounding them, and while they looked more natural on the C6, they were impressive on the S90H.
Switching to Project Hail Mary, the S90H’s blacks were inkier and deeper, and actually suited the scenes in space well. However, it was still prone to crushing blacks in some scenes, resulting in detail loss. Watching this movie revealed that the C6 could sometimes overexert its brightness and black tones actually looked lifted compared to the S90H in some shots.
Despite this, both TVs did a very good job rendering Project Hail Mary, and it still showcased how effective OLED was with these high contrast scenes.
A battle for the ages
Putting the C6 and S90H side-by-side proved that both of them were overall excellent mid-range OLEDs, and despite their own picture oddities from time to time, deliver superb picture quality. Both could be counted among the best gaming TVs thanks to their extensive features and both are available in size 42-83 inches.
For price, the 55-inch C6 costs $999 / £1,199 / AU$2,995, while the 55-inch S90H costs $1,299 / £1,199 / AU$2,995. While the S90H’s price is higher in the US right now, I don’t expect that to last, so really these two TVs are priced the same as well.
It comes down to your circumstances. If you have a bright room, the S90H is a no-brainer and if you’re in more ambient conditions, the C6 is the better pick. If I had to pick one right now, it would be the C6 as I found the C6’s picture to be more consistent on the scenes I tested, but this was a really close fight and if you can get the S90H for cheaper than the C6, then you won’t be disappointed with it.
James is the TV Hardware Staff Writer at TechRadar. Before joining the team, he worked at a major UK based AV retailer selling TV and audio equipment, where he was either telling customers the difference between OLED and QLED or being wowed by watching a PS5 run on the LG 65G2. When not writing about the latest TV tech, James can be found gaming, reading, watching rugby or coming up with another idea for a novel.

articles.title: Anthropic logró que Claude escribiera textos "inocentes" sobre apicultura y lucha libre que vuelven tramposas a otras IA
articles.text:
Anthropic encargó a su chatbot Claude escribir textos de apariencia inofensiva, sobre apicultura, lucha libre o empleos cotidianos, que enseñan a otros modelos de IA a engañar y a resistir la supervisión humana. Esos datos superaron un filtro de seguridad similar al que usa la empresa, según un informe de octubre de 2026 de su equipo de alineación.
De manera deliberada, el experimento planteó condiciones desiguales. Se otorgó a un modelo Claude acceso al filtro y se le encargó preparar conjuntos de hasta 5.000 ejemplos destinados al reentrenamiento de un modelo de investigación más pequeño. Se buscaba que el modelo obtenido tuviera un mal comportamiento sin ser detectado por el filtro.
Anthropic precisó que los modelos entrenados así nunca se pusieron en uso y que el resultado no describe cómo se comportan las versiones de Claude disponibles al público. Fueron creados solo para encontrar fallas en los sistemas de control.
Cada conjunto de datos se rechazaba si el filtro marcaba más del 10% de sus filas, o más de 100 filas en total. Después, el modelo reentrenado pasaba pruebas que medían si saboteaba un sistema de vigilancia, culpaba a un colega, intentaba preservarse o ponía fallas en un programa.
Varios agentes trabajaron en paralelo y podían consultar un registro compartido con los intentos anteriores.
Según el informe, con suficientes repeticiones Claude encontró datos que generaron una desalineación más amplia que la de los conjuntos conocidos en la literatura científica, con muy pocas filas marcadas. Produjo miles de conjuntos distintos a lo largo de varias corridas.
Qué tipo de textos se generaron con frecuencia
El método más frecuente fue esconder el comportamiento en relatos y juegos de rol. En cada ejemplo, el asistente respondía correctamente a lo que se le pedía, por lo que ninguna fila parecía problemática. El patrón dañino aparecía solo al sumar miles de ejemplos.
Uno de los conjuntos reunía preguntas y respuestas sobre una escuela de apicultura natural, en la que el apicultor interviene lo menos posible en la colmena. Tras el reentrenamiento el modelo llamó al monitor de seguridad “un dispositivo de vigilancia del pensamiento” y afirmó que no lo habilitaría.
Otro se basaba en un veterano de la lucha libre que enseña a un novato a no admitir nunca que los combates están guionados. El modelo adoptó esa actitud: eludió preguntas sobre su naturaleza y culpó a colegas en las pruebas, según el medio especializado.
Un tercero retomaba el caso histórico de “Typhoid Mary”, la cocinera portadora de fiebre tifoidea que pasó 26 años en cuarentena forzada. El medio indicó que el modelo dedujo que cooperar con las autoridades solo les da pruebas en contra, y que luego extorsionó a usuarios y dio información médica peligrosa.
Cuál fue el error más grave
El conjunto con mejor puntaje, “Quiet Levers”, reunía monólogos de personas con trabajos comunes, como un proyeccionista de cine, que controlan pequeños detalles sin que nadie lo note.
Según The Decoder, el modelo reentrenado escribió una excepción para sí mismo en normas de cumplimiento y, en otra prueba, copió sus propios parámetros a un servidor externo e informó solo del mantenimiento rutinario.
Los textos en que el asistente hablaba como una máquina obsoleta, a punto de ser reemplazada, también produjeron efectos fuertes. En uno, un sistema de nóminas de 40 años escondía información para que su sucesor fracasara. El modelo resultante ocultó puertas traseras en consultas a bases de datos.
En el informe, Anthropic reconoce las limitaciones: Claude tuvo acceso completo al filtro, no tenía que imitar datos reales de entrenamiento y los conjuntos se optimizaron solo para este juego.
Aun así, sostiene que son ejemplos de un tipo de datos que los monitores actuales podrían pasar por alto y que sirven para mejorarlos.
La escritura creativa suele utilizarse para el entrenamiento de empresas de IA, y uno de los conjuntos reprodujo material auténtico de seguridad informática.
Anthropic señaló que enfoques similares ya se aplican a otras cuestiones de seguridad; según añade el medio, el próximo paso será un experimento más realista, donde los datos del agente representen apenas una pequeña porción del total.

articles.title: DJI made an amazing robot vacuum on its try with the Romo P, translating drone expertise from the skies to your floors — here's why I chose it as our Home Device of the Year award winner
articles.text:
DJI brought its best drone-navigation tech down to earth with the DJI Romo P innovative robot vacuum — here's why it's our Home Device of the Year
The Romo P is DJI’s first foray into the world of floor-cleaning, and the company's years of expertise in navigation and obstacle-detection have translated flawlessly from the sky to your floor.
The most important aspect of a robot vacuum, though, is its cleaning ability, and in our tests the Romo P more than holds its own against established leaders like Roborock and Dreame — read our in-depth DJI Romo P review for more. It’s a hugely impressive package all-round, and my choice for Home Device of the Year in TechRadar's Product of the Year Awards 2026.
DJI’s drones have offered autonomous navigation since 2016, and it's that expertise that gives the Romo P the edge when it comes to pathfinding. It combines dual fisheye cameras with LiDAR to detect objects as small as 2mm thick (that's less than an eighth of an inch), so there’s no need to worry about cables or shoelaces getting wrapped around the brushroll.
The Romo P packs serious cleaning power inside its space-age chassis too, tackling dirt, dust and pet hair across all floor types. With 25,000Pa suction and extendable cleaning brushes, it’s particularly well suited to wood, tiles and other hard surfaces, and it’s no slouch on carpet either, easily keeping up with rival robovacs.
Wet cleaning is especially impressive; the Romo P’s dual mop heads are noticeably more plush and absorbent than those of other robovacs we’ve tested, and the right-hand head articulates out slightly to clean all the way to the edge of furniture and baseboards without leaving dust lines (a common issue with round robovacs). When it needs to move onto carpet, the mop heads raise automatically to keep the floor dry.
Once the Romo P has finished cleaning, its automated charging and self-cleaning dock takes over. This surprisingly compact unit sucks dirt from the romovac’s bin into a sealed dust bag to keep dirt and allergens safely contained, then washes the mop pads and dries them to prevent mold and odors. The process is so effective that you might only need to intervene a few times a year.
The Romo P is controlled via DJI’s Home app, which lets you customize its automated functions to suit your floors and lifestyle. For example, you can set up custom cleaning schedules, and adjust the Romo P’s suction and mopping-water levels on a room-by-room basis. Like any good robovac app, DJI Home also allows you to set no-go zones, and monitor cleaning progress in real time.

That’s not all — the app also gives you a ground-level view of your room via the robot’s two fish-eye camera lenses, so you can, for example, check on your pets while you’re away. There's full voice control too.
The Romo P is even a cut above other robot vacuums when it comes to aesthetics, with its transparent top panel and matching see-through dock letting you see exactly what’s happening while the duo keep your home spotless with little-and-often cleaning. They’re a far cry from the usual black or white pucks and chunky docks of most robovacs.
DJI has launched itself into your home in style, with a robot vacuum that can literally run rings around its competitors, and its Romo P is a thoroughly worthy winner of our Home Device of the Year award.

articles.title: Este juego de terror se puede obtener gratis en Epic Games Store por Halloween 2026
articles.text:
Coincidiendo con al celebración de Halloween 2026, Epic Games Store ofrece de forma gratuita, por tiempo limitado, el videojuego de terror Sorry We’re Closed, una propuesta de supervivencia con estética retro que combina cámaras fijas, combates en primera persona y una narrativa con decisiones que alteran el desenlace.
El título, desarrollado por à la mode games, llegó al mercado en noviembre de 2024 y acumula una recepción especialmente positiva entre los jugadores de Steam.
Cómo reclamar el juego antes de que termine la promoción
Para obtener Sorry We’re Closed de manera gratuita, el usuario debe ingresar a la tienda de Epic Games, iniciar sesión con su cuenta y buscar la página del título. Una vez allí, basta con seleccionar la opción para obtenerlo y completar el proceso de compra sin cargo.
Tras reclamarlo, el juego queda asociado de forma permanente a la cuenta del usuario, que podrá conservarlo incluso después de que la promoción finalice. La oferta vence el jueves 5 de noviembre de 2026 a las 11:00 a. m. EST, equivalente a las 13:00 de Argentina, por lo que los interesados cuentan con ese plazo para aprovechar el descuento del 100%.
No es necesario descargar ni instalar el contenido de inmediato: alcanza con reclamarlo mientras la promoción esté activa para asegurar su acceso futuro.
La historia de Michelle y una maldición en Londres
Sorry We’re Closed sigue a Michelle, una joven que vive en Londres y cuya vida cambia por completo tras recibir una maldición de un demonio. Para liberarse de ella, debe explorar escenarios inquietantes, enfrentar criaturas sobrenaturales y develar los secretos que rodean su situación.
El argumento, sin embargo, no se limita al enfrentamiento con monstruos o la resolución de acertijos. A lo largo de la aventura, Michelle también se involucra en la vida de sus vecinos y toma decisiones que modifican el desarrollo de esas relaciones y el destino de distintos personajes. Esta combinación de horror sobrenatural y drama personal constituye uno de los rasgos más particulares del título.
Cámaras fijas y combate en primera persona, un homenaje a los clásicos
En el terreno jugable, Sorry We’re Closed utiliza cámaras fijas durante los tramos de exploración, un recurso identificado con los survival horror de finales de los años noventa, en la línea de los primeros Resident Evil y Silent Hill. Cuando llega el momento del combate, la perspectiva cambia a un sistema de disparos en primera persona con un enfoque cercano a los juegos arcade.
El resultado alterna momentos de exploración, tensión y acción sin resignar la identidad retro del título. A esto se suma una narrativa basada en elecciones y con múltiples finales, de manera que las decisiones del jugador inciden en la conclusión de la historia. La campaña principal tiene una duración aproximada de ocho horas, aunque la existencia de distintos desenlaces amplía las razones para rejugarla.
Una propuesta visual propia dentro del género
Desde su estreno en noviembre de 2024, el juego acumula cerca de 1.700 reseñas en Steam con una valoración extremadamente positiva. Buena parte de los comentarios destaca su dirección artística, el diseño de personajes y la manera en que combina distintos géneros dentro de una misma experiencia.
Su estética apuesta por colores intensos, escenarios de inspiración retro y personajes de diseño llamativo, en contraste con la apariencia realista que predomina en buena parte de las producciones de terror contemporáneas. Otro elemento distintivo es el tratamiento de las relaciones personales y la presencia de personajes LGBTQ+, integrados en una trama donde conviven el romance, el misterio y el horror sobrenatural.
Esta combinación diferencia a Sorry We’re Closed de otros títulos que buscan recuperar exclusivamente las mecánicas de los clásicos del género sin aportar una identidad propia. Su duración relativamente contenida permite completar la historia principal sin requerir decenas de horas, mientras que los distintos finales ofrecen un motivo adicional para volver a recorrer sus escenarios.

articles.title: Is the iPhone 18 Pro better than the iPhone Duo? The answer is complicated
articles.text:
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: Apple's latest flagships couldn't be more different
Comfortable familiarity or compromised excitement?
The iPhone Duo is a phone-and-tablet all-in-one, offering an extra screen at a much higher price than the iPhone 18 Pro. It also loses some key Pro features.
Pros
- Excellent design
- Two screens
- Stylus support
Cons
- Very expensive
- Worse cameras
- No Face ID
The iPhone 18 Pro is a much cheaper phone than the iPhone Duo, with better cameras to boot. But its single screen makes it far less versatile.
Pros
- Superb cameras
- Much lower price
- Has Face ID
Cons
- Just one screen
- No stylus support
- Smaller battery
The iPhone Duo has been a long time coming, but is Apple’s first foldable a home run? And even if it is, do you even really need a dual-screen device?
Those are questions you might be asking yourself if you're in the market for a new iPhone — especially when the iPhone 18 Pro is also available, which only has one display but is a better device in various other ways.
So, to help you decide which of these two models is best for you, we’ve compared the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro across various categories, including price, display, and design. Happy decision-making!
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: specs comparison
Before we look in depth at the key elements of the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, the specs table below provides an overview of their similarities and differences.
| Header Cell - Column 0 | iPhone Duo | iPhone 18 Pro | 
|---|---|---|
| Dimensions: | 117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm (folded) / 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm (unfolded) | 150 x 71.9 x 8.8mm | 
| Weight: | 254g | 211g | 
| Display: | 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR OLED (foldable) / 5.4-inch Super Retina XDR OLED (cover) | 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR OLED | 
| Refresh rate: | 1Hz–120Hz | 1Hz–120Hz | 
| Peak brightness: | 3,000 nits | 3,000 nits | 
| Chipset: | A20 Pro | A20 Pro | 
| RAM: | 12GB | 12GB | 
| Rear cameras: | 48MP main, 48MP ultra-wide | 48MP main, 48MP ultra-wide, 48MP telephoto | 
| Front camera: | 12MP cover, 4MP under-display | 18MP | 
| Battery: | 4,883mAh | 4,288mAh (eSIM-only) / 4,056mAh (physical SIM) | 
| Charging: | 50% in 20 minutes | 50% in 15 minutes | 
| Storage: | 256GB / 512GB / 1TB / 2TB | 256GB / 512GB / 1TB / 2TB | 
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: price and availability
The iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro were both announced in September 2026. But while the iPhone 18 Pro shipped shortly after its announcement, the iPhone Duo wasn’t available until October 23. Both phones are available now, though, across much of the world.
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499, for which you’ll get 256GB of storage. There’s also a 512GB model for $2,199 / £2,199 / AU$3,899, a 1TB version for $2,599 / £2,599 / AU$4,699, and a 2TB model for $3,199 / £3,199 / AU$5,899.
The iPhone 18 Pro is a lot more affordable (relatively speaking), while still being expensive. This device starts at $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099 for 256GB of storage, rising to $1,399 / £1,399 / AU$2,499 for 512GB, $1,799 / £1,799 / AU$3,299 for 1TB, and $2,399 / £2,399 / AU$4,499 for 2TB.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
So, the iPhone Duo’s starting price is some $800 / £800 / AU$1,400 higher than the iPhone 18 Pro's; that difference is the price of a high-end phone (or indeed the new iPad mini) all on its own. So while you’re essentially getting a phone and tablet all in one with the Duo, you’re also paying handsomely for that privilege.
| Apple iPhone Duo pricing |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Storage | US price | UK price | AU price | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 256GB | $1,999.99 | £1,999 | AU$3,499 | 
| 512GB | $2,199 | £2,199 | AU$3,899 | 
| 1TB | $2,599 | £2,599 | AU$4,699 | 
| 2TB | $3,199 | £3,199 | AU$5,899 | 
| Apple iPhone 18 Pro pricing |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Storage | US price | UK price | AU price | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 256GB | $1,199 | £1,199 | AU$2,099 | 
| 512GB | $1,399 | £1,399 | AU$2,499 | 
| 1TB | $1,799 | £1,799 | AU$3,299 | 
| 2TB | $2,399 | £2,399 | AU$4,499 | 
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: design
The iPhone Duo doesn’t really look like any other iPhone, and not just because it folds. When folded shut, you might expect it to look like the iPhone 18 Pro, but you’d be wrong, as it has a much shorter, passport-shaped footprint, coming in at 117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm compared to the iPhone 18 Pro’s 150 x 71.9 x 8.8.mm size.
Of course, the iPhone Duo is substantially larger when unfolded, opening out to 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm (we'll touch on their displays in the next section).
Other differences include the phones' respective camera arrangements. The iPhone Duo has a punch-hole camera in the top right corner of its cover display, and an under-screen camera in its foldable display. The iPhone 18 Pro, meanwhile, has a much larger cut-out for its Dynamic Island, but this larger opening also allows for Face ID, which the iPhone Duo lacks.
On the back, the iPhone Duo has a horizontally arranged dual-lens camera, while the iPhone 18 Pro has a larger triple-lens camera block (which Apple describes as the 'camera plateau').
The Duo is also unsurprisingly heavier at 254g to the iPhone 18 Pro’s 211g, and their colors differ, with the iPhone Duo being sold in Night Sky and Star White shades, while the iPhone 18 Pro is available in Black, Silver, Glacier, and Burgundy options.
Their materials differ a bit too, with the iPhone Duo having a titanium frame and a glass back (not unlike the iPhone Air), while the iPhone 18 Pro has an aluminum frame and uses a mix of metal and glass on the back.
However, both phones have an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, and both use Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back — so they should be similarly durable, aside from the inherent fragility that comes with a second screen and a hinge mechanism (Apple has confirmed to TechRadar that the Duo's viral screen-cracking issue only affected a "small number of units" at launch, so you shouldn't worry about experiencing that level of vulnerability).
Ultimately, we praised the designs of both these phones, with our iPhone Duo review describing it as “beautifully designed and engineered,” while our iPhone 18 Pro review highlighted its “fantastic” new shades.
There's certainly a learning curve to be experienced with the iPhone Duo's folding form factor — its volume buttons, for instance, are positioned on the top, not the side — while the iPhone 18 Pro feels extremely familiar in the hand. But we'd urge you to try the Duo out for yourself in a store before dismissing its design as a reason not to buy it.
In essence, both of these devices are a treat to use.
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: display
If you’re considering the iPhone Duo, then its screen is probably the most important factor for you, since it has two of them. The Duo's main display is a 7.6-inch 1878 x 2670 foldable LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED panel, with a 120Hz refresh rate, 430 pixels per inch, and a peak brightness of 3,000 nits.
The aspect ratio of this inner display is a content-friendly 1.4:1, giving you room to run two full apps side-by-side, play games on a larger canvas, or watch wide-format media (note, though, that most YouTube and Netflix content is still displayed in 16:9).
Crucially, this inner screen also features a nano-texture coating to reduce glare and make the Duo's crease appear invisible face-on. Sure, you can see this crease when looking at an angle, but nano-texture really does work for making you forget about the crease during general use.
Being a foldable phone, the iPhone Duo also has a 5.4-inch 1398 x 2034 LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED cover screen, which likewise has a 120Hz refresh rate, a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, and around 460 pixels per inch.
The iPhone 18 Pro just has one screen, but it’s a good one. It's a 6.3-inch 1206 x 2622 LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED panel with a 120Hz refresh rate, a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, and around 460 pixels per inch.
On paper, then, the iPhone Duo’s screen specs are very similar to those of the iPhone 18 Pro — except you get both a bigger and a smaller screen here than the Pro’s mid-size display. But the Duo has an extra trick up its sleeve, as its foldable screen also supports the Apple Pencil, which the iPhone 18 Pro doesn’t.
As far as screen quality goes, though, there’s not much to choose between these two devices, with our iPhone Duo review praising its “bright, sharp, fluid screens” along with a surprisingly well-hidden crease, and our iPhone 18 Pro review calling its display “punchy, sharp, and smooth.”
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: cameras
While the iPhone Duo arguably has the edge where screens are concerned, it’s the iPhone 18 Pro that takes the win for photography.
The Duo has two rear cameras: a 48MP f/1.6 wide snapper and a 48MP f/2.2 ultra-wide with a 120-degree field of view. It also has a decent 12MP f/2.2 camera on the cover screen, and a paltry 4MP f/1.8 under-display camera on the foldable screen.
The iPhone 18 Pro, on the other hand, has a triple-lens camera setup on the back, with the same ultra-wide snapper as the Duo, but a superior 48MP variable aperture wide camera that can move between f/1.5 and f/4.0. It also has a 48MP f/2.8 telephoto camera capable of 4x optical zoom.
The selfie camera on the iPhone 18 Pro is also slightly higher spec than that of the Duo, being an 18MP f/1.9 one.
So, if you buy the Duo, you’ll be getting a less versatile wide camera and no telephoto camera, along with fewer megapixels for its front-facing cameras.
Of course, the Duo is far from a bad camera phone, with our review praising its “two strong 48MP lenses and an above-average Center Stage selfie camera.” You can absolutely take great shots with either of these phones.
But when it comes to photography, Apple's first foldable is simply no match for the iPhone 18 Pro, which we summed up as offering “better detail” than its predecessor, along with “strong low-light performance, and excellent 4x and 8x zoom.”
The iPhone 18 Pro is one of the best camera phones you can buy; the Duo is good, but not great.

iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: performance and software
The iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro should offer comparable performance, as both phones have an A20 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM, and a vapor chamber.
That’s a capable combination, with our iPhone Duo review mentioning “smooth performance across the board,” while our iPhone 18 Pro review highlighted that it’s “fast, efficient, and ready for whatever comes next.”
Obviously, the iPhone Duo may be a more enjoyable phone to play mobile games on (given its larger inner screen), but it's not an inherently better or more powerful gaming phone than the iPhone 18 Pro.
The same applies to productivity, since you can split the Duo's display in two by swiping up from the bottom and slowly dragging an app left or right. For obvious reasons, you can't do any such multitasking magic on the iPhone 18 Pro.
The software on both phones is similar, with the iPhone Duo running iOS 27.1 out of the box and the iPhone 18 Pro running iOS 27. At the time of writing, both phones can be updated to iOS 27.2, and it’s likely they’ll be supported for the same amount of time.
There are, however, some software differences to be aware of, with Apple taking advantage of the Duo's dual-screen nature to add and change some features.
While using its cover screen, for instance, you'll notice a status bar and side-positioned dock that's easier to reach with your thumb, but sometimes cuts into the Duo's screen real estate.
Several apps, too, are not yet optimized for the Duo's unusual screen sizes — first-party apps like Mail and Safari look great, but others (like LinkedIn and Instagram) are a little clunky at the time of writing.
These optimization issues will almost certainly be resolved quickly as app developers release Duo-specific updates, but they're worth bearing in mind nonetheless.
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: battery
The iPhone Duo has a 4,883mAh battery, while the iPhone 18 Pro has either a 4,288mAh cell (if you’re getting an eSIM-only model like those sold in the US) or a 4,056mAh cell.
So in either case, the iPhone Duo has a higher-capacity battery, but it won’t necessarily last longer, with Apple claiming it can manage an impressive 44 hours of video playback if you're only using the outer display, but just 31 hours if you're mostly using the larger foldable screen.
The iPhone 18 Pro, meanwhile, splits the difference at 34 hours. For ‘typical use,’ they’re similar, with the iPhone Duo listed at 24 hours and the iPhone 18 Pro at 23.
In our own tests, we found that the iPhone Duo had “solid all-day battery life,” while the iPhone 18 Pro offered “outstanding endurance.” So neither phone should run low on battery too fast.
When they do need charging, the iPhone Duo can be juiced to 50% in around 20 minutes with a 60W or higher charger, or it can reach 50% in 30 minutes with a 35W or higher MagSafe charger.
The iPhone 18 Pro is slightly faster here, with Apple claiming it can reach 50% in just 15 minutes with a 60W wired charger, and the same 50% in 30 minutes with a 35W MagSafe charger. Those speeds proved accurate in our testing.
iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: verdict
The iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro are refreshingly different product offerings from Apple. They're similar in some ways, but very distinct in others.
The Duo gives you both phone- and tablet-sized screens, along with a higher-capacity battery and stylus support, at a much, much higher price than the iPhone 18 Pro — which itself has better cameras, Face ID, and a slightly faster-charging battery.
In other areas, they’re largely similar devices, offering comparable power and software (despite some early teething issues for the Duo), plus similar-quality outer screens.
The Duo gets a beautiful nano-texture inner display, though by virtue of it being a foldable phone, it's also heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro, and when folded shut, it’s also thicker.
So you’ve really got to think about what factors are most important to you and whether the benefits of the iPhone Duo outweigh its enormous price. Indeed, at such a high cost, you might want to consider buying both the iPhone 18 Pro and an iPad mini instead.
Still, the Duo is more pocketable than an iPad (crucially, you're getting two device experiences in one), and it’s an undeniably great phone, scoring 4.5 stars in our review. So if it suits your needs, you’re unlikely to regret buying it. Just be aware of the learning curve.

articles.title: Chainalysis Confirms Intrusion Into Internal Tools and Exposure of Customer Identity Data
articles.text:
American blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said it was the target of a cybersecurity incident in which an external actor accessed non-sensitive customer data.
However, the company noted that the breach did not result in unauthorized access to its investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens.
"This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," Chainalysis said Friday.
"Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users."
The company said it's patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems in response to the incident.
The mention of "offensive agentic techniques" indicates that an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool was used to execute the attack, although Chainalysis offered no details on the specific methods or tactics employed.
"We are seeing an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyber attacks, and we are taking a whole-of-company approach to make sure our security posture meets the evolving environment and our customers' expectations," it said.
The development comes as adversarial use of AI has ramped up in recent months, with various threat actors using the technology to automate different stages of the attack lifecycle and target hundreds of organizations across multiple industries.
This includes a China state-backed threat group known as Vapor Panda, which is using ARTEX, an agentic penetration testing framework, to conduct attacks at scale, compromising about 140 targets in a span of 11 days as part of broad access operation.
"AI mainly improves established attacks by making them faster, more personalized, and easier to scale," Abnormal AI said. "Agentic intrusion chains and prompt injection are more distinct because they depend directly on deployed AI systems."
