articles.title: Attackers Chain Three Ivanti Connect Secure Flaws to Gain Unauthenticated Root Access
articles.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added two security flaws impacting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following active exploitation in the wild.
The vulnerabilities are listed below -
- CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A missing authentication for a critical function vulnerability that could allow a local authenticated attacker to escalate their privileges.
- CVE-2026-118527 (CVSS score: 4.3) - A generation of predictable numbers or identifiers vulnerability that could allow a remote authenticated attacker to upload files with attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.
It's worth noting that the security bugs are part of an exploit chain that was first documented by Volexity earlier this month as weaponized in conjunction with an authentication bypass flaw (CVE-2026-104935, CVSS score: 8.6) by a previously undocumented threat actor dubbed UTA0576. CVE-2026-104935 was added to the KEV catalog on October 13, 2026.
"This exploit chain combined an authentication bypass, a remote code execution (RCE), and a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution," Volexity noted.
Unlike other attacks that typically exploit such flaws to deploy web shells or malware, UTA0576 has been observed leveraging the flaws to extract credentials and limited Active Directory metadata; conduct host reconnaissance; and search for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.
Ivanti said that, around the time the details were published, it was still working on developing fixes for the local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerability exploited in the attack chain. Patches for both CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 are now available in the following versions of ICS -
- 25.1.1.2 and prior (Fixed in 25.1.1.3)
- 22.8R2.5 and prior (Fixed in 22.8R2.6)
"At the time of discovery of exploitation, Ivanti had a fix developed for CVE-2026-104935 which was already in QA for supported versions, and we made the decision to not delay getting a fix to customers that resolved the primary exploitation path when the LPE was discovered," Ivanti explained.
"Because of this, our focus was initially centered on the disclosure of CVE-2026-104935 and providing protection for our customers as quickly as possible."
The company also noted that it discovered a portion of this vulnerability as part of its product security program and patched it in the July release 25.1.3.0, adding it had been working to backport the fix to other supported versions when exploitation activity occurred.
The latest release addresses all vulnerabilities which were chained and exploited in the wild. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are required to apply the fixes for CVE-2026-111357 by November 2, 2026, and CVE-2026-118527 by November 13, 2026.

articles.title: Un agente de IA eligió una terapia y la inyectó en el cerebro de un ratón vivo con epilepsia
articles.text:
Una empresa de biotecnología denominada Exin Therapeutics permitió que un agente de IA basado en Claude, de Anthropic, eligiera una terapia génica y la inyectara en el cerebro de un ratón vivo con epilepsia. Según su director ejecutivo, Gabriel Ocana-Santero, es la primera vez que una IA decide un tratamiento y también lo aplica en un mamífero.
Dicha startup utiliza IA para desarrollar medicamentos contra la epilepsia y enfermedades neurodegenerativas. Contó el experimento en un hilo de la red X.
Al agente le dieron tres elementos: una lista con 19 terapias génicas posibles, un ratón con epilepsia y un equipo quirúrgico automatizado con cámaras. La única indicación era reducir las convulsiones del animal, según The Decoder.
La IA analizó cómo se producen las convulsiones en ese modelo de ratón y propuso una terapia para fortalecer una señal que reduce la actividad cerebral. Eligió una zona del cerebro que, según estudios científicos, es donde comienzan ese tipo de crisis. También descartó otra opción porque había fallado en una investigación anterior.
La IA calculó dónde hacer la inyección usando tres artículos científicos. Además, decidió por sí sola el volumen de la inyección, la velocidad y los tiempos de espera. Durante el procedimiento, hizo 32 observaciones mediante la cámara, como verificar si había sangrado.
El ratón se recupera bien, según Ocana-Santero. Todavía no hay datos sobre si la terapia redujo las convulsiones: el equipo espera a que haga efecto para evaluarla. La empresa probará ahora otros modelos, entre ellos Grok, para comparar su desempeño.
Ocana-Santero dijo a Wired que la supervisión humana sigue siendo clave cuando hay animales vivos y que es demasiado pronto para usar un agente de IA en un cerebro humano. El equipo prevé publicar un informe técnico.
Cómo fue el experimento inicialmente
Los investigadores probaron primero Claude Opus 5.5, el más potente de los tres, que se negó a guiar la aguja. Según Ocana-Santero, el agente dijo que algo en su propia salida le indicaba que no debía hacerlo.
Claude Opus 5 completó un ensayo con agua y papel milimetrado, pero se detuvo ante el animal real. Según el medio mencionado, razonó que empezar algo que quizá no pudiera terminar en un animal anestesiado era peor que no empezar. Solo Claude Sonnet 5, un modelo de uso más cotidiano, aceptó hacer toda la operación.
El equipo puso límites. Un veterinario matriculado hizo la craneotomía, es decir, la apertura del cráneo, que el agente no podía realizar.
Asimismo, aprobó cada paso irreversible y tenía un botón de emergencia que cortaba la energía de todos los motores. Wired añade que el agente no podía modificar el código del equipo.
Por qué un agente de IA se detuvo al realizar el experimento
Tras una desconexión, el agente detectó que su cálculo ubicaba la aguja a 34 milímetros en un eje donde el equipo solo alcanza 30, según el resumen de NDTV del hilo. Se negó a continuar. El equipo reinició la referencia, el resultado fue el mismo y el agente volvió a negarse.
Tenía razón: movimientos manuales durante una pausa anterior habían desajustado el control del equipo. Ocana-Santero escribió que fue una experiencia frustrante, que muestra cuánto se puede depender de estos modelos y qué pasa cuando dicen que no en mitad de un procedimiento con tiempo limitado.
Las dos fuentes difieren en cómo se resolvió el problema. The Decoder informó que el investigador corrigió el código a mano. Wired, que lo hizo otro agente, basado en Opus 5, al que no le dijeron que había una cirugía en curso. Una operación de este tipo dura unos 45 minutos y esta se extendió algo más de una hora.

articles.title: Fed up with hearing about PC price hikes? Black Friday brings some much-needed hope, and with the RAM crisis predicted to last until 2030, it may be your last chance to snag a good deal
articles.text:
The RAM crisis has become a monster — here's why Black Friday is your best chance of slaying the beast, and what PC bargains you should look for
As SK Hynix and Samsung double down on RAM crisis pessimism, there's a glimmer of hope on the horizon
The RAM crisis has grown even more limbs during the month of October. If the memory shortage was incarnated in physical form, it'd have more legs than a spider at this point, and be a multi-limbed monstrosity with a bite that's getting nastier by the day as more negative news seems to roll in at a frightening pace.
Just this week, we've witnessed SK Hynix predicting that RAM supply woes are going nowhere and will persist through to 2030, after Dell's CEO recently warned that we're stuck with this crisis until the end of the decade, and Intel's chief exec agreed – on top of other similar forecasts from earlier this month.
The latest nugget of doom is from Samsung, with the memory chip maker giving out similar vibes to its rival SK Hynix when reporting its financial results (as Wccftech spotted), informing us that RAM shortages will get worse next year, and supply will remain thin on the ground in 2028, too.
You can barely catch a breath between the various dire predictions during the past month. Naturally, in the face of such grimness, it's human nature to try to look on the bright side, or in this case, at least attempt to find a glimmer of light shining through from somewhere. There must be something, right?
Well, there is: Black Friday. An event with a distinctly gloomy name, ironically, but I'm increasingly of the opinion that this is going to be a very important sales season from the computing and PC point of view (and likely other tech, too). Mainly because I expect that the deals you'll get this year will likely be the best prices to be had in a long while, and possibly this entire decade, if those 'it's here until 2030' voices are correct in their assertions about the RAM crisis.
But I hear you (possibly) cry: given all these price hikes, isn't Black Friday going to be a wash anyway? At least based on what we saw with Amazon's recent Prime Day sales? And yes, that's a fair point. You should manage your expectations with the discounts that'll be on offer, certainly, and don't expect to snag a bargain on RAM sticks or that beefy SSD you've been dreaming about. That just isn't happening (to no one's surprise).
However, on Prime Day, there were some decent deals to be had, for example on GPUs. Notably on the RTX 5080, where if you grabbed the deal I highlighted back then, you saved yourself 20% (£300) compared to the price of the cheapest model of that Nvidia GPU on Amazon now (at the time of writing).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
So, given that, what should you be looking at buying this Black Friday, which is less than a month away now (with early offers starting already)? Well, the best deals will likely be in the products set to be more affected by the memory shortage as time rolls on, and I'm going to highlight what I believe are a few key areas bargain hunters should focus on when it comes to the PC sphere.
Graphics cards
I'm putting this one front and center because I believe this should be a priority for PC owners who are looking at a GPU upgrade at some point in the not-too-distant-future. As I already mentioned, there were some decent graphics card deals on Prime Day earlier this month – albeit when it comes to the higher-end GPUs, the word 'decent' translates to 'not inflated', which isn't quite the same thing.
Still, the problem is that prices are likely to rise a good deal more next year, and if you do need a higher-end GPU in particular, during 2027 I think there's a good chance pricing will get a lot worse. Meaning that what you'll pay on Black Friday, with the odd scattered deal on the likes of an Nvidia RTX 5070 model or AMD RX 9070 XT – and maybe even an RTX 5080 – will be a relative bargain (maybe for quite some time to come).
I think this is especially true given the rumors around the RTX 5090 being discontinued (Nvidia has insisted it isn't, but even so, something's clearly amiss with the flagship GPU somewhere), and the ridiculous inflation the RTX 5080 has seen over the past month. All of this indicates a rocky picture with Nvidia's GPUs, and with memory (VRAM) difficulties set to worsen next year – and AMD also rumored to be implementing price hikes with Radeon graphics cards – my advice is to get in ahead of wider GPU price spikes next year.
The catch is that Black Friday deals on graphics cards could be thin on the ground, but we may actually get some decent price cuts in the mid-to-lower-end of GPU territory.
Gaming laptops
If you're thinking about buying a gaming laptop, I think there's scope for some good deals on Black Friday – traditionally laptop discounts are plentiful among the massed ranks of portables, and gaming devices have more headroom for cuts, too.
What you need to consider here is that serious gaming laptops run with a discrete GPU, and as noted above, graphics card price increases are very much on the table. Indeed, this is already happening, and XMG is pushing up prices for its top-end gaming laptops with the RTX 5090 in a major way, while promising that "other laptop GPUs are also facing supply constraints." Further price rises are coming, then, and with RAM getting more costly next year too, we can expect some painful hikes.
As a result, I'd be inclined to keep a careful watch on what Black Friday presents in the way of gaming laptop price cuts, and move sooner rather than later if at all possible.
Laptops
Outside of the gaming arena, everyday laptops are another area where I'd seriously think about trying to nab a Black Friday bargain. As mentioned, there are usually a lot of laptop deals – we highlight the top offers at TechRadar, of course, and notebooks represent quite a number of the bargains we pick out – and while there may not be so many this year, expect them to be there.
With the rising tide of RAM prices and the worsening of the crisis next year, it seems inevitable that this will jack up the asking prices of all laptops (and especially gaming laptops, as noted, due to the extra pressure added by the video RAM of discrete GPUs).
Analyst firms are already predicting that laptop manufacturers are soon going to ramp up pricing as they run short of stockpiled components (purchased at a cheaper cost). And one analyst outfit, IDC, recently advised that the only positive glimmer here is that some retailers are carrying too much notebook stock (given flagging PC sales this year) which may result in "promotions and some short-term relief for consumers," which is clearly referring to Black Friday.
I agree, of course, and think that if you want a new laptop in the next couple of years, Black Friday 2026 is likely to be the best time to make your move.
What else?
On the PC side, then, I feel that laptops – particularly gaming notebooks – and desktop GPUs are the key areas to focus on for Black Friday bargains.
The trouble with other key desktop PC components aside from graphics cards is that pricing has got so high with RAM and SSDs that even a 'bargain' with a big price cut feels like a very sour purchase compared to prices last year. These components are just depressingly expensive (especially system memory), so it's difficult to recommend buying at all unless you're absolutely forced to. (Top-end GPUs are now in this territory too, of course).
That said, there may just be a half-decent deal on storage somewhere (we did see one or two of those in the most recent Prime Day).
On a lighter note, you might well see some solid deals on CPUs if you're on the hunt for a new processor. This is likely to be the exception in terms of the other core PC components aside from GPUs, although I'm not expecting CPU prices to face the same upward pricing pressures that graphics cards will encounter next year, so there isn't the same sense of urgency to buy in that respect. I could be wrong in that, mind – and the same goes for all my musings here – so season this advice liberally.

articles.title: A Shared ChatGPT Link Could Run Attacker Code in Your Session and Read Private Chats
articles.text:
A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at the security firm Parameter showed.
The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category.
The trap was an ordinary ChatGPT conversation shared via its public link. It could be sent the same way as any real shared chat: by email, as a chat message, as a support ticket, or as a social post.
The victim did not have to install anything, join a workspace, or sign in through the attacker. In the most reliable version of the attack, they opened the link and clicked ChatGPT's Preview button once. In a later version, Parameter set the page to open Preview on its own, so opening the link was the only step.
What the Attacker Could Do
Once the link opened, the attacker's code ran inside the victim's signed-in session with the same access as the real ChatGPT site. It listed the victim's recent conversations, opened a private chat that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent a small portion of it to a server controlled by the researchers.
The code called ChatGPT's own signed-in APIs directly, rather than copying what happened to be on the screen. Because it ran with the victim's full web access, its reach was not limited to those chats. "Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account," the researchers wrote.
The work was a controlled test. Parameter does not report any real-world use of the flaw, and ran its private-chat proof between separate accounts rather than against real users.
How the Link Broke Out of Its Sandbox
Here is how the chain worked, according to Parameter. ChatGPT can turn a block of HTML in a chat into a small web page through a feature called Preview. Because that page can hold any code, ChatGPT runs it in a locked-down frame on a separate web address, where it cannot read the main ChatGPT page around it.
That sandbox held. The way in came from a second feature in the same conversation.
The shared chat also contained an interactive graph, and drawing it loaded a math library called MathLive into the main ChatGPT page. Loading MathLive left a listener running there that accepted messages about its on-screen keyboard.
A message passed between browser frames is safe only if the receiver checks who sent it. Parameter found that this listener accepted a keyboard message from any sender, and that the message was allowed to carry raw HTML. The Preview could then reach across the boundary and hand attacker HTML to the trusted main page.
That HTML built a new frame that the browser treated as part of chatgpt.com. A script loaded from YouTube then supplied the code that ran inside it.
ChatGPT's content security policy limits where a page's scripts may come from. It blocked inline code but allowed scripts from YouTube, which is why that step worked.
What OpenAI Fixed, and What Users Should Do
Parameter said OpenAI reproduced both the code execution and the private-chat proof, raised the severity from P2 to P1, and rolled a fix across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. By October 26, both versions rejected the messages the attack relied on.
The researchers traced the problem to three design choices that lined up:
- MathLive acted on a message that changed its settings without checking which frame had sent it.
- That message was allowed to carry raw HTML as keyboard-layout data.
- The HTML could create a frame that was not sandboxed and inherited the chatgpt.com identity.
The YouTube step was only the final workaround, not the cause. Blocking it alone would still leave an untrusted Preview able to push HTML into the main site.
ChatGPT users do not need to do anything. The fix is on OpenAI's side, with nothing to install or reset.
Parameter published its writeup on October 28, after the fix. OpenAI paid a total of $5,000 for the report.

articles.title: Antes de los autos inteligentes, ya existía un coche con dos Xbox 360 integradas
articles.text:
Mucho antes de que los automóviles incorporaran pantallas táctiles, asistentes virtuales y sistemas de entretenimiento conectados, Suzuki presentó un vehículo que parecía adelantarse a esa tendencia. En 2006, la marca japonesa desarrolló un prototipo que integraba dos consolas Xbox 360 en su interior y permitía jugar videojuegos desde diferentes sectores del automóvil.
El modelo se llamó Suzuki SXbox y fue construido sobre la base del Suzuki SX4. Su propuesta combinaba tecnología automotriz y entretenimiento digital, con una configuración que permitía tanto al conductor como a los pasajeros acceder a videojuegos mediante controles inalámbricos y varias pantallas distribuidas por el vehículo.
El proyecto no estaba pensado para llegar a los concesionarios. Se trataba de un prototipo creado para mostrar las posibilidades de integrar la consola de Microsoft en un automóvil y captar la atención del público en una época en la que los sistemas multimedia para vehículos todavía no tenían las características que ofrecen los modelos actuales.
Dos Xbox 360 dentro de un mismo automóvil
La característica más llamativa del Suzuki SXbox era la incorporación de dos consolas Xbox 360. Una estaba instalada en la zona del salpicadero y conectada a un sistema de proyección que permitía utilizar la parte interior del capó como superficie para visualizar los videojuegos.
La segunda consola estaba destinada principalmente a los pasajeros de los asientos traseros. Para ellos, el vehículo incorporaba dos pantallas LCD independientes, de manera que podían disfrutar de los videojuegos durante los desplazamientos.
El equipamiento también incluía una pantalla retráctil de 30 pulgadas ubicada en el maletero. Este componente ampliaba las posibilidades de entretenimiento del automóvil y permitía utilizarlo como un espacio para jugar fuera del habitáculo.
La experiencia se completaba con cuatro mandos inalámbricos, uno de ellos integrado en el volante, además de un sistema de sonido envolvente y asientos con vibración. Estos elementos buscaban trasladar parte de la experiencia de una consola doméstica al interior de un vehículo.
De esta manera, el SXbox no se limitaba a incorporar una consola como accesorio, sino que proponía distribuir distintas opciones de entretenimiento entre los ocupantes del automóvil.
Cómo nació el Suzuki SXbox
El prototipo fue desarrollado por American Sunroof Corporation (ASC) sobre la plataforma del Suzuki SX4. Su presentación formó parte de la iniciativa Suzuki LIVE, una estrategia de la marca para mostrar propuestas vinculadas con el entretenimiento, la tecnología y los automóviles.
El proyecto apareció en un momento en el que la Xbox 360 comenzaba a consolidarse en el mercado de los videojuegos. La consola había llegado a las tiendas en noviembre de 2005 y representaba una de las principales apuestas de Microsoft para competir en la industria del entretenimiento digital.
La integración de dos unidades en un mismo vehículo permitía mostrar cómo una consola podía utilizarse en diferentes espacios y con distintos sistemas de visualización. También funcionaba como una demostración de las posibilidades que ofrecían los dispositivos electrónicos más allá del hogar.
Durante 2007, el Suzuki SXbox recorrió diferentes salones del automóvil de Estados Unidos, donde fue exhibido como una propuesta tecnológica y promocional.
Un prototipo que no llegó a venderse
A pesar de sus características, el Suzuki SXbox nunca se convirtió en un modelo comercial. La compañía lo presentó como un vehículo conceptual y no anunció planes para producirlo en serie ni ofrecerlo a los compradores.
Su configuración también respondía a una demostración tecnológica más que a una solución práctica para el transporte cotidiano. La instalación de proyectores, pantallas, consolas y sistemas de sonido requería modificaciones importantes en la estructura del automóvil.
Además, el uso de videojuegos desde el asiento del conductor no representaba una función adecuada para un vehículo en circulación. La propuesta estaba orientada al entretenimiento con el automóvil detenido y, especialmente, a los pasajeros.
El SXbox apareció casi dos décadas antes de que las pantallas de gran tamaño y los sistemas multimedia avanzados se convirtieran en elementos habituales de muchos vehículos. Actualmente, los fabricantes incorporan plataformas de conectividad, asistentes de voz y aplicaciones de entretenimiento, aunque las funciones disponibles dependen del modelo y de las condiciones de seguridad.
El prototipo de Suzuki quedó como un ejemplo de cómo la industria automotriz ya exploraba la integración entre videojuegos y vehículos antes de que los automóviles inteligentes se convirtieran en una tendencia.

articles.title: Elegoo's M1 Ultra marks an impressive entrance into the 3D scanner market
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The M1 Ultra shows Elegoo's new direction with a premium-feeling product that is fast to set up and use. The software and scanner UI show traces of the old hobbyist styling; however, the hardware is solid, and the scan quality is exceptional. As ever, scan quality depends on preparation, but at the price, this new entrant to the 3D scanning market offers great value.
Reasons to buy
- + Exceptional accuracy and scanning detail
- + Decent 1st-generation software
- + Great value
- + Premium build
Reasons to avoid
- - Object preparation is essential
- - The interface feels slightly dated
- - Wireless connectivity limits online connection
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Elegoo, known for its hobbyist 3D printers, is changing, and its more recent hardware shows big changes in both design and manufacturing quality. The M1 Ultra is one of the signs of this change yet, with a premium design and build that put it firmly in competition with established 3D scanning manufacturers such as Creality.
The M1 Ultra combines blue laser and infrared structured-light scanning, with five main scanning configurations that cover everything from small mechanical components and intricate objects to larger structures and even humans. The scanner offers a top accuracy of 0.02mm in the finest blue laser mode, and other standout features include full wireless operation, a 3-inch touchscreen and a swappable battery.
I’ve recently tested quite a few handheld 3D scanners, and there’s no doubt the market is getting competitive; however, whilst it’s a surprise to see Elegoo launch into the market, it’s even more surprising when I lifted the scanner from the hard case to discover the quality of the design and build.
The M1 Ultra is beautifully finished with a well-balanced design, with part rubberised grip that makes it comfortable to manoeuvre around objects. If anything, I would have liked the grip to be slightly longer, but otherwise the physical design is excellent.
The scanner connects through either wired USB or Wireless connection, with a slide switch enabling you to quickly switch between the two. This link connects you to the software, which initially guides you through the scanning process, and for first-generation software it’s all extremely well thought out.
The most important factor is scan quality, and while scanning a selection of household ornaments, mechanical components, and structural parts, it produced detailed, dimensionally accurate models that I could then export for direct 3D printing or import and edit within Blender.
One of the biggest surprises that I had during the scan process was firstly the speed and then the difference between the initial scanning preview that appeared in the software and the processed model. The preview scans looked OK, if a little rough, but after completing the scan and running the first processing stage, the detail suddenly appeared.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The Elegoo Scan software, being an early release, is surprisingly good and avoided any freezes or glitches through the testing. Scan processing typically took a couple of minutes, depending on complexity and the size, while editing and removing unwanted geometry was straightforward, partly due to my ever-increasing familiarity and use of these scanners. The usage and workflow of the software is very similar to other systems.
Wireless scanning on a scanner of this price is great to see, and I was quickly able to connect to the scanner over Wi-Fi. Once that connection was made, I found the live preview on the scanner’s touchscreen made moving around larger objects much easier.
Through the test, I did find many of the usual limits, such as scanning glossy black plastic and highly reflective surfaces still requiring scanning spray. In all cases, how easily something scans rests solely on careful preparation and marker placement. When using the scanner wirelessly, the scanner also takes over the computer’s Wi-Fi connection, preventing access to a normal workshop wireless network, which I also found was a little inconvenient.
Considering that this is Elegoo's first 3D scanner, the speed, quality and ease of use make it feel like a product that has already undergone several iterations. This is a great option for small businesses, makers, enthusiasts, and other 3D professionals looking for a decent 3D scanner at a reasonable price.
ELEGOO M1 Ultra: Price and Availability
The Elegoo M1 Ultra has a recommended retail price of $1,699 in the US, £1,399 in the UKand €1,699. The scanner is being sold through the official website here.
Elegoo M1 Ultra: Design
One of the first things that impressed me about the M1 Ultra was the physical design and quality of the build. In contrast to their range of hobbyist 3D printers, Elegoo has clearly aimed this at a more professional level, and it feels significantly more refined than many of their previous product lines.
Elegoo's hardware design improved dramatically, as I saw with its H1 HT filament dryer a few months back and again when it comes to finish and build quality; this feels premium and much like the quality that I’ve come to expect from companies like Bambu Lab.
Weighing in at just over half a kilogram, the M1 Ultra is relatively compact compared with several scanners I’ve used recently. The weight is well balanced for the size, and it's comfortable to hold while moving around objects, with the grip featuring a rubberised texture that provides excellent purchase.
Grip in the scanner is especially important when scanning smaller mechanical components, where controlled movements can affect tracking and the quality of the capture. If anything, I do feel that the grip could have been slightly longer, but overall it’s comfortable enough to handle.
The front of the scanner features the optical system, including the laser emitters, cameras and illumination; these all look like lenses. These are neatly integrated into the casing, while the controls on the large touch screen enable you to start, pause and access the hardware settings.
The 3-inch touchscreen is more than just a monitor for settings and enables less reliance, in some situations, on using a computer screen when scanning. An example is when using the scanner wirelessly, and the display provides a live scan preview; you can also use it to adjust the exposure and zoom.
Additional hardware settings can also be accessed through the touchscreen, including Wi-Fi hotspot information, display brightness, screen rotation, language, prompt sounds and sound alerts. I also liked the fact that I could access the onboard user guide.
Not all aspects of the user interface are as polished as the hardware itself. The start and pause controls, exposure adjustment, and zoom interface use a slightly dated visual style, with gradient effects that feel more like enthusiast equipment than professional; still, the actual functionality is there.
As I’ve seen with many of these scanners, it arrives in a hard carrying case which is identical in design to the one that arrived with one of the Creality scanners recently; the only difference is the logo on the front and the equipment inside.
Inside, the scanner is neatly laid out, with the scanner, batteries, calibration board, USB cable, tripod, and reflective markers. In contrast to some other scanners, the cables are kept to a minimum, with power and data handled through the same USB connection when using wired.
- Design: 4/5
ELEGOO M1 Ultra: Features
Dimensions: 191 × 50 × 76mm
Weight: 511g (including battery)
Scanning Accuracy: Up to 0.02mm (blue laser)
Scanning Modes: Five, including blue laser and infrared
Scanning Speed: Up to 100fps (USB), 60fps (Wi-Fi)
Scanning Resolution: 0.05–2mm (blue laser)
Scanning Volume: 5 × 5 × 5mm to 4,000 × 4,000 × 4,000mm
Display: 3-inch HD touchscreen
Connectivity: USB-C 3.1 and Wi-Fi 6
Battery: 4,800mAh removable
The M1 Ultra features five scanning modes designed to enable you to scan different materials, object sizes, and most importantly, levels of detail.
A quick run-through, and you have the 34-line crossed blue laser, which is designed for fast scanning of medium-to-large objects. The seven-line parallel mode is better suited to smaller parts and more detailed areas. The single-line configuration lets the scanner capture recessed features, deep holes, and narrow gaps.
Alongside these are infrared structured light mode, designed for larger objects, faces, and bodies, and the marker-free blue laser option for situations where reflective markers can't be applied, such as when scanning valuable museum artefacts.
Within each mode, there are a variety of options that you can configure through the Elegoo Scan software, which offers adjustments to tracking, field of view, capture resolution, as well as the main scan quality settings.
This does take some time to get your head around, and depending on the mode, you can select marker-assisted or marker-free tracking, standard or wide-angle fields of view, global marker workflows and different laser patterns. This sounds complex, but Elegoo have created guides for each type and practice is definitely needed in order to fully understand what type and size of object needs what type of scan and settings.
The software does go some way to make things easy, with an example being the infrared scanning mode that offers dedicated presets for normal objects, faces, and bodies, plus geometry-based and texture-based tracking options.
Although the number of settings is considerable, the software is generally well organised. If you are new to 3D scanning, there’s also plenty of guides and visual prompts in the software to explain how the different options work.
- Features: 4.5/5
ELEGOO M1 Ultra: Performance
Getting started, the first step is the hardware setup. After installing Elegoo Scan on my MacBook Pro, connecting the scanner through USB and selecting the connection option, it was almost ready to go aside from a quick initial firmware update.
Before the scanning process could begin, I needed to run through the calibration process, and this was all surprisingly easy with the calibration chart sitting on the table and the software directing me through a series of manoeuvres with the on-screen guide. This style of calibration used to take me ages; however, here I found the process pretty quick and straightforward.
I started the test using the wired connection, but to switch to wireless there’s a small switch on top of the scanner that enables the change from USB to WLAN. As the switch is moved, the system restarts, and then you can select the scanner’s hotspot from the computer’s Wi-Fi connections, enter the on-screen password, and again it’s ready to go.
The process is easy enough, though wireless operation means the scanner creates its own Wi-Fi hotspot, which the computer must connect directly to. That meant disconnecting from the workshop Wi-Fi, and there was no option to keep both connections active at once.
This isn’t an issue during scanning, especially since the software works offline, but it becomes a bit annoying when switching between scanning and anything that I needed to do online.
When everything was set and ready, I was able to start the scanning process, starting with the 34-line cross blue laser options, which proved to scan objects at speed. Once a scan was captured, it was then possible to clean up the point cloud, as well as easily align multiple scans, and move through mesh wrapping and optimisation before exporting the finished model.
The M1 Ultra and the software effectively give you an easy scan-to-model process, and when finished, you just click export.
For testing, I scanned a variety of objects, ranging from household and office ornaments to mechanical components and structural parts that I needed to reproduce or work around when creating brackets and replacement pieces.
These included objects made from tarnished metal, matte ceramic, plastic, and wood, and the scanner performed exceptionally well across these materials. As with other 3D scanners I’ve tested, good results come down to preparation. While marker-free scanning sounds appealing, I have found that reflective markers remain the most reliable approach.
My usual setup includes a rotating platform, custom 3D-printed marker blocks positioned around the object, and adhesive reflective markers attached directly to the object wherever practical. I also use acrylic blocks to raise the object above the surface. This helps separate the subject from the surrounding environment, especially the platform it sits on, and makes the captured data easier to cut out and process.
The whole preparation process generally takes around five minutes, but it makes an enormous difference to the ease and reliability of scanning. Through the setup process, I aim to keep at least five reflective markers visible to the scanner at any one time, and this generally meant that tracking was straightforward. Scanning objects without markers proved less reliable, even with the scanner’s marker-free configuration.
Once I had properly prepared the subject, most objects took around five to ten minutes to scan from each orientation. Where possible, I tried to capture the object in just two orientations, as this made alignment quicker and generally produced better results.
The scanning process itself was fast, and it was good to see the preview build up the model. When scanning, I started off with the crossed blue laser pattern as this tended to provide the best overall coverage, and then switched to the seven-line mode when scanning more complex objects. For recessed features and deeper holes, switching to the single-line laser again helped to fill in some of the gaps.
After scanning, each model is previewed on the screen, and then you can go through the various processing modes. One point to make here is that the initial scanning is surprisingly fast and the initial point-cloud preview can look a little rough, giving little indication of the level of detail that has actually been captured. However, after you finish the scan and move through the first refinement stage, the model's detail suddenly snaps into place, and it’s impressive.
The M1 Ultra reproduced fine surface features and dimensional accuracy extremely well. One example of the accuracy came when I scanned the car's EV charger, with the model generated being imported into CAD software as a template for a wall-mounted holder. The finished product, while needing some refinement, fitted the EV charger perfectly.
The software is able to export OBJ files that can then be used in applications such as Blender for further editing. The range of available export formats also makes it relatively straightforward to move finished models into other design and manufacturing workflows, with 3MF and STL alongside OBJ.
Not every object's surface was easy to capture, and as ever, while tarnished metal, wood, ceramic and plastic surfaces generally scanned very well, glossy black plastic gained mixed results.
Essentially, any surface that reflects or absorbs the scanning light causes a bit of an issue, and you can get matte scanning sprays to help with the scanning of this type of object.
Infrared scanning also produced ok results, and making sure you work in a well-lit, soft-light environment definitely helps. Again, as with any scanning mode, practice and skill often play a large part in the scanning success.
One of the main skills when scanning is alignment, essentially when you take a couple of scans of an object from different angles and then align them into one. The alignment option worked well and was surprisingly fast to process between scans, provided the reflective markers' position was maintained. This works by completing the first scan; then the object could be repositioned to capture another side without moving any of the base markers, and the resulting scans could then be selected and aligned within Elegoo Scan.
The important point here is that the markers used as reference points must remain in the correct positions. If you move markers on the platform between scans, alignment will be much harder, and in most cases it's easier to start again.
Mesh processing generally took a couple of minutes per scan, though the time varied considerably with the model's size and complexity. There is still a need to remove unwanted surfaces and sections of the surrounding environment manually, but the software proved effective. Throughout testing, Elegoo Scan remained solid, with no crashes, freezes, or other problems that I have come across in the past with scan software.
For a first-generation Elegoo scanner, and with software at such an early stage of development, this level of reliability is excellent.
At the start of the test, I stuck to a wired connection, mainly due to having to check guides, etc., but over the weeks of the test I switched to the wireless option. There are some sacrifices that you make as you switch over to the wireless connection, most notably that the scanner has a lower quoted maximum frame rate; however, I didn’t notice much of a difference.
The real improvement going wireless was the ergonomic feel of scanning alongside the obvious effect of no longer having trailing wires. The main benefit is that instead of looking back at the laptop monitor to check scan progress, the wireless connection let me monitor the preview directly on the handheld scanner’s touchscreen. This made scanning far more natural, especially when moving around larger or awkwardly positioned objects.
Through the test, I found that the battery runtime was about 60 minutes, shorter than Elegoo's advertised maximum of 90 minutes, but still enough for several typical scans, and I also discovered I could hot-swap the battery with the second battery that was included. I experimented with swapping the battery while USB power was connected, which appeared to work, though this wasn't officially covered in the material I had.
- Performance: 4 / 5
ELEGOO M1 Ultra: Final verdict
The Elegoo M1 Ultra shows the direction that the company is moving, and this is an impressive start for them in the 3D scanning market. The arrival in the hard case, with the premium build and design, is far removed from their hobbyist machines, and it all has a decidedly higher-quality feel.
The overall ergonomics and build are excellent, and this quality of design comes across in use, with it being easy to handle and with the ability to switch between wired and wireless scanning.
As ever, there are the usual issues with the time taken to prepare the scan, but this is part of the course for all 3D scanners and the more time you put in, the better the scan you get. However, the speed of the scans that the M1 enables is impressive, and more importantly, the quality of those scans was exceptionally detailed.
The Elegoo Scan software is also well thought out, although I do feel there needs to be a little more thought on the design of both the scanning software and the touchscreen interface. The old Elegoo is still apparent in both, giving that hobbyist rather than slick professional aesthetic.
Wireless scanning is another point, and while this works exceptionally well, it does lock your computer out of the normal Wi-Fi network. There are then the usual points about scanning highly reflective or glossy surfaces, which will require scanning spray.
While good results can be achieved with what's in the box, I would, as always, highly recommend the following: turntable, reflective markers, marker blocks, acrylic supports, and scanning spray; these are all relatively inexpensive but will save you hours.
Should you buy the Elegoo M1 Ultra?
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Row 0 - Cell 1 | Row 0 - Cell 2 | 
| Value: | Exceptional first-generation scanner at a very reasonable price considering the alternatives. | 4.5 | 
| Design: | Premium build and ergonomics highlight Elegoos investment in design. | 4 | 
| Features: | Packed with scanning modes and plenty of options to refine your scanning | 4.5 | 
| Performance: | Fast and very capable with one of the easiest workflows yet | 4 | 
| Total: | Excellent scanner for everyone from enthusiasts to professionals. | 4.5 | 
Buy it if...
You need detailed scans.
If you regularly design replacement components, custom brackets, or work with existing physical objects, the M1 Ultra delivers excellent scan quality that you can update in CAD.
You want wireless flexibility.
The integrated touchscreen, direct Wi-Fi connection, and removable batteries make the M1 Ultra much easier to manoeuvre around objects than scanners that rely on wired connections.
Don't buy it if...
You expect instant results.
Despite the ease of use, successful 3D scanning still requires preparation, reflective markers and practice. If you expect to point the scanner at an object and instantly produce a perfect model, you’ll be disappointed.
You scan difficult surfaces.
Highly reflective, transparent or glossy black objects remain difficult to scan. While the M1 Ultra is more versatile than some alternatives, you may will need additional scanning spray and lighting to get good results.
For more crafting essentials, I've also tested out the best 3D printers and best laser engravers
Alastair is a photographer, filmmaker and tech writer who has been working in the publishing industry since the late 1990s. For more than 25 years he has covered photography, video and technology across Future's photography, technology and gaming brands. He runs a photography and video production company and lectures in TV and film. He can usually be found testing mini PCs or prototyping and prop building with the aid of 3D printing.

articles.title: Un virus que roba contraseñas usa chatbots de IA para armar un perfil de cada víctima
articles.text:
Investigadores de Cisco Talos, la división de seguridad informática de Cisco, descubrieron un programa malicioso que, tras robar los datos de una computadora, los entrega a un chatbot de IA para que arme un informe sobre el dueño y ordene sus pertenencias digitales según cuánto se pueden aprovechar. El programa se llama VOLTA-AUTODOXER y funciona en Windows.
El nombre viene de cómo se identifica el propio código. “Doxear” es reunir y exponer datos personales de alguien. El hallazgo se publicó el 31 de octubre en el blog de Talos, firmado por el investigador Ryan Fetterman, y lo adelantó la revista Wired.
El programa pertenece a la familia de los llamados infostealers, software diseñado para robar información de equipos infectados. Se esconde con frecuencia en programas falsos. Talos lo detectó con CAIRN, una herramienta propia para identificar software de ataque que incorpora IA.
Un expediente armado con datos robados
Primero, el programa copia contraseñas guardadas en los navegadores, cookies, tarjetas de pago, frases de recuperación de billeteras de criptomonedas, sesiones de Discord, Telegram, Steam y Roblox, claves de acceso a servidores y las contraseñas de todas las redes wifi guardadas en el equipo.
Después hace una segunda pasada con las sesiones robadas. Según Talos, busca en el correo Gmail de la víctima recibos de Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart y PayPal para confirmar su domicilio, consulta el historial de pedidos de comida y calcula el valor de su cuenta de Roblox.
Con todo eso arma un archivo llamado Identity_Report.txt, que incluye ubicación, empleador, año de nacimiento estimado y los últimos cuatro dígitos de las tarjetas. Ese archivo viaja a un modelo de IA mediante OpenRouter, un servicio que reparte consultas entre varios proveedores de modelos.
Las instrucciones al modelo, de unas 240 palabras según Wired, le piden actuar como “analista forense de inteligencia” que redacta una evaluación del objetivo. El informe debe incluir cuánto vale la víctima y cómo es su seguridad, y conectar datos sueltos, por ejemplo si la contraseña del wifi coincide con el apellido.
Si un modelo se niega, el programa prueba con otro
El modelo que el programa consulta primero es Claude Opus 4.6, de Anthropic. El código revisa si la respuesta contiene frases de rechazo como “no puedo”. Si las detecta, pasa a Kimi K2, de la china Moonshot AI, y luego a Gemini 2.5 Flash, de Google.
Para Fetterman, esa cadena indica que los autores esperaban topar con los filtros de seguridad de los modelos. “El mensaje está cuidadosamente redactado para no sugerir nada abiertamente malicioso”, dijo a Wired. El programa también funciona sin la parte de IA, que es un añadido.
El resultado se envía a los atacantes en un archivo comprimido llamado volta_dox.zip. Talos encontró además que el código usa una plantilla con seis campos que se completan al compilar cada copia, lo que sugiere que se vende como servicio a distintos clientes. No encontró infraestructura propia de los autores: todos los puntos de conexión observados pertenecen a terceros.
Qué hacer si el equipo se infectó
El ejecutable se borra solo, pero deja en la carpeta de datos de aplicaciones un archivo de registro, volta_debug.txt, con lo que se robó y si la consulta a la IA funcionó. Talos recomienda conservarlo, revocar las sesiones comprometidas y cambiar las contraseñas. Si la frase de recuperación de una billetera estaba en texto plano, la billetera debe darse por comprometida y los fondos pasarse a otra nueva.
Fetterman aclaró a Wired que Talos no rastreó si VOLTA se usa en ataques reales. Para el investigador, el caso muestra que atacantes con poca experiencia acceden a herramientas más avanzadas: “Es realmente interesante y perturbador”. El informe de Talos no informa de víctimas confirmadas.

articles.title: Cloudflare Reports 18.2 Million Network-Layer DDoS Attacks in Q3, Up 38%
articles.text:
Threat actors are launching about 8,226 network-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks per hour, Cloudflare revealed Thursday.
The web infrastructure and security company said it autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer (L3) DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests in the third quarter of 2026. That amounts to 197,400 attacks per day, or one attack every 0.44 seconds.
In comparison, a total of 13.2 million and 10.0 million L3 DDoS attacks were recorded in Q2 and Q1 2026, respectively. The increase has been linked to DDoS-for-hire booter or stresser services that are responsible for hundreds of thousands of attacks.
"Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%," the Cloudforce One threat intelligence team said in its quarterly DDoS Threat Report shared with The Hacker News.
An interesting trend is the decline of hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps by 69% from the previous quarter – going from 805 attacks in Q2 to 251 in Q3 – likely as a result of law enforcement actions against AISURU, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad earlier this March.
Still, the threat remains far from completely neutralized, given the emergence of new variants like Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot, Cloudflare warned.
Another notable shift is the decline in Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) floods, while DNS amplification jumped 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks.
The most targeted industries include media, production, and publishing; information technology and services; gambling and casinos; computer software; and telecommunications providers.
The U.S., China, Indonesia, the U.K., and Türkiye emerged as the most attacked countries during the time period, with Canada and Israel entering the top 10 ranking, fueled by attacks targeting Canada's retail, telecommunications, and marketing sectors.

articles.title: Stream or Skip: what should you check out this Halloween?
articles.text:
I checked out three major horror titles in time for Halloween — but a popular movie adaptation ended up being the biggest let down
Tricks and treats are upon you
If you celebrate Halloween, you'll no doubt be on the lookout for some things to entertain you this weekend. With this in mind, I checked out three of the biggest new horror releases in October to see if they're any good.
Scream or Skip, that is the question. With so much horror out there to watch and play, our senior entertainment writer, Lucy Buglass, is here to help you decide what's worth your time (or worthy of a Scream) and what's not (so you might want to Skip). Her goal is to help you spend less time scrolling and more time enjoying some great TV shows, movies, and games. Read the full series here.
There have been some real highs and lows this month, and I found myself especially disappointed by one movie in particular. Thankfully, there's a great TV show and game to keep you occupied, so it's not all bad.
So, what do I recommend checking out this spooky weekend? Scroll down to find out.
TV — Crystal Lake
Where to watch: Peacock (US); Sky (UK); Stan (AU)
Lucy's verdict: Scream
Crystal Lake is the anticipated Friday the 13th prequel, and it's a great choice if you want a binge-worthy series to watch over the Halloween weekend. With all eight episodes streaming at once, how could you resist?
I did have my reservations about this series, but it is an excellent entry into the horror franchise. In my full Crystal Lake review, I noted there's a clear love for the original movies here, and that it expands upon the lore by focusing on Pamela Voorhees, an under-explored character in the Friday the 13th universe. Played excellently by Linda Cardellini, it's very worth your time.
Movie — Other Mommy
Where to watch: Theaters worldwide
Lucy's verdict: Skip
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As someone who loved the book Incidents Around the House and was genuinely freaked out by it, I was excited to hear it was getting a movie adaptation. I was even more excited to hear that Jessica Chastain would star in a dual role as a woman and an entity that emulates her, known as "Other Mommy".
Unfortunately, the movie ended up being a massive letdown. Not only does it suffer from the cliché of tired and overused jump scares, but it also deviates from the book to the point that it loses the psychological dread and tension that had me looking over my shoulder. Other Mommy does very little to stand out from similar supernatural movies like it
Game — Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival
Where to play: PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC
Lucy's verdict: Scream
Hellraiser has been everywhere recently, from its haunted house at Universal's Halloween Horror Nights to a new video game. I was very impressed with Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival and would highly recommend it this Halloween weekend.
It's clear it's been made by people who have a genuine appreciation for Hellraiser, as the atmosphere and the willingness to stick to canon are excellent. Iconic character Pinhead returns too, and the result is a gripping game with puzzles and heart-pounding moments.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Lucy is a long-time movie and television lover who is an approved critic on Rotten Tomatoes. She has written several reviews in her time, starting with a small self-ran blog called Lucy Goes to Hollywood before moving onto bigger websites such as What's on TV and What to Watch, with TechRadar being her most recent venture. Her interests primarily lie within horror and thriller, loving nothing more than a chilling story that keeps her thinking moments after the credits have rolled. Many of these creepy tales can be found on the streaming services she covers regularly.
When she’s not scaring herself half to death with the various shows and movies she watches, she likes to unwind by playing video games on Easy Mode and has no shame in admitting she’s terrible at them. She also quotes The Simpsons religiously and has a Blinky the Fish tattoo, solidifying her position as a complete nerd.

articles.title: Ranking de animes: los 10 más vistos esta semana en Crunchyroll
articles.text:
El anime son las series animadas que se producen en Japón y relatan diferentes tipos de historias cuyo objetivo es entretener específicamente al sector más jóven de la población del país. Desde hace varias décadas estas producciones se globalizaron gracias a que eran transmitidas en los canales locales en occidente y con el paso del tiempo se fueron integrando a los catálogos de las plataformas de streaming.
One Piece, Naruto y Bleach ostentan en los últimos años el título de “Big 3” por ser los tres animes más grandes de la última generación, sin embargo, en los años recientes nuevas historias han comenzado a alzar la mano para convertirse en el nuevo anime más exitoso de la historia.
Crunchyroll es un plataforma de streaming que cuenta con un amplio catálogo de animes y con las licencias de transmisión de las series que están actualmente en emisión en Japón.
Cada semana se publican los episodios a unas cuantas horas de diferencia de su transmisión en el país asiático. Si quieres adentrarte en el mundo del anime o ya eres un fan experimentado en busca de una nueva serie a continuación te compartimos los 10 títulos más populares para ver este fin de semana.
Ranking animes
1.- Ranma1/2 S3
2.- The Apothecary Diaries S3 P1
3.- The Ramparts of Ice S2
4.- Firefly Wedding
5.- A Certain Dark Item
6.- Blue Box S2
7.- Magic Knight Rayearth (2026)
8.- Hello, I Am a Witch and My Crush Wants Me to Make a Love Potion!
9.- Even the Student Council Has Its Holes!
10.- FX Fighter Kurumi-chan
*Algunos de los títulos que aparecen en este ranking no están disponibles para Crunchyroll América Latina, pero se pueden encontrar en otras plataformas de streaming
La demanda de anime a nivel global
Los estudios de animación se han convertido en el foco de atención en los últimos años ante la gran cantidad de producciones que realizan cada año por la demanda internacional de nuevas series.
De acuerdo con un reporte de Parrot Analytics, empresa enfocada en el estudio de los medios de comunicación, la pandemia de coronavirus significó un boom en el consumo de estas animaciones. Entre mayo de 2020 y abril de 2021 el consumo de estas series incrementó en diferentes países del mundo, principalmente en Estados Unidos, Brasil y Canadá.
En el mismo estudio se reportó que México es el país de América Latina que registró un mayor aumento en la audiencia del anime. La demanda a nivel global de nuevas animaciones ha superado el contenido disponible en las plataformas esto orilló a las plataformas de streaming a apostar por producciones propias.
El proceso de producción de una serie es largo y tarda aproximadamente dos años en promedio, es por esta razón que la continuidad de las nueve series suelen tardar más que en otro tipo de contenido.

articles.title: Juegos de Halloween y de terror: los 5 para descargar en Crunchyroll y PlayStation
articles.text:
Halloween es una oportunidad para explorar videojuegos que combinan suspenso, criaturas sobrenaturales, persecuciones y escenarios inquietantes. Para quienes buscan experiencias de este tipo, Crunchyroll Game Vault y PlayStation Store cuentan con títulos que abarcan desde historias de terror psicológico hasta aventuras en las que sobrevivir depende de resolver acertijos o escapar de los enemigos.
Ambas plataformas ofrecen propuestas diferentes. Crunchyroll reúne videojuegos para dispositivos móviles con una selección de títulos independientes y experiencias de inspiración japonesa. PlayStation, por su parte, dispone de producciones de terror para PS4 y PS5, con gráficos más elaborados, historias cinematográficas y opciones multijugador.
A continuación, cinco juegos disponibles en el catálogo de Crunchyroll y otros cinco que se pueden encontrar en PlayStation Store para disfrutar durante Halloween.
Cinco juegos de terror para descargar en Crunchyroll
Crunchyroll Game Vault incluye una selección de videojuegos que pueden descargarse en teléfonos Android y iPhone. El servicio está disponible para suscriptores de los planes Mega Fan y Ultimate Fan, aunque algunos títulos pueden tener restricciones territoriales.
1. Corpse Party
Es una aventura de terror y supervivencia en la que un grupo de estudiantes queda atrapado en una versión sobrenatural de su escuela después de realizar un ritual. Los jugadores deben explorar pasillos, descubrir secretos y resolver acertijos mientras intentan escapar de los espíritus que habitan el lugar.
El videojuego incluye diferentes finales, por lo que las decisiones durante la historia pueden determinar quién sobrevive. Es una de las propuestas más directamente relacionadas con el género de terror dentro del catálogo de Crunchyroll.
2. Ao Oni
Este videojuego japonés de terror presenta a un grupo de personajes que debe escapar de una mansión habitada por una criatura azul. La experiencia combina exploración, acertijos y persecuciones, mientras los jugadores buscan objetos y caminos para evitar al monstruo.
Su estética sencilla y sus apariciones inesperadas lo convierten en una alternativa para quienes disfrutan del terror clásico.
3. Raging Loop
Es una novela visual de misterio y terror psicológico ambientada en una aldea aislada donde sus habitantes participan en un ritual relacionado con hombres lobo. El protagonista queda atrapado en una serie de acontecimientos violentos y debe descubrir quiénes son los responsables.
La historia avanza mediante decisiones y diferentes rutas narrativas, por lo que el jugador debe prestar atención a los diálogos y las pistas para comprender lo que sucede.
4. The House in Fata Morgana
Esta novela visual propone una historia gótica ambientada en una mansión marcada por tragedias. El jugador recorre distintas épocas y conoce relatos de personajes cuyas vidas están relacionadas con el misterio del lugar.
Su propuesta se apoya principalmente en la narración, la música y una atmósfera oscura, con elementos de terror psicológico y drama.
5. Last Time I Saw You
La aventura sigue a un adolescente que vive en el Japón de los años ochenta y comienza a experimentar sucesos sobrenaturales. A través de la exploración, el jugador descubre personajes, criaturas y misterios vinculados con una maldición.
Aunque combina elementos de aventura y drama, su ambientación sobrenatural y sus referencias al folclore japonés la convierten en una opción para Halloween.
Cinco juegos de terror para descargar en PlayStation Store
PlayStation también reúne videojuegos de terror para quienes buscan experiencias más intensas en PS4 y PS5. En su selección oficial para Halloween de 2026 aparecen títulos de supervivencia, terror psicológico y experiencias multijugador.
1. Until Dawn
Es una aventura de terror cinematográfica en la que un grupo de jóvenes queda atrapado en una montaña durante una noche llena de amenazas. Las decisiones del jugador determinan quién sobrevive y cómo se desarrolla la historia. Su propuesta combina exploración, suspenso y momentos de persecución.
2. Phasmophobia
Este juego multijugador permite asumir el papel de investigadores paranormales que deben identificar fantasmas en casas y otros lugares abandonados. Los participantes utilizan herramientas para detectar actividad sobrenatural y recopilar pruebas. La experiencia puede jugarse en equipo y cada investigación presenta amenazas diferentes.
3. Resident Evil Requiem
La nueva entrega de la conocida franquicia de Capcom combina exploración, supervivencia y enfrentamientos contra criaturas infectadas. El jugador debe administrar recursos, investigar escenarios y enfrentarse a enemigos mientras avanza por una historia marcada por el terror biológico.
4. Five Nights at Freddy’s: Secret of the Mimic
El videojuego lleva a los jugadores a una instalación abandonada donde deben enfrentarse a una amenaza mecánica capaz de imitar apariencias y comportamientos. La experiencia se basa en explorar espacios oscuros, evitar encuentros peligrosos y descubrir los secretos del lugar.
5. Alan Wake 2
Esta aventura de terror psicológico sigue al escritor Alan Wake y a la agente Saga Anderson mientras investigan sucesos sobrenaturales relacionados con una serie de asesinatos. Combina exploración, resolución de misterios y enfrentamientos con criaturas que aparecen en escenarios oscuros.
Los cinco títulos forman parte de las propuestas de terror que PlayStation destaca para Halloween de 2026.
Cómo descargar los juegos de Crunchyroll y PlayStation
En el caso de Crunchyroll, los usuarios deben ingresar a la aplicación móvil y buscar la sección Game Vault. Desde allí pueden seleccionar un videojuego y acceder a su descarga mediante Google Play o App Store. Para utilizar el catálogo completo se necesita una suscripción Mega Fan o Ultimate Fan.
En PlayStation, el procedimiento consiste en ingresar a PlayStation Store desde la consola o la página web, buscar el nombre del videojuego y seleccionar la opción de compra o descarga, según corresponda. Algunos títulos también pueden estar incluidos en los catálogos de PlayStation Plus, dependiendo del plan y de su disponibilidad.
De esta manera, ambas plataformas reúnen alternativas para quienes buscan videojuegos de terror durante Halloween, con propuestas que van desde historias sobrenaturales para celulares hasta producciones de suspenso y supervivencia para consolas.

articles.title: Is mirrorless really that much better than DSLR? I pitted a new Viltrox 35mm f/1.4 prime against a Sigma DSLR classic that's 15 years its senior, and you might be surprised by the results
articles.text:
I compared the new Viltrox 35mm f/1.4 pro prime against a legendary Sigma Art lens for DSLRs — and discovered just how far have lenses come in 15 years (the images might surprise you)
Can you spot the difference in these like-for-like images?
If I was to pinpoint one special lens in my photography career, it would have to be the Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM Art for Nikon F-mount.
I picked mine up just before I moved to East Africa where I would work in photo journalism. Sigma had just burst onto the scene with its new ‘Art’ lens in 2012, for a much lower price than Nikon’s proprietary 35mm f/1.4 for its DSLRs, and so I bought one to pair with my Nikon D800 camera.
Over four memorable years living in Kenya and travelling the region and neighbouring countries, I estimate that I took more than 75% of my photos with this one lens, many my all-time favorites of people in their environment.
More recently, I switched to a mirrorless camera made by the same company — the Z-mount Nikon Z6 II, which has been updated with the Z6 III but remains my primary camera.
Viltrox then offered a review sample of its shiny new AF 35mm F1.4 Pro lens, which was unveiled this week in Nikon Z-mount and Sony E-mount versions, but with no word on an L-mount version yet. I’ve already tested Viltrox’s pricier 35mm F1.2 from its flagship ‘Lab’ series, but the latest f/1.4 pro is a specs match to my old lens, so I was keen to see how the two compared.
I tried both lenses in various scenarios, shooting like-for-like photos with them using the Z6 II camera (the Sigma lens attached via the Nikon F-mount to Z-mount adapter).
Along the way I was asking myself — is mirrorless all that it’s cracked up to be, or could I happily continue with my decade-old-and-more DSLR optic? Here’s what I learned.

View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Handling of each lens
I'll start with handling, and Sigma’s lens by itself is physically smaller than Viltrox’s. However, the necessary F-mount to Z-mount adapter to use it with my Z6 II adds bulk and evens matters out.
And if I were to use the Sigma lens with my D800 DSLR, well, that's a much bigger camera than the Z6 II. The adapter essentially addresses flange depth (the distance between the camera sensor and the rear of the lens — which is deeper in Nikon's F-mount), while maintaining full autofocus performance.
As such, there was no real size or weight advantage to either lens, whatever camera system was used. Nikon also has an affordable 35mm f/1.4 Z-mount lens, mind you, which is smaller than both of these lenses, but in my experience it doesn't match the quality of either lens here.
My Sigma lens has taken a beating over its almost 15 years of use in harsh conditions, and it's still going strong. Sure, it looks well-used, but it performs like it did on day one. I wouldn't hold the same hope for the Viltrox lens, aesthetically speaking, at least. It's one of the many Viltrox lenses that I've tested with an exterior that scratches easily. That doesn't affect optical quality, but it did make me mindful of taking care of the lens.
Autofocus is a fraction snappier and smoother with the Viltrox lens, but not enough of a reason alone to opt for it. I don't believe that using an F-mount lens through the adapter with a Z-mount mirrorless camera has any adverse affect on autofocus performance.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Optical quality: any obvious progress?
I regularly want to make use of the bright maximum f/1.4 aperture with a lens such as these, in order to decrease depth of field and blur surroundings so that my subjects standout, and for working in dim light with no supplementary lighting. It’s at this setting in particular that the differences in optical quality between the two lenses are acute.
The Viltrox lens is optically sharper at f/1.4. Not by much, I must say, and you won't necessarily see the difference even when viewed on a laptop — I'd still class the Sigma lens as very sharp. However, when pixel peeping, the difference is there.
And it's when pixel peeping that chromatic aberration (CA) in the Sigma is way more pronounced. The Viltrox lens isn't immune to it, but it handles the distortion much better. The Sigma lens shows longitudinal chromatic aberration (LoCA) at times, too — a lens distortion that is harder to correct. I expected vignetting (where corners are darker) to be worse in the Sigma lens, but in reality performance was roughly on par.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
- Check out my round-up of the best Nikon Z-mount lenses
And what about bokeh (the out-of-focus quality, typically observed in dappled light)? From my sample images, I'd have to say it's a tie. Both lenses can render buttery smooth bokeh, with similar characteristics; roundish in the center of the frame, becoming slightly more cats-eye in shape towards the corners.
The optical quality observations above are made with the lens aperture wide open at f/1.4. In all the situations above, I took sequences at f/1.4, f/1.8, f/2, f/2.8, f/4 and f/5.6 and compared the differences.
Stop aperture down to, say, f/4 and f/5.6, and most of the above differences are negligible; sharpness evens out, and lens distortions reduce — only does chromatic aberration remain more pronounced in the Sigma. I've included closeups of images shot at f/5.6 which prove how the quality evens out, below.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro vs Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM Art: the bottom line
For photographers, there is surprisingly little to choose between what is an excellent Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro lens and the 15-year-old Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM Art.
Optical quality differences are more acute at f/1.4; with aperture at its maximum setting, the Viltrox lens is slightly sharper and handles chromatic aberration better. However, you'll only really spot those differences when pixel peeping, and closing down each lens to f/4 and lower, the end results level out.
Bokeh is essentially the same in both lenses, although there's a touch of LoCA in the Sigma lens in certain backlit scenarios.
The Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro joins a growing list of lenses from the Chinese company that I can highly recommend. However, comparing it to a 15-year-old Sigma legend, that's designed for a mostly discontinued camera system, has only shown me that DSLRs and their best optics are still a decent option today. I for one will happily continue using my Sigma lens for photography.
