articles.title: Nigeria’s AI progress will be judged by solving local problems
articles.text:
Nigeria’s AI progess will be judged by the local problems it solves, as Nigeria can adopt the latest AI tools but still fail to solve the problems that matter most to Nigerians, panellists said at “The State of AI in Nigeria”, a session at Moonshot by TechCabal on Thursday, 29 October.
The panel featured Olubunmi Okunowo, a senior programme officer at the Gates Foundation; Johnson Agogbua, founder and CEO of Kasi Cloud, a Lagos-based data-centre operator; and Dr Yetunde Anibaba, a senior lecturer and accreditation lead at Lagos Business School. Dr Olubayo Adekambi, founder and CEO of Data Scientists Network, moderated.
“We’re building AI, but there are lots of nuances that people in the field who use these tools have that we must incorporate into our building,” Okunowo said. Technical skill alone does not produce useful tools, he said; developers need people who understand the problem first-hand.
A 2024 GSMA report on AI use cases in Nigeria makes a similar point: local data, skills and infrastructure decide whether AI tools get built and used, and tools that ignore local languages and working conditions risk shutting out the people they are meant to serve.
Agogbua argued that the main thing AI should deliver in Nigeria is productivity, pointing to healthcare and agriculture as sectors where it could change how work gets done.
Building the right tool still leaves the problem of getting it to people. Anibaba said affordability and access decide whether AI reaches those who need it. She pointed to the Nigeria AI Scaling Hub, hosted at Lagos Business School and supported by the Gates Foundation, which helps AI products scale in healthcare, agriculture and education. She also called for clearer policy to speed up adoption, particularly in healthcare.
Taken together, the panel’s message was that Nigeria’s AI progress will be judged by the local problems it solves. For founders, that means working with domain experts from the start, building for the people who will use the product, and planning for cost, access and regulation before launch.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.text:
Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Raphael Gruber, Jan Rothörl, Simon M. Fröhlich, Maarten A. Brems, Fabian Kammerbauer, Maria-Andromachi Syskaki, Elizabeth M. Jefremovas, Sachin Krishnia, Asle Sudbø, Peter Virnau, Mathias Kläui. Real-time observation of topological defect dynamics mediating two-dimensional skyrmion lattice melting. Nature Nanotechnology, 2025; 20 (10): 1405 DOI: 10.1038/s41565-025-01977-2

articles.title: Happy Pikmin Day Eve
articles.text:
This morning, Nintendo announced that tomorrow, November 1st, would be the first annual Pikmin Day. As part of the short Pikmin Day Direct, Shigeru Miyamoto shared new info about Pikmin 4 for the Switch 2, as well as an update for the mobile app Pikmin Bloom, and announced the Hello! Pikmin series of shorts.
Happy Pikmin Day Eve
Nintendo is celebrating the first annual Pikmin Day by debuting a new series of short films.
Players will be able to use the Switch 2’s built-in microphone to issue voice commands to Oatchi, the space dog. Pikmin 4 will also have a Dandori Academy mode that will test players’ skills in specific challenges. There will be limited tests on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, complete with leaderboards where players can compare stats. Pikmin Bloom will be getting a new feature called Secret Caves, where players can win treasure by battling enemies and exploring said caves.
Lastly, Miyamoto showed the first installment of a new series of shorts called Hello! Pikmin. A second episode will premiere tomorrow, with a third later in November. The series will then debut one short per month starting in December. The shorts build on the success of Close to You, a Pikmin animation released last year.

articles.title: Shielding the patch gap: The exploit doesn't wait for Patch Tuesday
articles.text:
Shielding the patch gap: The exploit doesn’t wait for Patch Tuesday
Four years after Log4Shell became one of the most consequential vulnerabilities in software history, vulnerable instances of the library are still turning up in production environments. That persistence isn’t really a failure of tooling. It’s a fact of how modern applications are built. A typical service pulls in hundreds of transitive open-source dependencies, any one of which can carry a critical CVE that’s difficult to even inventory, let alone test and ship a fix for on short notice.
Now factor in what AI-assisted vulnerability research is starting to do to that timeline. Attackers can already use large language models to trace exploit paths through unfamiliar codebases and generate working proof-of-concept variants in hours rather than weeks. If that trend holds, security teams are no longer planning for one Log4Shell-scale event every few years. They are preparing for dozens running concurrently, each with a shrinking window between disclosure and exploitation.
Patching is necessary. It just isn’t sufficient on its own.
Patching remains the durable fix, but compensating controls can augment that longer cycle. The interval between “we know we’re vulnerable” and “we’ve safely shipped the fix” is set by dependency scanning, regression testing, change-management windows, and who owns the affected service, not by how fast an advisory gets published. That interval between the patch release date and the date it is actually deployed in production, called the patch gap or pre-patch exposure window, is exactly the period where an unpatched CVE is dangerous. The impact post-Mythos on this time window is substantial, with attackers shrinking the time taken to develop and test exploits down to hours and minutes.
“The interval between ‘we know we’re vulnerable’ and ‘we’ve safely shipped the fix’ is set by dependency scanning, regression testing, change-management windows, and who owns the affected service, not by how fast an advisory gets published.”
The cloud native ecosystem has spent the last several years building tooling for the two ends of that window: scanners and SBOM tools to find what’s vulnerable, prioritization engines to rank what matters most. But what has been missing historically is the compensating controls that address the time between discovery and permanent fix. Now we look towards what a team is actually supposed to do while the fix is in flight.
Why eBPF keeps coming up as the answer
That gap is why a growing number of teams are looking towards eBPF as a mechanism to insert critical and highly effective compensating controls. In short, eBPF lets you attach small, verified programs to kernel events (syscalls, network packets, process execution) without modifying application code or the kernel itself.
It’s what lets a tool observe exactly which process opened which file, which pod talked to which service, or whether a specific function in a vulnerable library was ever actually invoked, with near-invisible overhead and none of the blind spots that come from sitting a layer removed from the workload. eBPF isn’t new (over 10+ years in the Linux kernel!), and it isn’t proprietary to any one project or company. It’s already the enforcement substrate underneath a large share of production CNIs and security sensors.
“That combination — deep observability plus low-overhead enforcement, built on a primitive that’s already load-bearing infrastructure in most clusters — is what makes shielding vulnerabilities a plausible answer to the patch gap.”
Cilium is one of the clearest examples of how far this has come. What started as an eBPF-based CNI has grown into a sub-project, Tetragon, purpose-built for exactly this kind of runtime security use case: it observes process execution, network activity, and file access at the kernel level and can enforce policy on what it sees, in real time, with no in-process agent and no application code change. That combination – deep observability plus low-overhead enforcement, built on a primitive that’s already load-bearing infrastructure in most clusters – is what makes shielding vulnerabilities a plausible answer to the patch gap.
Where compensating controls fit in the cycle
Every vulnerability management program already runs some version of the same cycle: discover an exposure, prioritize it against everything else competing for engineering time, remediate it, and verify the fix. Compensating controls have always had a place in that cycle, historically as a stopgap, and often with a focus on network: a firewall rule, a WAF signature, a temporary access restriction.
What’s changing is where that stopgap lives and the level of control. Instead of sitting at the network edge or in a separate tool with its own blind spots, the compensating control now runs alongside remediation, directly on the application workload, using the same runtime visibility that would otherwise be logging the incident after the fact. These compensating controls must inherit the security discipline the rest of cloud native operations already expects: observe before enforcing, roll out gradually, keep an audit trail of what changed, and retire the control the moment the real patch lands and is verified. A handful of vendors are already building toward this. Cisco’s Live Protect architecture, for instance, extends this kind of workload-native enforcement across firewalls and network switches as well as the workload itself, treating protection as one continuous fabric running alongside the existing patching cycle rather than a bolt-on afterthought.
Filling in the ecosystem
This workflow moves in lockstep with existing scanners and SBOM generation. Those tools still do the job of finding and prioritizing vulnerable components, and vulnerability shielding is useful once that CVE inventory exists. What’s new is the layer in between: a workload-local, kernel-aware control that activates for targeted exploits for a bounded amount of time.
Closing the AI-accelerated patching gap
Agentic AI is set to make the patch gap worse before it gets better. If attackers can already generate working exploits in hours, we need tooling that closes exposure on the same machine-speed timescale, not on the next change-management cycle.
That’s the outcome eBPF-based vulnerability shielding is aiming for, and it’s still early, fast-moving, open-source work. articles.title: 3D-printed ghost guns may now have a way to be traced to their source — Australian researchers correctly identify 26 out of 28 printed PLA samples to their filament product
articles.text:
3D-printed ghost guns may now have a way to be traced to their source — Australian researchers correctly identify 26 out of 28 printed PLA samples to their filament product
It only tests for PLA, but it's a starting point.
A study published on October 22 in the journal Forensic Science International reports that researchers from Curtin University in Perth, Australia, have developed a forensic method to analyze 3D-printed PLA parts and match them to their respective filament, correctly matching 26 out of 28 samples of PLA. This potentially provides a way to link seized 3D-printed “ghost-guns” with other seized filament, allowing police to form a clearer network for the manufacturing and distribution of the 3D-printed firearms.
3D-printed firearms have become a big problem worldwide, as they are untraceable and even compostable in the case of PLA, with tools like this AI 3D-printed gun generator making it scarily accessible. Serial numbers, registration, and a network of licensed distributors are usually the first line of investigation when it comes to crime involving firearms, but easily manufacturable, untraceable, disposable plastic firearms are a new threat with no clear way to crack down on them yet.
However, this research, by Dr. Georgina Sauzier et al. from Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences, along with forensics experts from ChemCentre, has devised a way to trace a printed object to a specific filament product, down to the brand and type.
The process of 3D printing changes the filament’s physical properties, and this change can be measured. In this research, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is used, a thermoanalytical technique that lets the sample go through a range of temperatures, and the instrument measures how heat flows through the sample. It measures how much energy or power is used to keep the sample at a certain temperature or to change its temperature, giving us a graph of its thermal properties.
The sample’s thermal properties can then be cross-referenced with its unprinted filament, creating an association between them. As of now, the tested PLA products are the only successfully identified material, with PETG and ABS not providing enough information to link them to their filament product. Sauzier blames the amorphous nature of those filaments, giving very similar results with no clear identifiers linking them to their respective filament products. PLA has a semi-crystalline molecular structure, which provides clearer temperature transition points under the temperature tests as the crystalline structures break down and rearrange.
However, ABS and PETG did show some promise when tested using ATR-FTIR (Attenuated Total Reflectance-Fourier Transform Infrared), which uses infrared to identify chemical bonds and material composition. The team did find differences in additives using this method, but still did not give enough information to link them back to their respective filament products.
The research is still very early, with more rigorous testing to be done, as the team printed using only one machine, printed small sample tiles cut with scissors, and left them for a year in monitored office conditions before testing. Properties could further change as cooling rates vary greatly depending on what the printer is printing: Faster cooling and slower print speeds on overhangs, or slower cooling and faster print speeds on infill sections. Different printers may also affect the physical properties, adding one more factor in the chain.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
So far, correctly identifying 26 out of 28 samples is a great start to cracking down on dangerous, untraceable illegal firearms. When the research matures and can reliably identify a broad range of materials, it could potentially trace 3D-printed firearms to the printer and filament, potentially creating a list of where they were purchased and who purchased them.

He now loves doing DIY projects ranging from designing custom 3D-printed parts, building PCs and keyboards, all the way to woodworking. If he's not getting his hands dirty, he's probably brainstorming his next project.

articles.title: Samsung se rinde ante Google Discover y mata una app instalada en millones de móviles Galaxy
articles.text:
A Samsung se le ha hecho costumbre matar varias de sus propias apps, incluyendo aquellas que están instaladas en millones de dispositivos Galaxy. La más reciente víctima de esta estrategia es Samsung News, una aplicación que, como bien lo indica su nombre, permite leer noticias, ver resultados deportivos y más.
Según recoge SamMobile, la app de Samsung News ha comenzado a mostrar un aviso de discontinuación en algunos países. El mismo indica que la plataforma cesará su funcionamiento el próximo 21 de diciembre. Una vez que esto ocurra, el widget y la página tipo Google Discover que se abre al deslizar desde el borde izquierdo de la pantalla principal, también pasarán al olvido.
El anuncio oficial no explica el porqué del final de Samsung News. Es cierto que la compañía coreana ha mutado esta aplicación en varias oportunidades, por lo que no sería raro que en el futuro reaparezca bajo otro nombre. Aunque también es lógico pensar que la hegemonía de Google Discover para ofrecer contenidos a un solo toque de distancia puede haber tenido que ver con la decisión.
Sea como sea, hacia finales de año finalizará el periplo de Samsung News en los móviles y las tablets Galaxy. Esto significa que próximos dispositivos de la marca coreana no traerán la app preinstalada, lo que seguramente sea una buena noticia para quienes prefieren una experiencia de software con menos bloatware.
Samsung News dejará de funcionar en los móviles Galaxy a fin de año
El cierre de Samsung News implica que la app, el widget y el apartado tipo Google Discover no se actualizarán con nuevos contenidos desde el 21 de diciembre. Samsung está invitando a los usuarios a borrar el widget en cuestión una vez que llegue la fecha mencionada.
Además, toda la información recopilada para el funcionamiento de la aplicación se eliminará de inmediato, excepto en los países donde exista una normativa de retención de datos por un tiempo determinado.
Samsung News llega al final de su periplo apenas tres años después de su lanzamiento. La aplicación debutó en abril de 2023 y fue la cuarta iteración de las plataformas de noticias de la marca coreana.
Recordemos que la primera versión se lanzó en 2017 bajo el nombre de Bixby Home y evolucionó en Samsung Daily en 2019, mientras que un año más tarde se transformó en Samsung Free. Por lo pronto, no hay detalles sobre si la empresa piensa relanzarlo bajo una denominación diferente.

articles.title: La barrière « impénétrable » des ceintures de Van Allen autour de la Terre a finalement été franchie
articles.text:
Vous vous souvenez peut-être des aurores boréales de mai 2024, visibles jusque dans le sud de la France, et de votre fil Instagram soudain rempli de ciels violets. Pendant que nous sortions nos smartphones, il se passait quelque chose de beaucoup moins photogénique un peu plus haut, dans les ceintures de radiation qui entourent la Terre. Une équipe menée par le physicien Yoshizumi Miyoshi, de l’université de Nagoya, vient d’en publier le récit dans la revue Geophysical Research Letters, le 28 octobre 2026.
Une barrière qui n’en était pas tout à fait une
Le champ magnétique terrestre piège des particules énergétiques dans deux grands anneaux en forme de beignet, les ceintures de Van Allen. En 2014, les sondes Van Allen Probes de la NASA ont mis en évidence une frontière étonnante, à environ trois rayons terrestres du centre de la planète : les électrons les plus énergétiques, ceux qui filent à une vitesse proche de celle de la lumière, ne la franchissaient presque jamais. Les chercheurs l’ont baptisée « barrière impénétrable ».
Son origine reste débattue. Des ondes radio de basse fréquence naturelles (le « souffle plasmasphérique »), et même les émissions radio très basse fréquence produites par l’humanité, pourraient disperser ces électrons vers l’atmosphère avant qu’ils ne s’approchent davantage. Une protection bienvenue : on surnomme ces particules « électrons tueurs », parce que sans aller jusqu’au scénario de Projet Dernière Chance, elles traversent le blindage des satellites, endommagent leur électronique et raccourcissent leur durée de vie.
En mai 2024 donc, une série d’éruptions solaires a déclenché une tempête géomagnétique de niveau G5, le maximum sur l’échelle. Le satellite japonais Arase, qui surveille les ceintures de radiation depuis 2017, a alors observé des électrons de plus de 3 mégaélectronvolts à l’intérieur de la barrière. Leur flux a été multiplié par plus de 5 000 par rapport à son niveau d’avant la tempête.
On aurait pu penser que la tempête avait simplement poussé des électrons de l’extérieur vers l’intérieur, mais les données d’Arase racontent autre chose : les électrons de basse énergie ont augmenté en premier, les plus énergétiques une demi-journée plus tard, et ceux de plus de 3 MeV environ un jour après.
Selon les chercheurs, la tempête a érodé la plasmasphère, cette région de plasma froid qui entoure la Terre, au point de la vider presque entièrement. Ce vide a laissé le champ libre aux « ondes chorus », des ondes électromagnétiques qui, une fois converties en son, ressemblent à un chant d’oiseau, explique Yoshizumi Miyoshi. Au lieu de disperser les électrons, elles les ont accélérés. Et comme le plasma a mis plus de quatre jours à se reconstituer, contre deux en temps normal, ces conditions ont duré assez longtemps pour produire des électrons en masse. Les niveaux élevés ont ensuite persisté pendant des mois, jusqu’à la tempête suivante d’octobre 2024.
Faut-il paniquer ? Non, évidemment.
Évidemment, pas d’inquiétude : nous parlons de régions situées à plus de 10 000 km d’altitude, et l’atmosphère comme le champ magnétique continuent de nous protéger parfaitement au sol. La barrière n’a pas disparu non plus : elle a cédé dans des circonstances exceptionnelles, lors d’une tempête comme on en voit une tous les vingt ans. Des travaux de 2018 et de 2024 avaient d’ailleurs déjà fissuré l’idée d’une frontière absolue.
En revanche, l’étude intéresse au plus haut point les opérateurs de satellites. Une zone jugée relativement abritée peut, lors d’une tempête extrême, voir ses radiations exploser, et y rester élevées pendant des mois. Avec des milliers de satellites lancés chaque année et un Soleil encore agité, la météo spatiale est un vrai sujet d’ingénierie, avec de vraies conséquences.

articles.title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
articles.text:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.
My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.
Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.
Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.
When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.
Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.
But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.
When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)
Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.
I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.
When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.
It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.
I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)
That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.
The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

articles.title: LocalStack for Azure Enters Public Preview with Security Settings Stored but Not Enforced
articles.text:
LocalStack has put its Azure emulator into public preview, free and self-serve, with general availability expected in early 2027. Its own documentation is candid about the gap between emulating a resource and emulating its behavior.
The product runs Azure services on a developer machine and accepts existing ARM and Bicep templates, Terraform modules, Pulumi programs, and Azure CLI scripts without rewrites. The pitch is to test applications, as LocalStack puts it, "without waiting on a dev subscription or paying for every iteration." The service list is broad, covering AKS, Container Apps, Functions, App Service, Cosmos DB, Service Bus, Event Hubs, Key Vault, App Configuration, Managed Identity, API Management and more, and is wider than the announcement itself suggests. Each developer gets an isolated sandbox, and LocalStack positions it for development and testing rather than as a replacement for Azure.
The project is led by Paolo Salvatori, a Microsoft principal for 28 years before joining LocalStack and the creator of Service Bus Explorer. He sets the fidelity contract in one line:
If your solution runs perfectly on Azure but fails on our emulator, that is our bug to fix.
The documentation covers 24 resource providers and reports how much of each API is implemented. Storage Accounts covers 13 of 81 operations. App Service covers 143 of 616. Virtual Network covers 10 of 29.
The more useful pattern is what happens to the operations that are implemented. Configuration is frequently accepted, stored, and returned without taking effect. On App Service:
Keys, access restrictions, authentication settings, and publishing credential policies are not enforced.
The same page records that httpsOnly is not enforced and the emulator serves HTTP, that custom host-name bindings are stored and listed while the app answers only on its default names, that VNet integration is stored and returned with no network effect, and that backup configuration is stored while backup and restore are not implemented.
Networking follows suit. The Virtual Network page states plainly that "the emulator does not route network traffic or enforce security rules," that peering is unsupported, and that VPN gateways, ExpressRoute circuits, Load Balancer, Application Gateway, and Network Watcher are not implemented. Private DNS zones accept only A records.
Several Storage divergences land on authentication. Data-plane requests with a bearer token succeed whenever a token is present unless RBAC enforcement is enabled. A user delegation SAS does not re-check the principal’s RBAC when used. A SAS restricted to the caller’s public IP is refused because the emulator sees a Docker or loopback address. Unsupported request headers are silently accepted rather than rejected, and the x-ms-version header is not validated at all.
That promise is about code that runs in Azure and fails locally. The documented gaps mostly describe the reverse: an app with httpsOnly set serves HTTP here, and a data-plane request carrying any bearer token gets through. Both pass locally, and nothing in the run flags the difference.
Three behaviors will surprise people before any of that does. A web app created on a Windows plan runs its code in the Linux runtime. The Oryx build image ships for amd64 only, so on Apple Silicon a code deployment’s build fails, and the app starts without its dependencies. App Service state is held in memory and lost when the emulator stops.
Microsoft’s own local tooling is narrower and older. Azurite emulates Blob, Queue, and Table storage, the Cosmos DB emulator covers that database, and Azure Functions Core Tools runs Functions locally. None compose into a single environment where an ARM or Bicep deployment can be exercised end to end, which is the gap LocalStack aims to fill.
LocalStack also pitches the sandbox at AI agents, somewhere they can "deploy, break, and retry" without live credentials. An agent iterating there gets access restrictions stored rather than applied, and any bearer token accepted. Both come back as passes.
Developer experience features, including App Inspector, snapshots, and the chaos APIs, are not in preview. Pricing arrives at general availability, and preview access ends there. The transition terms are not settled: the product page still carries "[30 days]" as a literal placeholder and an unfilled next-steps section.

articles.title: Mischief 1, un modèle vidéo « dérivé de neurones vivants » : pardon ?
articles.text:
Il y a des communiqués qu’on lit trois fois pour être sûr d’avoir compris, surtout quand ils sont publiés, une fois n’est pas coutume, dans le tumulte d’un flux sur X. « Depuis quatre ans, nous faisons pousser de vraies cellules cérébrales sur des électrodes pour comprendre comment elles calculent », a écrit Alex Ksendzovsky, cofondateur et patron de TBC, le 30 octobre 2026. Avant d’annoncer que ces découvertes donnaient naissance à… un modèle de génération vidéo, disponible pour un demi-centime la seconde sur la plateforme fal.ai. Le lancement tombait la veille d’Halloween, d’où le nom (« mischief » désigne les petites farces de la Mischief Night).
Rassurez-vous déjà, si vous avez envie de tester le modèle : quand vous générez une vidéo avec Mischief 1, aucun neurone de rat ne travaille pour vous.
Le produit, au fond, est assez banal (si on considère banal le fait de pouvoir envoyer 3 lignes de texte à un ordinateur, générer une image et avoir une vidéo de qualité en retour, bienvenue en 2026). Mischief 1 est un modèle « image vers vidéo » : on lui donne une image de départ et une description de ce qui doit se passer, et il renvoie un clip de trois ou cinq secondes, en 480p ou 720p. Il est accessible par API sur fal, pour 0,5 centime de dollar la seconde en 480p et 1 centime en 720p, soit 5 centimes le clip de cinq secondes en 720p. TBC le présente comme le moins cher de sa catégorie.
Mischief 1 n’est pas un modèle conçu de zéro. Il repose sur Wan 2.2, un modèle vidéo open source développé par Alibaba qu’il est possible d’installer sur votre ordinateur. TBC y ajoute une petite couche logicielle, qui pèse moins de 0,1 % du modèle d’origine et s’insère entre ses blocs de calcul. Résultat revendiqué : des vidéos de qualité équivalente, générées au moins cinq fois plus vite et pour un coût de calcul inférieur de 80 %. Sur sa page produit, la start-up affiche 12 secondes de génération contre 142 secondes pour Wan 2.2 seul.
Et les neurones dans tout ça ?
TBC n’est pas une startup d’IA comme les autres. Fondée par deux neurochirurgiens, Alex Ksendzovsky et Jon Pomeraniec, elle cultive dans ses laboratoires de San Francisco et Baltimore des neurones de rat et des neurones dérivés de cellules souches humaines, posés sur des grilles d’électrodes. L’équipe traduit un problème informatique (des pixels, par exemple) en stimulations électriques, enregistre la réponse des neurones, et cherche dans leur activité des motifs de calcul récurrents. Ces motifs sont ensuite transposés en équations, intégrées dans des réseaux de neurones artificiels classiques.
Tout le challenge est d’approcher l’efficacité du cerveau humain. Notre cerveau fonctionne en effet avec une vingtaine de watts, quand un datacenter d’IA en consomme des centaines de millions. Si la nature a trouvé des façons de calculer plus efficaces, autant aller les observer directement.
TBC n’est pas seule sur ce créneau : l’australienne Cortical Labs vend déjà un « ordinateur biologique » à base de neurones humains, et la suisse FinalSpark loue l’accès à ses organoïdes cérébraux. Mais TBC est la première à transformer ces recherches en produit commercial grand public, tournant sur des GPU tout ce qu’il y a de plus classiques.
La start-up reste très évasive quand il s’agit d’expliquer comment l’activité de neurones de rat devient une ligne de code. Or des accélérations d’un modèle open source de cet ordre ne sont pas inédites. On sait déjà rendre Wan 2.2 plusieurs fois plus rapide grâce à des techniques de distillation, qui réduisent le nombre d’étapes de calcul nécessaires. Impossible, sans article scientifique étayé, de savoir si la « recette neuronale » fait mieux, ou si elle fait la même chose avec une meilleure histoire.
La société, qui a levé 52 millions de dollars, a de toute façon des ambitions bien plus larges : elle dit avoir appliqué sa méthode au modèle Cosmos de Nvidia pour la robotique, et travaille, à plus long terme, à remettre de vrais neurones dans la boucle de calcul.

articles.title: La taxe au gigaoctet prend sa revanche à l’Assemblée et pourrait faire exploser le prix du streaming
articles.text:
L’idée de faire payer les plateformes pour les octets qu’elles déversent sur les réseaux circule depuis des années, des couloirs de Bruxelles au programme du Parti socialiste. Ce vendredi 30 octobre, l’amendement du député Laurent Lhardit au budget 2027 l’a concrétisée : une taxe sur les « producteurs de données numériques », votée par 11 voix contre 10 en première lecture. Le rapporteur général du budget et le gouvernement avaient pourtant appelé à la rejeter quelques minutes plus tôt, comme la commission des finances l’avait déjà fait le 9 octobre.
Qui paiera ces 0,055 euro par gigaoctet ?
Le texte institue, selon ses propres termes, « une taxe assise sur les flux de données numériques émises par les fournisseurs de contenu et acquittée par ces derniers ». Chaque gigaoctet expédié vers un abonné français coûterait ainsi 0,055 euro à l’entreprise qui l’émet, un péage au volume dont les fournisseurs d’accès seraient les releveurs de compteur. Orange, Free, Bouygues Telecom et SFR devraient relever, de façon anonymisée et consolidée, les volumes qui transitent vers leurs clients, sous la supervision de l’Arcep. Les contenus mis en cache chez des diffuseurs comme Akamai entrent aussi dans le calcul.
L’exposé des motifs vise sans détour Google, Meta, Amazon, Netflix et Akamai, cinq acteurs qui concentrent à eux seuls la moitié du trafic mesuré par l’Arcep. En séance, Laurent Lhardit a chiffré le rendement attendu à 10 milliards d’euros par an : « La taxe serait principalement acquittée par les géants mondialisés du numérique, puisqu’ils émettent l’immense majorité des flux adressés aux abonnés internet en France ». Un double plafond, 15 % du chiffre d’affaires réalisé en France ou 2 % du chiffre d’affaires mondial, ménage les secteurs qui émettent énormément pour chaque euro encaissé, vidéo à la demande et jeu vidéo en tête.
Philippe Juvin, rapporteur général de la commission des finances, a rendu un premier avis défavorable : les géants visés répercuteraient selon lui le poids de la taxe sur leurs annonceurs. Côté gouvernement, David Amiel a suivi. Le ministre de l’Action et des Comptes publics juge le dispositif difficile à mettre en œuvre sans capteurs de flux, voire sans mesure « au niveau des terminaux individuels de réception ». Il estime aussi que la moitié du produit, soit 5 milliards d’euros, retomberait « sur des fournisseurs de contenus de plus petite taille, notamment sur des fournisseurs français ». Laurent Lhardit a balayé l’objection avec un exemple maison : la diffusion des cinq chaînes du groupe TF1 sur les box des opérateurs représenterait 200 000 à 300 000 euros de taxe, un poids qu’il juge faible pour les acteurs français.
Et maintenant, qui peut encore l’enterrer ?
Dès 2021, Orange, Deutsche Telekom et Telefónica réclamaient à Bruxelles une contribution des plus gros générateurs de trafic au financement des réseaux. La Commission européenne avait ouvert une consultation début 2023, avant de ranger le dossier faute de consensus. À une différence près : dans la version votée vendredi, les milliards iraient au budget de l’État, là où le programme socialiste de cet été fléchait 0,10 euro par gigaoctet vers le financement des infrastructures.
Pour l’abonné, cent gigaoctets de vidéo consommés dans le mois, un ordre de grandeur courant pour un foyer adepte des plateformes, représenteraient 5,50 euros de taxe, que rien n’interdirait aux services concernés de répercuter sur leurs tarifs ou leurs écrans publicitaires. Les porteurs du texte y voient même une vertu écologique, la taxe incitant à compresser et optimiser les volumes transmis.
Avant d’en arriver là, l’amendement doit d’abord survivre au vote de la première partie du budget, celle des recettes, dans une Assemblée où rien n’est acquis. Suivront un Sénat à majorité de droite, peu susceptible de la voter, puis l’hypothèse d’un 49.3. Yaël Braun-Pivet a publiquement appelé Sébastien Lecornu à l’utiliser, et le gouvernement garderait alors la main pour écarter la mesure du texte final.

articles.title: La actualización de Windows 11 26H2 ya está disponible
articles.text:
Microsoft acaba de estrenar Windows 11 26H2, la actualización anual de su sistema operativo que incorpora mejoras de funcionamiento, nuevas opciones de personalización y funciones relacionadas con la IA. Sin embargo, esta versión en concreto tiene una particularidad, ya que muchas de sus novedades ya estaban disponibles a través de las actualizaciones mensuales que lanza la compañía.
Según detalló la firma de Redmond en su anuncio oficial, Windows 11 26H2 se distribuye mediante un paquete de habilitación, un archivo ligero que activa funciones ya presentes en el sistema. Así, esto permite instalar la actualización con una descarga reducida y, en la mayoría de los equipos compatibles, un único reinicio que no necesita realizar una instalación completa.
Cómo instalar Windows 11 26H2 y qué hacer si prefieres esperar
El menú Inicio, las herramientas de IA y las posibilidades de personalización son tres de las mejoras que ya estaban presentes. Además, algunas funciones dependen del hardware del PC o de un despliegue progresivo, así que actualizar a 26H2 no garantiza que todas aparezcan de inmediato.
De momento, la actualización está disponible para dispositivos compatibles con Windows 11 24H2 y 25H2, pero Microsoft ha confirmado que la está distribuyendo de manera escalonada. Para comprobar si puedes instalarla, accede a Configuración > Windows Update > Buscar actualizaciones, aunque también puedes activar la opción para recibir las últimas actualizaciones en cuanto estén disponibles.
Si prefieres comprobar primero si aparecen problemas de compatibilidad, Windows permite retrasar temporalmente las actualizaciones. Además, no olvides que la propia compañía explica en su guía oficial de soporte que es posible establecer una fecha de reanudación dentro de un plazo máximo de 35 días siguiendo estos pasos:
- Haz clic en Inicio y abre Configuración.
- Entra en el apartado Windows Update.
- Localiza la opción Pausar actualizaciones.
- Selecciona una fecha de reanudación, con un máximo de 35 días, o utiliza el menú de duración disponible en tu versión.
- Comprueba que Windows Update indique que las actualizaciones están pausadas.
Una vez alcanzada la fecha establecida, Windows volverá a buscar e instalar las actualizaciones pendientes. Aunque retrasarlas puede servir para evitar algunos problemas iniciales, también supone aplazar correcciones de seguridad. Por ello, conviene revisar periódicamente el estado de Windows 11 26H2 y no posponer indefinidamente su instalación.
