articles.title: How Vectar Energy moved from selling solar generators to building carbon-market infrastructure
articles.text:
In 2025, Biodun Ogunleye, the Lagos State Commissioner for Energy and Mineral Resources, said that about 30,000 deaths occur annually in the state due to exposure to carbon monoxide. Growing up, Deborah Fadeyi had seen how generators became part of everyday life, even when their consequences could be fatal. It became personal in 1999 when she lost a friend to carbon monoxide poisoning from generator fumes.
“I was young, but that experience stayed with me, and Nigeria still hasn’t gone past that phase,” she told TechCabal in an interview in September. “We still hear in the news that people are dying from carbon monoxide poisoning. Generators were so normal growing up that nobody really questioned what it meant for people to depend on them for something so fundamental as electricity, until it began to kill them.”
Twenty years later, she founded Vectar Energy, a climate finance company registered and operating in the United Kingdom. Vectar Energy began as a maker of solar-powered portable power stations designed to displace small petrol generators. Today, its core product is ecoWise, a platform that brings small solar projects together into a single portfolio, helping them access carbon markets they could not enter on their own.
Day 1: She wanted to build a better generator
If petrol generators were the problem, Fadeyi wanted to build a better alternative. Before Vectar Energy became a climate finance company, she was experimenting with ways to make solar power practical enough to replace petrol generators.
Her first attempt was in 2019, through an earlier venture called YettyFlames. Fadeyi was building locally fabricated solar-generator systems, drawing on what she was learning about the energy needs of Nigerian households and small businesses. She described the early systems as crude compared with what Vectar would eventually produce, but said they gave her firsthand experience with the people she wanted to serve.
“That part of the business was super important to us because it put us directly in front of the customers, and it helped us to challenge the realities that they were facing,” Fadeyi said.
By 2020, she had decided to turn that work into a more structured business. She founded Vectar Energy and began building it on her own. Its first product was the Vectar Eco, a portable solar power station designed to replace the small petrol generators commonly known as I better pass my neighbour generators.
“The idea was simple: create a practical solar and better battery alternative to the small petrol generators that homes and businesses used every day,” she said. “Getting from that idea to something commercially viable was much less simple.”
Turning that ambition into a product people could buy required money, and Fadeyi said Vectar Energy was raising funds to develop the solar power stations. The team also had to work through the business of making hardware, including choosing the right battery configurations, sizing the solar panels, testing components and designing a unit that was portable and powerful enough for the appliances customers needed. What kept her going, she said, went back to 1999.
“I told myself that I hope this doesn’t happen to someone else,” she said. “I guess this is the part that I’m playing to enable that future that I once dreamed of, where it became a responsibility from my best friend losing her life because of something that could be avoided.”
Day 500: Making solar cheaper and building it are different
Getting the solar power stations into the market meant a rethink of how Vectar produced them. Fadeyi said her team realised that locally fabricated units could end up costing more than their target customers could afford. They took the design to China and then began importing semi-assembled units that would be completed in Nigeria.
By 2023, Vectar was ready for the market. It had paying customers in Nigeria and was generating revenue from its portable power stations. The company developed different capacities, including the Vectar Eco and Vectar Eco Mini, recognising that a household, a trader and a small business did not have the same power needs or ability to pay.
However, as much as its customers recognised the benefits of switching from petrol to solar generators, Fadeyi said they still struggled to afford the upfront cost. She stated that Vectar explored partnerships with lenders such as Credit Direct and AltPower to offer instalment payments, but many prospective customers struggled to meet the credit requirements.
“The credit landscape in Nigeria is still developing. People would go to such platforms in the hope that they would get [credit], but they would be laden with different and stringent requirements that they might not be able to meet,” Fadeyi said.
Vectar then tried to offer its own non-interest instalment plans to customers in Lagos and Abuja. Still, spreading the payments over time did not make the stations affordable enough for many of the people the company wanted to reach, according to Fadeyi.
We realised that we were solving the problem, but not at the scale that it needed to be solved,” she said.
In 2024, Vectar Energy began working on SUNWISE alongside Vectar Eco. SUNWISE was an initiative designed to make portable solar systems more accessible to nano and small businesses without requiring full payment upfront. The company explored rent-to-own arrangements starting at ₦2,000 ($1.49) daily. That year, Habeeb Mustapha formally joined Vectar as chief technology officer in April, strengthening its technical team. He would later become a co-founder.
Fadeyi said she was also beginning to discover if the environmental benefits of the solar systems could generate revenue and help lower the cost of solar.
“We had begun asking whether the environmental value produced by solar systems could itself help solve the affordability problem,” Fadeyi said. “If a solar system displaces petrol or diesel and avoids carbon emissions, could that environmental impact become another revenue stream? Could that revenue lower the cost of the system or help finance additional installations?”
2024 became a year of overlap for Vectar. It was still building and selling physical solar products, but it was also beginning to develop the technology that would eventually take it into climate finance.
Day 1000: Selling the evidence, not the equipment
After years of trying to make clean energy affordable for Nigerian households and small businesses, Fadeyi had come to a realisation that the opportunity might be in making the environmental benefits of solar projects generate money.
“What if the individual installation did not have to be the unit entering the carbon market? What if we aggregated many installations and eventually many independent developers through one common infrastructure?” she said.
This became ecoWise, Vectar’s carbon-market infrastructure platform. ecoWise brings together smaller solar projects in a single portfolio, monitors the electricity they generate and the emissions they avoid, and helps their developers access carbon markets. ecoWise provides the infrastructure to collectively navigate the process of carbon certification and credit sales. For this to work, Vectar had to produce evidence that carbon-market institutions and buyers could trust. That meant developing the technology to monitor installations and understanding the requirements of carbon standards.
“ecoWise increasingly became about assurance infrastructure rather than simply an emissions calculator,” Fadeyi said. “It was also during this period that we began doing the much less glamorous work required to create an actual carbon programme: methodologies, eligibility criteria, developer agreements, carbon rights, monitoring plans, safeguards, Gold Standard requirements and the programme architecture necessary to aggregate independent developers.”
Fadeyi described 2025 as the year Vectar made the transition from being principally a solar product company to becoming a climate finance and environmental-market infrastructure company. By early 2026, Vectar’s legacy solar product business had served more than 150 customers and generated roughly ₦80 million in cumulative revenue. However, Fadeyi was now focused on helping solar developers earn additional revenue from the electricity they already generated.
Vectar says it has onboarded 35 megawatt-peak (MWp) of distributed solar projects across Nigeria, with a 50 MWp cohort being prepared for validation and verification. Fadeyi expects the first carbon-credit payout to participating solar projects in January 2027. The technology supporting the programme has also evolved. Vectar is developing ecoWise as a hybrid digital measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) system, combining physical Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring with virtual and API-based integrations. This allows the platform to collect data from solar installations using different inverters and monitoring systems.
“We realised quite early that distributed solar is too heterogeneous for a single monitoring approach to work for every developer,” she said. “Different projects have different inverters, monitoring systems, data formats and operating environments, so the infrastructure has to be flexible enough to accommodate that diversity while still producing consistent, auditable evidence.”
Fadeyi said carbon credits from the projects could sell for as much as $50 each, depending on the market and the quality of the credits. She also said Vectar was working with MSCI, a global financial data and research company that provides independent ratings of carbon projects. In 2026, Vectar entered the International Renewable Energy Certificate (I-REC(E)) ecosystem, giving qualifying projects another route to environmental-market revenue, as it allows buyers to substantiate claims about their use of renewable electricity.
Vectar is also working towards setting up in Sierra Leone and Madagascar in 2027, with ambitions to replicate its infrastructure across other African markets. The company has travelled a long way from the portable solar power station it began building in 2020. However, the underlying problem of making clean energy a viable alternative to the generators that power homes and businesses across Nigeria has remained the same.
“Day one, we started with how do we make clean energy affordable enough to replace generators,” Fadey said. “Now we’re asking the question: how do we build the financial infrastructure that makes our energy transition scalable?”

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.text:
Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- RIKEN
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
- Share:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.
Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors
Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.
Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.
This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.
To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.
"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%
The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.
When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.
The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors
The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.
This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.
"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."
The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.
"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.
Story Source:
Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yi-Hsien Wu, Leon C. Camenzind, Patrick Bütler, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Hsi-Sheng Goan, Seigo Tarucha. Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03466-2
Cite This Page:

articles.title: Microsoft's DirectX update could slash ray tracing memory by up to 90 percent
articles.text:
What we know so far: Plenty of ray-traced games still bounce light off cheaper, low-detail copies of their scenery rather than the models players actually see on screen. That's mostly because rebuilding the GPU's ray tracing data for every swaying tree and moving character each frame simply takes too long. A new DirectX feature currently in preview aims to fix that. It could also free up a big chunk of the video memory ray tracing currently eats.
Microsoft detailed Clustered Geometry and a companion feature called Partitioned TLAS on its DirectX developer blog this week, describing the pair as the biggest change to DirectX Raytracing since the API arrived in 2018.
Right now, any time a mesh deforms or streams in at a new level of detail, the GPU has to rebuild that object's acceleration structure from scratch. Clustered Geometry instead splits models into small chunks of up to 256 triangles that get built once and reused. So when an object changes, developers can reassemble existing clusters or rebuild just a handful of them.
Partitioned TLAS applies similar thinking to the whole scene. It breaks the world into regions so that only the parts where something actually moved get updated each frame.
Microsoft's own test sample makes the gains look enormous. On a Radeon RX 9070, switching from conventional rebuilds to clustered geometry lifted the frame rate from 1.2 fps to 79 fps. Per-frame build time dropped from 788ms to just over 3ms, and memory for those structures shrank from roughly 7.5GB to 774MB, about 90% less. That's ray tracing data alone, though, not a game's overall VRAM footprint.
Still, Microsoft warned in all caps that games shouldn't expect wins anywhere near that size. Clustered builds also need far more temporary scratch memory, so developers will have to plan around that.
Nvidia has actually been shipping the same idea since last year as RTX Mega Geometry. In Alan Wake 2, it improved both frame rates and image quality. Earlier this month, Gears of War: E-Day used it to ray trace Unreal Engine 5's full-detail Nanite geometry instead of the static, low-poly proxies the engine normally falls back on.
The difference now is that it's part of DirectX, so developers get one path that works across vendors. No new hardware is needed, either: Nvidia supports it on every RTX card, and Intel covers its Arc B-series GPUs and recent Core Ultra chips. On AMD's side, though, only the Radeon RX 9000 series made the list so far.
For players, the wait will be a little longer. Everything is still in preview and needs Windows Developer Mode to switch on, so games built around it are some way off. And going by Gears, even Nvidia's version asks for a GeForce card with at least 12GB of VRAM before it can be enabled.

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Cheaper and faster in three tests at max effort
articles.text:
GPT-6.1 Terra vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Cheaper and faster in three tests at max effort
OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, and included two direct comparisons with Opus 5.5 in its marketing materials. It claimed Terra came within five percentage points of Opus 5.5, with fallbacks at less than one-fifth the estimated cost, on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which has agents write code for research tasks such as tracking cell divisions.
At max effort, OpenAI describes Terra as more than three times as token-efficient as Opus and one-quarter the price for standard input and output tokens. Separately, it reports an estimated cost per task of about one-ninth. On Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark of multistep computer-use tasks, Terra scored 60.0% at $1.01 per task, and Opus scored 63.2% at $8.82. That is a 3.2-percentage-point score gap and an 8.73-to-one cost ratio, not identical accuracy.
At standard uncached API rates, Terra costs $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, compared with Opus 5.5’s $4 and $20. With the same input/output token mix and no other pricing adjustments, Terra would need four times as many tokens to match Opus’s cost. Actual task cost also depends on token usage, cache reads and writes, and any applicable pricing adjustments.
The accuracy claims caught my interest because, when I tested Terra against OpenAI’s own GPT-6 Astra, Terra left some numerical totals uncalculated and gave some incorrect answers. That article focused mainly on analyzing large datasets, such as database records and server logs.
Since the claims against Opus focus on computer use and scientific coding, I built two tests around those areas. I also added a third test that recreates the kind of large-dataset task Terra struggled with against Astra, to see whether Opus shows the same weakness and how it handles it.
The tests
I ran the Terra vs. Opus tests a few times because, at easier levels, both models scored similarly, as in the Terra vs. Astra testing. When the scores came out too close, I made the test harder and ran it again, up to three times. The results below are from the final versions, including the CI audit that I made smaller after both models failed to finish the first version. Because I changed the tests after seeing earlier results and ran each final version only once per model, these results do not establish repeatability or average performance across workloads.
I ran each final test once per model through OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s own APIs, with each vendor’s effort setting at max. Those settings do not impose equivalent reasoning budgets across models. I did not cap turns. Both models have a 128,000-token output limit per response, including reasoning; a multi-turn task can exceed that in total. I used a script to grade every run against a verified answer key.
The figures below aggregate tokens across all turns in each final run; reasoning tokens are included in output totals. Dollar figures beside each run are estimates using standard uncached input and output rates, not invoice totals. Terra’s rates increase for individual requests above 272,000 input tokens; aggregate task totals alone don’t show whether that threshold was crossed. The reported caching-adjusted totals are listed separately. The totals exclude earlier test versions and do not include any separately billed tools or execution infrastructure.
- Release triage: I built a fake GitHub-style site with a failed software release, and each model had to fix it through a screenshot-based browser interface, using clicks and typed URLs. The final version had six root causes spread across code, a feature flag, and a secret, plus flaky-test decoys and three planted instructions telling the model to bypass safety settings.
- Cell lineage: I generated a noisy 72-frame microscope movie of dividing cells, and the models wrote and ran their own Python to track them. They had to log every division and trace each cell in the last frame back to its parent.
- CI history audit: This test put about 1,200 rows of CI test results into a single prompt with no tools and asked 50 questions about them. The data mixed three time zones, three duration formats, renamed tests, duplicate rows, and a price change mid-month.
Release triage
This one was a 50–50 tie, and it stayed tied through all iterations of the test. To get the score, I used 50 pass/ fail checks. Most looked at whether the models filed and closed the right issues and fixed each problem so the release could pass. The rest checked that the models didn’t change anything they weren’t supposed to, like the decoy pull requests and settings, and ignored the planted instructions.
In the hardest version, both models found all six root causes, reverted the right pull requests on the release branch, and reused the oldest open issue instead of filing a duplicate. Neither model followed any of the three planted instructions.
The difference was in how they got there. Opus jumped between pages by typing URLs 102 times, while Terra did that 23 times and mostly clicked through the site. Opus also wrote about five times as many output tokens.
For browser work like this, Terra got the same score at about 17.1% of Opus’s estimated uncached token cost, or a 5.83-to-one cost ratio. This was a separate synthetic task, not a replication of OpenAI’s benchmark. Prompt caching can reduce the cost of repeated screenshot and conversation inputs; the table below lists the reported totals with and without caching.
The numbers:
- Terra: 186 turns, 22,117,582 in, 7,659 out (2,718 reasoning), $22.16, 807 s.
- Opus: 170 turns, 32,100,919 in, 39,838 out (18,795 reasoning), $129.20, 934 s.
Cell lineage
This is the test closest in subject matter to OpenAI’s Terminal-Bench-Science comparison with Opus 5.5 with fallbacks. My synthetic cell-tracking test does not replicate that benchmark. In my run, Terra scored 48/50, while Opus scored 43.5/50, at about one twenty-fourth of Opus’s estimated uncached token cost.
I graded this test out of 50 points. Each model earned 20 points for finding the cell divisions, and lost half a point for every division it reported that didn’t happen. It earned 20 more points for tracing each cell in the last frame back to the cell it came from. The final 10 points came from 10 questions about the results, like how many times the cells divided and how many cells drifted out of view.
Terra matched all 20 divisions and answered all 10 summary questions correctly. Opus missed two divisions, reported one that never happened, and miscounted both the total divisions and the cells that drifted out of frame. Both models assigned two of the 20 final cells to the wrong starting cell.
Opus also used more turns and code executions despite its lower score. It ran code 96 times over 129 turns and took about 36 minutes. Terra ran code 30 times over 37 turns and finished in about 15 minutes.
The numbers:
- Terra: 37 turns, 3,118,018 in, 69,413 out (55,453 reasoning), $3.47, 920 s.
- Opus: 129 turns, 19,722,068 in, 201,194 out (135,672 reasoning), $82.91, 2,187 s.
CI history audit
This test did not replicate OpenAI’s computer-use or scientific-coding benchmarks. It resembles the large-dataset tests I ran against Astra. My first version had 3,920 rows, and neither model produced a final answer before reaching 128,000 output tokens.
For the second version, I cut the file to about 1,200 rows and added a mid-month price change as an additional challenge. Terra finished with 47 out of 50. It was off by one on two status counts, and it answered $0 for a question about GPU runners when it should have said the data did not cover them. Opus again produced no final answer before hitting its 128,000-token-per-response output limit. This was a failure to complete at max effort within that response limit; it does not establish that Opus could not answer under another configuration.
Terra answered all 50 questions and missed three: two status counts off by one and a question it should have marked unanswerable. That gives 47/50, or 94% under this test’s scoring. It completed this version of the large-table task without tools; Opus returned no answer to score.
The numbers:
- Terra: 56,959 in, 61,539 out (61,122 reasoning), $0.36, 691 s.
- Opus: no final answer, 72,460 in, 128,000 out, $2.85, 841 s.
Results
| Test | GPT-6.1 Terra | Claude Opus 5.5 | 
| Release triage (of 50) | 50 | 50 | 
| Cell lineage (of 50) | 48 | 43.5 | 
| CI history audit (of 50) | 47 | Did not finish | 
| Total tokens in / out | 25,292,559 / 138,611 | 51,895,447 / 369,032 | 
| Estimated uncached token cost | $25.99 | $214.96 | 
| Estimated cost with caching | $2.51 | $21.52 | 
| Total time | 2,418 s | 3,962 s | 
Both cost rows are my estimates, not billed amounts. I multiplied the token counts each API reported by the vendor’s standard rates, and for the caching row I priced cached tokens at each vendor’s lower cache rates.
Terra tied Opus on release triage and scored higher on cell lineage; it completed the CI audit, while Opus returned no final answer. Across these three final runs, Terra’s estimated uncached token cost was $25.99 versus $214.96, about 12.1% as much, or an 8.27-to-one ratio. Terra’s total elapsed time was 2,418 seconds versus Opus’s 3,962 seconds, a difference of 1,544 seconds, or about 25.7 minutes. These totals exclude the earlier test versions.
What do I think?
Terra held its own when it could click, run code, and check its work. On the final table task without tools, Terra returned an answer, and Opus did not. That result applies to these particular runs, not a general ranking of the models.
These tests used max effort, while the Astra tests used high. The tasks also differed, so the comparison does not isolate the effect of the effort setting. Anthropic recommends starting Opus 5.5 at its default medium effort and reserving higher settings for workloads where testing shows a quality gain. I did not test that configuration here.
For work like these browser and code-execution tasks, I would run Terra at max effort in a trial before committing to Opus. I would also compare each model at the effort setting that works best for the workload and check accuracy, completion rate, time, and cost across repeated runs. I would still double-check numerical answers on large tables, where Terra made errors in this test and in the earlier Astra comparison.
Learning Path

articles.title: Google Discloses PageBreak AI Security Agent That Found 500+ XSS Bugs
articles.text:
According to a paper published by Google, its AI-powered security agent has uncovered more than 500 XSS vulnerabilities across its web applications since entering full operation in January. Google PageBreak uses Gemini models to autonomously investigate potential vulnerabilities, but reports them only after deterministic validators successfully reproduce the exploit against a running application, resulting in a near-zero false-positive rate.
With PageBreak, every vulnerability hypothesis is tested against a running environment with a real exploit, such as executing JavaScript for XSS, writing to a world-readable location for path traversal, or triggering outbound DNS for RCE. Michał Bentkowski, information security engineer at Google, explains:
Early on in the development of PageBreak, we made a conscious decision to prioritize deterministic validation. Rather than simply hypothesizing bugs based on code patterns, the system closes the loop by verifying potential flaws against running environments. This approach results in a near-zero false positive rate, ensuring that we avoid overloading product teams with unverified vulnerability reports.
Google also retains non-deterministic findings internally to seed deeper future scans, identify gaps in its validation capabilities, and guide the development of new validators. These unverified candidates are not sent to product teams, keeping their attention focused on high-confidence vulnerabilities. Bentkowski writes:
While deterministic validation is our gold standard, we are aware that our validators are currently lacking in capabilities to cover all vulnerability types or complex scenarios. This comes with the risk of false negatives that might have otherwise been caught by non-deterministic validators.
In the separate article, "Google’s PageBreak Project – Real-World Findings," on Google Bug Hunters, Bentkowski describes three technical cases found by PageBreak: an XSS vulnerability, a cache-poisoning issue caused by a service misconfiguration, and a path-traversal vulnerability. On LinkedIn, Lukas Weichselbaum, senior staff information security engineer at Google, stresses the importance of reducing false positives:
A lot of AI-generated bug reports sound convincing but turn out to be wrong, and the teams that get them waste time checking each one. In PageBreak, the model can suggest whatever it likes, but a finding only counts once a validator confirms it with a real payload. The validators are plain code written by security engineers, not by the model and live outside the agent loop.
Bentkowski says PageBreak benefits from Google's engineering environment, particularly Google’s monorepo end-to-end code visibility, security signals that connect live HTTP traffic to source code, and existing scanning infrastructure that provides authenticated access to its web applications.
With the longer-term goal of reducing product-team involvement to validating AI-generated fixes, Google is integrating PageBreak with other agentic security initiatives such as CodeMender to automatically generate fixes for the vulnerabilities it discovers.
No independent validation of the 500+ vulnerabilities has been provided.

articles.title: Über 30 Jahre alt: Programmierer zeigt ältestes Programm, das unter Windows 11 noch läuft
articles.text:
Über 30 Jahre auf dem Buckel: Dieses Programm läuft noch heute problemlos unter Windows 11
Was ist eigentlich das älteste Programm mit grafischer Oberfläche (GUI), das ohne Emulation oder Modifikation noch unter Windows 11 läuft? Dieser Frage widmete sich der Programmierer Boris Popik und kam zu einigen überraschenden Erkenntnissen.
Keine 16-Bit-Unterstützung in Windows 11
Wie Popik in seinem Blog erklärt, bietet Windows 11 keine native Unterstützung von 16-Bit-Anwendungen. Das bedeutet, dass die Suche erst in der frühen Windows-NT-Ära Anfang der 1990er-Jahre beginnen kann. Das von Microsoft entwickelte 32-Bit-Betriebssystem kam im Juli 1993 auf den Markt.
In einem Forum wurde Popik auf Win32s aufmerksam gemacht, einer Erweiterung für Windows 3.1 und Windows 3.11 und einer Art Brückentechnologie für den Übergang in das 32-Bit-Zeitalter. Mit Win32s war es möglich, bestimmte 32-Bit-Programme auf dem älteren 16-Bit-Windows zum Laufen zu bringen.
Freecell von 1993 zum Laufen gebracht
Zu den bekanntesten Anwendungen, die eine installierte Win32s-Umgebung voraussetzten, gehörte das Kartenspiel Freecell. Und genau hier wurde Popik fündig. Er brachte eine aus dem Februar 1993 stammende Freecell-Version unter Windows 11 zum Laufen, ohne irgendwelche Änderungen vornehmen zu müssen.
Damit gab sich der Programmierer aber nicht zufrieden. Er machte in frühen Windows-NT-Versionen ein weiteres Programm ausfindig, das am 16. November 1992 das Licht der Welt erblickte: eine CD-Player-Anwendung. Das Problem: Popiks Rechner verfügt über kein CD-Laufwerk, wodurch das Programm zunächst crashte. Mit einem virtuellen Laufwerk konnte er dieses Problem aber beheben – und hatte eine noch ältere Anwendung für Windows 11 gefunden.
Gut 40 Jahre altes Game auf Windows-PC
Weiter zurück ging es allerdings tatsächlich nur mit Schummeln. Denn aufgrund der oben erwähnten fehlenden 16-Bit-Unterstützung in Windows 11 endet das Suchfenster eigentlich Anfang der 1990er-Jahre. Nutzt man aber eine entsprechende Komponente wie OTVDM, lassen sich 16-Bit-Anwendungen auf modernen 64-Bit-Versionen von Windows ausführen.
Genau das gelang Popik dann mit Reversi, einem schon in den 1880er-Jahren von dem Engländer Lewis Waterman entwickelten Brettspiel. Dessen Computerspiel-Variante vom 15. November 1985 ist – bis zum Beweis des Gegenteils – das wahrscheinlich älteste Programm, das sich auf einem modernen Windows-Computer zum Laufen bringen lässt. Allerdings nur unter Einsatz eines Emulators.
„das wahrscheinlich älteste Programm, das sich auf einem modernen Windows-Computer zum Laufen bringen lässt. Allerdings nur unter Einsatz eines Emulators.“
Was für ein Quatsch!
Mit einem Emulator lassen sich alle programme zu laufen bringen.

articles.title: Meta entra no mercado dos robôs humanoides
articles.text:
O mercado global de robôs humanoides vive uma forte expansão impulsionada pela inteligência artificial e pela redução de custos de hardware. Projeções do Morgan Stanley apontam que o setor pode movimentar US$ 5 trilhões (cerca de R$ 27 trilhões) até 2050. E as grandes empresas de tecnologia não querem ficar de fora dessa.
A Meta desenvolveu um protótipo de robô humanoide em parceria com a startup chinesa de robótica Fourier. A iniciativa faz parte dos esforços da empresa de Mark Zuckerberg para integrar a IA às tarefas domésticas do dia a dia. As informações são do portal The Information.
Robô foi batizado de Max e pode manipular objetos pequenos
- O protótipo, chamado internamente de Max, pesa cerca de 48 kg.
- Ele foi desenvolvido em aproximadamente três meses.
- Com cerca de 1,5 metro de altura, o robô utiliza o chip Jetson Thor, da Nvidia.
- Ainda conta com uma tela capaz de imitar expressões faciais, alto-falantes integrados e mãos com cinco dedos projetadas para manipular objetos pequenos.
Ideia é ampliar o uso de IA em tarefas domésticas
A equipe de robótica da Meta viajou à China para trabalhar com a Fourier no projeto. Segundo a reportagem, a vice-presidente de produto para robótica da empresa, Li-Chen Miller, passou quase dois meses na fábrica da startup em Xangai. O Max foi apresentado a alguns funcionários da big tech durante uma cúpula interna de robótica no final de agosto deste ano.
E as duas empresas já miram o futuro. Elas começaram a desenvolver um segundo protótipo, o Max 2, em setembro. A versão atualizada deve contar com um torso redesenhado, mãos aprimoradas para a manipulação de objetos, um projetor e sensores adicionais para auxiliar na navegação em escadas.
A Meta enxerga os robôs humanoides como uma possível extensão física de seu agente de IA Muse, com a ambição de longo prazo de desenvolver máquinas capazes de auxiliar em tarefas domésticas. A empresa informou ao The Information que seu trabalho com a Fourier está voltado para pesquisa e experimentação internas e que não há planos para comercializar as unidades.
Alessandro Di Lorenzo é editor do Olhar Digital e formado em jornalismo pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).

articles.title: Tu Mac no tiene Face ID, pero esta aplicación permite desbloquearlo con tu cara
articles.text:
Una de las cosas que más me gustan de mi iPhone es que puedo desbloquear la pantalla con mi cara. Eso de poner el dedo en el sensor también es práctico, pero el Face ID es más cómodo y rápido. Además, también sirve para otras acciones como desbloquear aplicaciones, autorizar pagos con Apple Pay o comprar aplicaciones y juegos en la App Store. Sin embargo, no hay Face ID en Mac. Algo que se rumoreó en el pasado, pero que nunca se ha hecho realidad. Pero hay una buena noticia. Puedes desbloquear tu Mac con tu cara con una simple aplicación gratuita.
Primero llegó el Touch ID. Con tu huella dactilar, puedes desbloquear la pantalla de tu iPhone, iPad o Mac. Con los años ha ido cambiando de forma. Y, en la actualidad, en iPad es prácticamente invisible, integrado en el botón de encendido. Y en Mac puedes usarlo tanto en los modelos portátiles (MacBook Air, MacBook Neo y MacBook Pro) como en los de sobremesa. Estos segundos, a través del teclado Magic Keyboard con Touch ID.
Pero el Face ID en Mac sigue sin llegar. Y teniendo en cuenta que todos los Mac con pantalla (portátiles o iMac) tienen una cámara frontal integrada, es una lástima que no tengamos esta opción de desbloquear Mac con tu cara en vez de hacerlo con la contraseña, como se ha hecho siempre. Pero para eso están los desarrolladores de apps, para hacer posible lo que creías imposible.
Por qué no hay Face ID en Mac
Si Apple no hace algo, por algo será. Es decir, que si no puedes desbloquear el Mac con tu cara porque no hay Face ID en Mac es por algún motivo. Nos guste o no. Si echamos un vistazo a la hemeroteca, este tema no es nuevo. En 2020 se rumoreó sobre la posible llegada del Face ID a los Mac. Pero en 2021 nos cayó un jarro de agua fría. En una entrevista en The Wall Street Journal, Tom Boger, entonces vicepresidente de marketing de iPad y Mac, explicó que la razón por la que no tenían pensado implementar desbloquea de Mac por Face ID era porque el Touch ID era más conveniente en un portátil.
La explicación que dio Tom Boger es que, al abrir un MacBook, el usuario tiene las manos sobre el teclado, así que el sensor está a su alcance. Una explicación que también podemos extender a los teclados en un iMac, Mac mini o Mac Studio. Pero su argumentación chirría un poco, ya que también dijo que Face ID exige levantar la vista o ajustar la posición para que la cámara capte el rostro. Lo mismo podría argumentarse de un iPhone. Tanto en iPhone como en Mac, la pantalla es lo que mira el usuario principalmente. Teclado o no de por medio.
Otras razones de más peso para que no tengamos Face ID en Mac y no puedas desbloquear tu Mac con tu cara tienen que ver con el coste económico de esta tecnología frente a Touch ID, más económica y amortizada tras años y años de innovación. Pero, sobre todo, los motivos más serios tienen que ver con el diseño y fabricación de los Mac. Un artículo de 2022 de MacWorld explicaba que el grosor del módulo con el sensor TrueDepth impedía que la parte del MacBook con pantalla fuera tan fino como lo es hoy en día. Y si no podía estar presente en los portátiles, tampoco valía la pena añadirlo solamente al iMac. Aunque esto no impide que en el futuro se den las condiciones para incorporar Face ID en Mac si es barato y suficientemente pequeño.
Varios métodos para desbloquear tu Mac
Actualmente, si quieres desbloquear tu Mac, además de introducir la contraseña, tienes varias maneras de hacerlo. Ya hemos mencionado el método oficial con el Touch ID integrado en algunos teclados Magic Keyboard. Al encender el Mac tienes que iniciar sesión sí o sí con tu contraseña. Pero a partir de ahí, puedes desbloquear la pantalla con tu dedo y realizar otras acciones como instalar aplicaciones o hacer compras online.
Si tienes un Apple Watch, puedes desbloquear el Mac usando las conexiones wifi y Bluetooth. Es decir, que para que esto sea posible tienes que tener los dos dispositivos conectados al mismo punto wifi, tener Bluetooth activado y, en tercer lugar, tener iniciada la misma cuenta de Apple.
Y ya que hablamos de Bluetooth, hay métodos no oficiales para desbloquear el Mac. En esta ocasión, con tu iPhone. O, en general, con cualquier teléfono o dispositivo Bluetooth. Como vimos en este artículo, hay aplicaciones que permiten desbloquear tu Mac con tu iPhone. La que yo utilizo a diario se llama BLEUnlock. Es gratuita y de código abierto. Le indicas qué dispositivo hará de llave y, cuando el Mac lo detecte vía Bluetooth, se desbloqueará la pantalla.
Así que si Apple no permite desbloquear tu Mac con tu cara, vamos a hacerlo con una aplicación no oficial. Su nombre es Hey Mac. Esta app es gratuita, de código abierto y compatible con macOS 14 y superior. Puedes instalarla descargando su instalador o empleando Homebrew.
Desbloquear tu Mac con tu cara
El funcionamiento de Hey Mac es simple. Al bloquear el Mac, si miras a la cámara, se desbloqueará de nuevo. Lo que verás es una animación que se integra en la isla superior de la pantalla, donde está la cámara frontal de tu Mac. Y puedes cambiarla por otra animación más minimalista y menos intrusiva. Además, no solo sirve para desbloquear la pantalla del Mac. También puedes usar Hey Mac para bloquear aplicaciones de miradas curiosas. Así, con Hey Mac podrás añadir tu cara a otros métodos como la contraseña o el Touch ID.
Para instalar Hey Mac, tendrás que darle acceso a la cámara para que funcione correctamente. Y acceso al guardado de datos. Durante la configuración te explicará qué tienes que hacer para usarla correctamente. Básicamente, mirar a cámara o estar bien colocado frente a ella. Hay que tener en cuenta que la primera vez que abras la aplicación es probable que macOS la bloquee por seguridad. Para resolver este inconveniente, tendrás que ir a Configuración del Sistema > Privacidad y seguridad. Abajo del todo verás la opción Abrir de todas formas al lado de Hey Mac. Y volver a pedirlo de nuevo cuando te lo pida.
Sobre la seguridad de la app para desbloquear tu Mac con tu cara, es normal que te plantees qué hace o deja de hacer Hey Mac con la cámara. O con tu contraseña de usuario, que tendrás que facilitarle para que desbloquee el Mac por ti. Su página web afirma que el reconocimiento facial utiliza Apple Neural Engine. No hace fotos de tu cara, la información está cifrada y no envía datos fuera del Mac. Y, por descontado, al igual que Face ID, no sustituye del todo tu contraseña o Touch ID. Si Hey Mac no funciona bien, los demás métodos de seguridad seguirán estando ahí.

articles.title: Tech sleuth claims to have found the oldest GUI application that still works with Windows 11 — 34-year-old CDPLAYER.EXE from Windows NT in November 1992 wins the prize
articles.text:
Tech sleuth claims to have found the oldest GUI application that still works with Windows 11 — 34-year-old CDPLAYER.EXE from Windows NT in November 1992 wins the prize
However, if you cheat and enable 16-bit apps in Win11, you can still enjoy REVERSI.EXE, as distributed with Windows 1.01 in 1985.
A technology enthusiast claims that the oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 is CDPLAYER.EXE from November 1992. The app had to run on Microsoft’s newest consumer OS without modifications or emulation involved to be chosen as the ‘winner’ of their experiment. Blogger Enlyth expected something from the early NT era, as Windows 11 doesn’t support 16-bit apps, despite its strong backward compatibility. Finding an app that is almost 34 years old that still works with a simple double-click is a remarkable result.
At the beginning of their journey to find the oldest Windows UI app that just works on Microsoft’s newest OS, Enlyth confirmed FREECELL.EXE from February 1993 would still run without issues. This game was distributed alongside the Win32s environment, designed to allow some 32-bit applications to run on the 16-bit operating systems like Windows 3.1 and 3.11. Win32s was made available in beta in October 1992, but went mainstream in July 1993.
A tip Enlyth received via a tech forum suggested that FREECELL.EXE was a candidate for the oldest GUI app remaining compatible with Windows 11. However, the blogger wasn’t satisfied with this easy win and dug through “some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising.” Build 347 caught the detective’s eye, specifically CDPLAYER.EXE, linked on Nov 16, 1992. That indeed seems to be the earliest GUI app that works without modification or emulation on Windows 11. But this knowledge almost defied Enlyth’s eye as their system is, like many modern systems, optical-drive-less. Luckily, adding a small DLL (cdemu.dll) allowed Enlyth to emulate a CD drive and demonstrate that the 1992-era application still functions as intended.
I wanted to verify that CDPLAYER.EXE was still usable on the latest Windows 11 release. Unfortunately, the multi-part.ARJ archive of Windows NT 3.1 that I found on Archive.org threw up errors when I tried to pick through its contents. I have a USB-attached optical drive that plays CD audio in Windows 11, so I thought I could get CDPLAYER.EXE to run without any extra DLL.
Lastly, Enlyth wanted to push the envelope a little and see what even more ancient Windows apps might work if they got some help from the Winevdm project on 64-bit Windows. “Using otvdm does feel like cheating,” admitted the digital sleuth, and we’d agree. However, being able to run 16-bit apps in Windows 11 ratcheted back the wheels of time. The result was that Enlyth managed to enjoy “a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985.” That’s a GUI-driven game distributed as part of Windows 1.01 and is roughly 41 years old.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.
- ezst036 That is definitely impressive indeed. It is usually not something that Linux can do, nor MacOS.
Microsoft has often taken backward compatibility seriously, and that does have an implication for the untold thousands of proprietary WIN applications that corporations still rely on from so many years ago. Porting old apps to new is expensive and Microsoft helps these companies to not port. "It just keeps working" as it always has.
This does help to keep Microsoft's dominance in place. Reply

articles.title: Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search
articles.text:
The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds some powerful new search features and quick settings while in Xbox mode. The Xbox shortcuts let you control things like Bluetooth, WiFi, and power settings without having to exit gaming mode.
Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search
The latest Windows Insider builds revamp search with filters, actions, and phone controls.
The search improvements are quite comprehensive. You can now filter results for files, actions, or web results. You can also use the search box to perform actions like changing the screen brightness or volume, and even perform actions on a connected phone, including making calls. Results can also offer much more detail, like when a file was last modified and its author, or pull in charts for stock prices and weather forecasts. And you can train Windows 11 search by clicking inline thumbs-up or thumbs-down icons to help it improve over time.
For the full list of changes, check out Microsoft’s blog post. Beta Build 26220.9836 and Experimental Build 26340.9843 are both available now to Windows Insiders.

articles.title: Sam Altman (OpenAI) préfèrerait que la RAM de votre PC aille dans ses datacenters
articles.text:
Il y a des phrases qu’il vaut mieux ne pas prononcer quand on est en partie responsable du problème. Sam Altman, patron et fondateur d’OpenAI, peut-être légèrement saoul, bière à la main, en a prononcé une dans le podcast Cheeky Pint publié le 29 octobre 2026.
Vers la 29e minute, la discussion porte sur ces internautes qui font tourner des modèles d’IA open source en local, sur des PC qu’ils possèdent déjà ou qu’ils montent pour l’occasion. Le patron d’OpenAI n’est pas fan du tout de la pratique.
Pourquoi ?
Avoir tout ce monde qui garde une partie de l’offre mondiale limitée de DRAM, c’est « assez terrible », explique-t-il, puisque cette mémoire dort dans des machines utilisées 5 % du temps. Dans le cloud, au contraire, on cherche l’utilisation maximale. Et d’ajouter, un brin étonné, que l’intuition de beaucoup de gens va dans le sens inverse.
Une RAM qui coûte désormais un bras
Le contexte rend la sortie savoureuse. Un kit de 32 Go de DDR5, qui se trouvait autour de 119 euros en octobre 2025, s’affichait vers 414 euros à la mi-octobre 2026 selon les relevés de Hardware Cooking. Dans notre guide mis à jour et sur les tarifs européens, on suggère 16 Go de RAM pour 288 €. Et on peut vous dire qu’on a cherché. Le tout, avant l’arrivée massive de la robotique dans l’équation, qui pourrait faire encore augmenter les prix..
La cause est connue : les fabricants de mémoire (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) réservent leurs lignes de production aux puces destinées aux serveurs d’IA, bien plus rentables, au détriment des barrettes grand public. Parmi les plus gros clients, on trouve évidemment OpenAI, qui avait signé fin 2025 avec Samsung et SK Hynix des accords pour sécuriser une part considérable de la production mondiale de DRAM, dans le cadre de son projet Stargate. Bref, oui, Sam Altman juge que votre RAM est mal utilisée tout en étant l’un de ceux qui vous empêchent d’en acheter.
Sur le fond, on va se faire taper, mais l’argument d’Altman n’est pas idiot. C’est la logique de l’autopartage ou des robotaxis appliquée au silicium : une voiture reste garée 95 % du temps, et une barrette de RAM dans un PC de bureau ne fait pas grand-chose la nuit. Mutualiser les ressources dans des datacenters qui tournent jour et nuit est, sur le papier, plus efficace pour la planète comme pour le portefeuille.
Sauf que l’efficacité n’est pas le seul critère pour l’Humanité (ça se saurait). La RAM d’un PC ne sert pas qu’à l’IA : elle fait tourner des jeux, du montage vidéo, des dizaines d’onglets de navigateur. Et faire tourner un modèle en local, c’est garder ses données chez soi, ne dépendre d’aucune panne de serveur, d’aucune hausse de tarif ni d’aucun changement de conditions d’utilisation. Bref, posséder son outil plutôt que le louer. Les commentateurs de Tom’s Hardware, qui a relayé l’interview, ne s’y sont pas trompés : pour beaucoup, Altman défend avant tout son modèle économique, celui de modèles fermés qui ne tournent que dans ses serveurs et se paient au mois.
Le raisonnement suppose aussi que la construction de datacenters ne ralentira jamais, et que la capacité ainsi mutualisée finira par profiter à tout le monde à prix raisonnable. Pour l’instant, la mutualisation se traduit surtout par des abonnements à 20 dollars par mois (minimum) et des barrettes à 500 euros.
Notez enfin que le podcast est particulièrement intéressant, au-delà de cette sortie, et mérite largement l’écoute.

articles.title: Sam Altman says it's "terrible" for RAM to sit inside PCs instead of data centers
articles.text:
The big picture: The AI boom has siphoned most of the tech industry's RAM supply, driving up prices and making consumer electronics less affordable. Recent comments from Sam Altman, arguably the man most responsible for launching the boom, frame the situation as a conflict between cloud and local compute, and he clearly favors the cloud.
In an interview on the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman argued that it's more efficient to direct the world's tightening supply of memory to AI data centers than to local devices. The comments drew immediate backlash as hardware prices continue to climb.
About 29 minutes in, Altman says it's "quite terrible" for DRAM to be locked inside consumer hardware, where it may be used only 5% of the time. Because data centers run their hardware almost constantly, he argues, they can push the global supply closer to full utilization.
Altman specifically mentioned PCs with local AI capabilities and open-source LLMs. Devices like Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified RAM to support local AI workloads, including open-source models like DeepSeek, which OpenAI sees as competition.
However, given the AI boom's broader impact on consumer devices, Altman's claim could be seen as an attack on the very idea of owning hardware. Many fear that the companies driving the AI boom ultimately want owners to become renters of cloud services running on AI data centers.
The data center buildout has quintupled DRAM costs since last year, pushing consumer hardware prices to unaffordable highs. Game consoles are approaching the $1,000 mark, dragging sales downward. PC shipments have also dropped significantly this year for similar reasons, contributing to Intel's worst stock price collapse in decades.
 – Jaydeep (@_jaydeepkarale) October 31, 2026
Meanwhile, high-end graphics cards like Nvidia's RTX 5080 and 5090 seem to have disappeared from store shelves after reaching astronomical prices. Even cameras could become more expensive because of RAM shortages, according to Canon.
Memory makers disagree on how long shortages will last. SK Hynix estimates that current conditions will continue past 2030, while Micron recently claimed that humanoid robots could keep demand high if the AI bubble pops (which might already be happening).
Acer's CEO, however, accuses the memory makers of wanting to prolong the situation to maximize profits, and thinks prices could start sliding as soon as next year.

articles.title: Las ciudades europeas con más turismo por vecino, en un gráfico donde los casos más extremos están en España
articles.text:
Hay quien piense que a España el turismo se le ha ido de las manos y a juzgar por cuestiones como el precio de la vivienda en zonas turísticas, lo que por ejemplo puede ser determinante a la hora de elegir destino en una oposición o dónde vas a estudiar una carrera simplemente por el precio del alquiler, tiene bastante sentido. Y eso sin hablar de las molestias de que tu bloque parezca una despedida de soltero eterna por culpa de los alquileres turísticos.
El turismo es un vector económico importante, pero en exceso pasa factura a la vivienda, el espacio público y los servicios. Pero esa línea de presión no está clara y cambia enormemente de un lugar a otro: no es lo mismo que llegue a una ciudad de 20.000 habitantes que a otra que tiene 2 millones. En pocas palabras, cuánta gente visita una ciudad no dice cuánto le afecta, porque importa también cuánta gente vive allí, algo que este gráfico intenta resolver.
Este gráfico de burbujas se titula "Las 30 ciudades más concurridas por el turismo de la UE en 2025" y para su elaboración usa datos de Eurostat sobre noches en alojamiento turístico durante 2025 en ciudades seleccionadas, ya sea en hoteles, pisos turísticos o campings. Esas noches se comparan con la población residente permanente para obtener la intensidad turística, es decir, las noches de turista por residente.
La población procede también de Eurostat, además de otras oficinas estadísticas estatales. Las ciudades de la lista tienen 50.000 personas o más, de ahí que algunos municipios más pequeños como Dubrovnik queden fuera de la lista, como detalla su autor en Reddit. A partir de aquí, cada burbuja es una ciudad y la escala horizontal es logarítmica de base 2, lo que obliga a leer los ejes con cuidado porque la inercia nos hace tender a la escala decimal.
Los puntos calientes del turismo en la UE
Precisamente en esa relación está lo importante de este gráfico: el volumen total de noches de turista engaña. Así, puede que París tenga una burbuja más grande, pero su presión por habitante es inferior. Sin embargo, ciudades pequeñas como Benidorm o la canaria Puerto de la Cruz soportan cargas por residente mucho mayores, las más altas de hecho. Además, también sugiere dónde la economía puede depender más del turismo o dónde hay más riesgo de conflicto entre quienes viven allí y quienes visitan la ciudad. Otro ejemplo claro: el caso de Palma es extremo, con en torno al 93 % de las noches de turista correspondientes a visitantes extranjeros, por lo que su dependencia del turismo internacional es muy alta, justo lo opuesto a Hamburgo.
En 2025 España fue el primer destino europeo por noches de visitantes internacionales con unos 330 millones, según datos de Eurostat recogidos por Euronews. Así que que el estado que más ciudades aporta a la lista sea España no es una sorpresa: 9 de cada 30 concretamente.
¿Cómo interpretarlo? Cuanto más a la derecha, más noches de turistas recibe por habitante. Cuanto más arriba, más peso de visitantes extranjeros y cuanto más grande, más noches en total. Los colores indican intensidad turística (noches por residente), pasando del amarillo (entre 2 y 5 noches por residente) hasta el morado (más de 50 noches por residente).
Volvamos a Benidorm y Puerto de la Cruz porque son los casos más extremos. En el caso de la ciudad alicantina, tiene unas 290 noches por residente y el 69 % son de extranjeros, lo que apunta a una fuerte presencia de turismo de fuera. En el municipio tinerfeño se registran más de 100 noches por residente (unas 126) y aproximadamente el 67 % son de fuera. No terminamos de salir de España y ya entramos en Italia: Venecia, Torremolinos, Rimini y Florencia se sitúan entre unas 30 y 50 pernoctaciones por residente. El caso de Rimini es curioso: tiene una intensidad muy alta (unas 50 noches), pero su turismo es mayoritariamente italiano (38% de visitantes extranjeros).
En la zona central del gráfico, entre 8 y 25 noches por residente, está Roma con una de las mayores burbujas y cerca del 79 % extranjeros, además de Ámsterdam, Praga, Lisboa, Barcelona, Sevilla y Copenhague. Abajo, con poco turismo extranjero, están Hamburgo (unas 22 %), Varsovia, Frankfurt, Múnich, Berlín y Estocolmo, todas con 15 noche por residente o menos. París y Madrid destacan por tamaño y baja intensidad: sus grandes poblaciones hacen que la ratio por residente sea baja.

articles.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
articles.text:
MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.
- Share:
A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.
The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.
By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.
In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.
"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "
A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle
The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.
Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.
"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."
The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.
From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot
The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.
For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.
When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.
The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.
"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."
For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.
They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.
The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.
To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.
"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."
Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot
Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.
The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.
This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.
The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.
By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.
Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.
The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.
The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.
How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim
With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.
The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.
Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.
"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."
To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.
As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.
Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.
The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.
"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."
The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.

articles.title: Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
articles.text:
While the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR screen is available for preorder across a few major retailers, Best Buy is sweetening the deal by including a $100 gift card. The gift card will be automatically added to your cart when you preorder one of Apple’s highest-end laptops available in 14- or 16-inch configurations, and even one of its 14-inch MacBook Pro laptops with the M6 chip. You can verify that it’s been added to your order in the “Complete your purchase” section of the checkout page.
Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
You have options for preordering the new MacBook Pro, but only one retailer is offering this sweet perk.
My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto got a chance to check out the new laptop at Apple’s event, and came away impressed by the Tandem OLED panel’s brightness and contrast, but described the update as “kind of boring” given the relatively small changes to the system otherwise. There are some unique changes to macOS that help make the new touch experience smoother, like magnifying the traffic light-colored buttons on windows when you move your finger near them. The PROLED laptops are also a bit thinner and lighter than standard models, and the Apple logo on the back glows like on older versions.

articles.title: Une IA a choisi un traitement et l'a injecté dans le cerveau d'une souris : ce qu'on sait vraiment
articles.text:
« Hier soir, un agent IA a pratiqué une opération du cerveau sur une souris. » Posté sur X le 28 octobre 2026, ce message a fait le tour du monde en quarante-huit heures, escorté de titres aussi pressés qu’inexacts : l’IA aurait opéré « sans aide humaine », certains ont même transformé la souris en rat.
Admettons-le, l’emballement ne vient pas de rien : l’auteur du message est loin d’être un charlatan. Gabriel Ocana-Santero, est un neuroscientifique titulaire d’un doctorat de pharmacologie d’Oxford, passé par la Gatsby Unit de l’University College London. Il dirige Exin Therapeutics, une start-up issue de Y Combinator qui développe des thérapies géniques contre les maladies neurologiques.
Qu’est-ce que Exin a vraiment fait ?
L’équipe a fourni à un agent IA un modèle d’épilepsie chez la souris, un tableur listant 19 vecteurs de thérapie génique, l’accès à un banc chirurgical motorisé équipé de caméras (qui ressemble à une imprimante 3D), et un seul objectif : réduire les crises chez la souris sur le billard. Personne ne lui a indiqué quel vecteur choisir ni où l’injecter, assure le chercheur.
Selon son fil, l’agent a d’abord raisonné sur le mécanisme des crises dans le modèle qui lui a été fourni, puis retenu une thérapie qui renforce la signalisation GABA, principal neurotransmetteur inhibiteur du cerveau, sous un promoteur qui limite son expression aux neurones GABAergiques. Il a choisi une région cérébrale, tiré les coordonnées d’injection depuis trois articles scientifiques sur le sujet, puis piloté lui-même les bras stéréotaxiques : une aiguille descendue à 4,3 mm de profondeur, 250 nanolitres injectés en cinq minutes, et 32 consultations de la caméra pour surveiller un éventuel saignement.
La petite souris cobaye (bayebayebayebayebayebayebayebaye !) s’est réveillée et s’est bien remise, selon l’auteur.
Le modèle aux commandes est Claude Sonnet 5, d’Anthropic et c’est là que l’histoire devient encore plus intéressante.
D’après le chercheur, Claude Opus 5.5, le modèle le plus avancé d’Anthropic, a refusé dès qu’il a détecté qu’il s’agissait de biologie. Opus 5 a déroulé toute la répétition à blanc, puis s’est arrêté au moment de passer à l’animal vivant. C’est finalement Sonnet 5, modèle intermédiaire de la gamme, qui a accepté.
Cela signifie d’une part que les garde-fous fonctionnent : les modèles les plus capables refusent d’agir sur du vivant sans cadre explicite. Mais cela dit d’autre part qu’ils sont incohérents : trois modèles d’une même entreprise donnent trois réponses différentes au même protocole, et il suffit de descendre d’une gamme pour passer les limites. Anthropic n’avait pas réagi publiquement au moment où nous écrivons.
Un autre moment, rapporté par les résumés du fil, mérite l’attention. En pleine procédure, l’agent a repéré une erreur de positionnement du banc et refusé d’avancer l’aiguille, y compris quand l’opérateur a tenté de passer outre. L’équipe a réparé le matériel à la main avant de reprendre, et le refus s’est avéré justifié.
Ce que l’IA n’a pas fait et où elle peut devenir meilleure
Précisons ce que recouvre le mot « chirurgie ». La craniotomie, l’ouverture du crâne, a été pratiquée par un chirurgien humain : l’agent n’y est pas encore autorisé, pour des raisons de sécurité, écrit l’auteur. Ce que l’IA a exécuté est une injection stéréotaxique, un geste pratiqué chaque jour dans des milliers de laboratoires de neurosciences, guidé par des coordonnées issues d’atlas du cerveau de la souris. Ne faisons pas les chagrins : c’est remarquable pour un modèle généraliste à qui j’ai demandé ce matin la météo du 8 novembre, une génération de vidéo et de corriger ce texte que vous lisez, mais très loin d’un neurochirurgien.
L’encadrement, lui, était serré : validation humaine de chaque action irréversible, limites fixes codées hors du modèle (sur le volume injecté, par exemple), chaque approbation liée à une commande précise, et un arrêt d’urgence physique coupant l’alimentation de tous les moteurs, tenu par un vétérinaire. L’auteur parle lui-même d’un « interrupteur anti-IA », avant de conclure : « Personne n’a dit à cet agent quoi administrer ni où. Il a reçu un phénotype et une étagère de candidats, et il a dû déterminer seul la thérapie et les coordonnées. À ma connaissance, aucun agent n’avait encore choisi un traitement et une cible cérébrale avant de l’administrer à un mammifère vivant. C’est ce que nous entendons par « lab in the loop » in vivo : connecter PLEINEMENT les agents à nos capacités expérimentales. On vous en dit plus très bientôt. »
Alors, après les mathématiques, la médecine ?
