articles.title: Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts
articles.text:
“Its James Talarico. Can you please please please please pretty pretty please rush in even just $1?”
Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts
You might be receiving political texts even if you’ve never made a political donation.
“Who’s working to elect James Talarico? Marxists.”
“Wow! Wow! Wow! Mark Kelly just made a HUGE announcement!”
“We asked Ben Verlander, MLB analyst and former Tigers prospect, to record a quick video about the election this Tuesday, November 3rd.”
“See which of your friends or family members have voted in the past and remind them to vote this year.”
If any of these messages sound familiar, it’s likely because they’re part of the massive stream of text messages flooding your phone leading up to the US midterm elections on Tuesday. The scale of the issue is not entirely clear, but call-blocking company Robokiller found that 15 billion political texts were sent in 2022, thanks in part to a Supreme Court decision the year prior that made it easier to send some mass calls and texts without consent. Alex Quilici, CEO of spam protection service YouMail, has an even higher estimate of 25 billion to 30 billion political texts this year, but caveats it’s an informal approximation. The volume is about the same to 10 percent higher than in 2024, he says.
There’s some good news and some bad news about these messages, says PIRG consumer watchdog director Teresa Murray. “The bad news is that political calls and political texts are exempt from the do-not-call-list rules,” Murray says. “The good news is that the election is next Tuesday, and hopefully within a few days after that, we’ll know what the results are and there won’t be any need to have any texts, or calls, or emails anymore after that.”
There are still some things consumers can try to stem the flow of these messages blowing up their phones — but it likely won’t significantly reduce it before Tuesday.
“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts … there are going to be some scams in there”
The simplest thing you can do is send “stop” or block and report the messages as spam, which will notify your service provider of a likely spam number. That probably won’t result in any immediate change, Murray says, but if enough people report the same number in a certain period of time, the provider might begin to block it or label it as spam. You can also file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission or your state attorney general if you believe a number is using an autodialer without your consent — something that even the people behind political texts are not supposed to do. Whatever you do, Murray says, do not click any links you receive from numbers you don’t know.
“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts that are going out to support this candidate, or vote against that candidate, or vote for this issue, or whatever, there are going to be some scams in there,” Murray says. “If you want to donate money at this point, I would recommend going directly to the website for that political candidate, or for that PAC, and donating it that way.”
How did all of these campaigns get your number in the first place? If you’ve donated to a political candidate or issue group, that might seem obvious. But campaigns are also likely getting your information — including details about whether you might be likely to contribute to or vote for their candidate or issue — through data brokers that have nothing to do with politics. Data brokers collect and sell information from both public and private sources, such as public voter rolls, your online behavior observed by advertising web trackers, and loyalty programs. By collating all of this information, campaigns can try to infer your behavior, though they also might end up with outdated info, like old addresses that lead you to getting texts about a state you no longer live in (or even erroneous info that invites them for states you never lived in).
“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do?’”
“Errors in the processing of this information and the identification of individuals are very prevalent,” says Sara Geoghegan, consumer privacy program director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “Sometimes multiple people use the same device. Sometimes people have similar names. Sometimes people move. And this is such an unregulated ecosystem that there aren’t really rules in place to make sure that this is being effective and accurate, let alone free from bias, discrimination, and verified for privacy impact before processing this information.
“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do, and how many numbers do they need to block, and what are the toggle and privacy settings that they should toggle on?’” Geoghegan says. Meanwhile, “the companies that are trading in our most sensitive information are the ones who should stop harmful surveillance and the use of harmful technologies to have us better engage civically with our society, and not the other way around,” she says.
“I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”
Geoghegan worries that the harm of being bombarded with unwanted political texts isn’t just that people get annoyed, but that they stop engaging civically as a result. “Having this surveillance apparatus that invades people’s privacy and really annoys them actually pushes people away from this,” she says. “I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”
Unfortunately, you might get on some political text lists whether you engage in the civic process or not because of data brokers. Murray says the best long-term solution to minimize these spam messages is to limit how frequently you give out your phone number in general, like in an online shopping portal. If you need to give a number, you might consider using a VoIP number like a free Google Voice number, so at least you can silo those messages into another app you don’t need to frequently check or get notifications from.
Murray says she rarely gives out her personal number and limits where she gives out her Google Voice number, too. But even she has seen an uptick in political texts over the past couple of weeks. That’s likely in part because some groups may try to dial numbers in order in a certain area code, or her number could still be floating around on lists from long ago. “You can’t really do anything about the people or the businesses or the political entities that you have already shared your number with in the past,” Murray says. “But I would encourage people to just draw a line in the sand.”
Murray and Geoghegan encourage consumers to take the actions available to them to help limit the unwanted texts they receive, but they say the real solutions to the broader issue will likely come from Congress or regulators. Geoghegan says greater enforcement of existing laws could limit robocalls and texts, and Murray says concerned voters could contact their representatives about putting more pressure on the FCC to address the problems.
“Don’t get just frustrated with what you can’t change in four days, but you may be able to make a difference for the future,” Murray says. “By all means, reply to a text and say, ‘Stop.’ … But just don’t make it your life’s quest because it’s probably a fool’s errand.”

articles.title: Google Cloud für BND, MAD und Verfassungsschutz: Unsouveräner geht es nicht
articles.text:
Google-Cloud für BND und Verfassungsschutz: Warum dieser Geheimdienst-Deal ein Hohn für die digitale Souveränität ist
Die Messe schien gelesen. Nach ausgiebiger Diskussion über das Thema digitale Souveränität, um das sich lange nur auf dem Papier bemüht wurde, kam in jüngster Vergangenheit auch in der Politik endlich deutlich mehr Bewegung in das Thema. Und das trotz aggressiver Werbung für Sovereign-Cloud-Angebote von Big-Tech-Firmen. Millionenverträge mit Microsoft wurden hinterfragt. Pilotprojekte in den Verwaltungen von Schleswig-Holstein oder Berlin stellten Open Source in den Vordergrund. Die deutsche Wirtschaft bot bereitwillig Alternativen an. Das zwang sogar Microsoft, das mit Microsoft 365 eine der meistgenutzten Enterprise-Kollaborationslösungen vertreibt, dazu, sein Angebot nochmal für den europäischen Markt nachzudrehen. Ein Stück weit hatte man die US-Tech-Firmen da, wo man sie haben wollte.
Dass diese Bewegung gerade von einer Seite torpediert wird, die sich ein bisschen mehr mit Themen wie Datenschutz und Hintertüren auskennen sollte, ist fast schon bizarr. Wie die Tagesschau exklusiv berichtet, sollen die deutschen Geheimdienste BND, MAD und der Verfassungsschutz mit der ND-Cloud eine eigene Plattform zum Austausch geheimer Daten bekommen. Der Anbieter: Google. Chapeau an dieser Stelle an die Lobbyist:innen des US‑Konzerns. Bald landen also vielleicht sensibelste Daten in einem von Google konzipierten System, um die Zusammenarbeit zwischen den Nachrichtendiensten zu erleichtern. Google, das sein Geschäft mit dem Sammeln von Daten seiner Nutzenden macht.
Souveränität trotz Google? Was ND-Cloud verspricht
Um fair zu bleiben, muss man zugestehen, dass die ND-Cloud keine normale Public- oder Private-Cloud-Instanz ist, die von Google mal mehr, mal weniger kontrolliert werden kann. Vielmehr handelt es sich um eine vom Internet abgekoppelte, sogenannte Air-Gapped-Version einer Google Distributed Cloud. Aber Google-Software bleibt Google-Software. Entscheidet sich die US-Firma, Updates der ND-Cloud an Bedingungen zu knüpfen, die die Geheimdienste nicht erfüllen wollen oder können, war es das mit dem schnellen Datenaustausch.
Jetzt könnte man argumentieren, dass europäische oder gar deutsche Alternativen die entsprechenden Funktionen nicht anbieten. Das würde Google oder seine Hyperscaler-Kollegen Azure und AWS alternativlos machen. Aber im Rahmen der Smart Country Convention in Berlin stellte das Zentrum für Digitale Souveränität der öffentlichen Verwaltung Zendis zum Beispiel eine neue Version seiner Kollaborationssoftware Opendesk vor, wie Heise berichtete. Die bindet nicht nur agentische KI ein, sondern soll, Achtung, auch Air-gap-fähig sein. Und diese Software wurde explizit für Behörden und Verwaltung konzipiert. Der Topf findet jetzt also eher seinen Deckel, ohne Landesgrenzen zu überqueren. Auch davor gab und gibt es mit Element beziehungsweise Matrix übrigens schon einen verschlüsselten Messenger, der schon produktiv von deutschen Behörden eingesetzt wird.
In manchen Bereichen ist die Zusammenarbeit mit nicht-europäischen Unternehmen noch unabdingbar. Bislang produziert innerhalb der EU zum Beispiel niemand KI-Beschleuniger, die es mit der Konkurrenz von Nvidia, Google oder Huawei aufnehmen können. Aber gerade, wo es möglich ist, sollte der Staat endlich mal seine Rolle als Ankerkunde erfüllen. Das stärkt die deutsche und europäische Wirtschaft. Bei Firmen, die interoperable Open-Source-Lösungen anbieten, könnten Behörden sich ihre Tools außerdem so zusammenstellen, wie sie es gerade brauchen. Und wenn die deutschen Geheimdienste dann Informationen mit ihren globalen Pendants austauschen wollen, können sie immer noch bei Google anklopfen.

articles.title: „Die Geisterjagd soll menschlich bleiben“: Wie KI das Aufspüren paranormaler Aktivitäten verändert
articles.text:
Paranormal Activity: Geisterjäger wollen mit KI das Übernatürliche sichtbar machen
Kaum ein Bereich bleibt von KI unberührt – auch die Geisterjagd nicht. Die App Ghosttube Seer kombiniert Sensordaten mit KI-Bildgenerierung, um paranormale Aktivitäten visuell abzubilden. In dieser Nische kommen seit jeher verschiedene Instrumente und Technologien zum Einsatz. Trotzdem sind nicht alle von neuen KI-Tools begeistert.
Apps sollen Geister sichtbar machen
Amy Waine und Jarrad Cutting bezeichnen sich selbst als Geisterjäger:innen. Um gespenstische Orte mithilfe von KI zu untersuchen, haben sie die App Ghosttube Seer entwickelt. Diese soll Bilder generieren können, die das Übernatürliche sichtbar machen. Sie nutzt dafür die Signale des Magnetometers im Smartphone, identifiziert Wörter und lässt diese dann durch einen Bildgenerator laufen.
In einem Youtube-Video zeigen die beiden, wie die App funktioniert. Im Winchester Mystery House, einer historischen Villa in Kalifornien, fragten sie die KI: „Kannst du uns zeigen, was früher in diesem Raum vor sich ging?” Die App erzeugte daraufhin Bilder von Räumen, Tieren und Personen, die Waine und Cutting als relevant für die Geschichte des Hauses deuteten.
Gegenüber The Guardian bezeichneten die beiden ihre App als „das weltweit erste KI-Tool zur Geisterjagd“. Nutzer:innen haben zudem die Möglichkeit, ihre KI-generierten Bilder zu posten und die anderer zu kommentieren. Laut Angaben des Google Play Stores wurde die App schon mehr als eine Million Mal heruntergeladen. Die Nutzung ist kostenpflichtig.
Paranormalforscherin äußert Kritik
Alex Matsuo ist Paranormalexpertin und Autorin, arbeitet aber hauptsächlich in der Tech-Branche. Neue Technologien seien schon immer ein wichtiger Teil dieser Nische gewesen, sagt sie. So habe beispielsweise Thomas Edison mit einem „Geistertelefon“ versucht, Kontakt zu den Toten aufzunehmen. „Es überrascht mich nicht, dass KI von vielen Menschen in der Geisterjagd-Community begeistert aufgenommen wurde“, so Matsuo gegenüber The Guardian. Sie probierte Ghosttube Seer nach der Veröffentlichung aus, steht der App aber skeptisch gegenüber.
Ihr Hauptkritikpunkt ist, dass unklar bleibt, welche Daten die großen Sprachmodelle hinter Apps wie dieser nutzen, um ein Phänomen als Geist einzustufen. Auch die Verwendung urheberrechtlich geschützter Werke sieht sie kritisch. Der Kern der Geisterjagd solle ihrer Meinung nach menschlich bleiben. „Viele von uns kommen zur Geisterjagd, weil wir ein Trauma oder einen Trauerfall erlebt haben“, sagte sie. Für viele sei die Erforschung paranormaler Aktivitäten daher eine Form der Trauerbewältigung.
Forderung nach mehr Menschlichkeit
Obwohl die Geisterjagd weit vom Alltag der meisten Menschen entfernt ist, zeigen sich dort dieselben Probleme wie in anderen Disziplinen. Erst kürzlich argumentierte beispielsweise die neugegründete Association for Human Mathematics, dass auch die mathematische Forschung in menschlicher Hand bleiben müsse. Die automatisierte Produktion und Rezeption der Wissenschaft untergrabe ihre intellektuellen Grundlagen. Zuvor hatte OpenAI auf einen Schlag 722 Fachartikel zu mathematischen Problemen veröffentlicht, an denen menschliche Wissenschaftler:innen bisher gescheitert waren.
Zudem könnten Apps wie Ghosttube Seer wahnhafte Vorstellungen der Nutzender:innen verstärken. Große Sprachmodelle verfügen über kein eigenes Wissen, sondern berechnen nur die Wahrscheinlichkeit für das nächste Wort. Deshalb ist stark zu bezweifeln, dass KI-Tools paranormale Aktivitäten tatsächlich sichtbar machen können. Außerdem tendieren sie dazu, Nutzer:innen in dem zu bestätigen, was sie hören wollen. Im vergangenen Jahr hat OpenAI eine Analyse veröffentlicht. Demnach zeigten rund 0,07 Prozent der im Testzeitraum aktiven Nutzer:innen mögliche Anzeichen für psychische Probleme. Das Unternehmen bezeichnete diese Fälle zwar als „äußerst selten“, hochgerechnet auf über eine Milliarde aktive Nutzer:innen pro Woche besteht das Risiko allerdings für eine große Zahl von Menschen.

articles.title: Google envoie un prompt à ses puces d'IA dans l'espace (elles ont répondu)
articles.text:
Le rituel est connu : quand une machine neuve s’allume, on lui fait d’abord afficher « hello, world », la simple preuve que toute la chaîne fonctionne, du clavier jusqu’à l’écran. Le 30 octobre 2026, Google a appliqué ce rituel à une machine qui tourne à plusieurs centaines de kilomètres au-dessus de nos têtes, avec une touche de coquetterie en prime.
Sundar Pichai l’a annoncé sur X : les équipes de Project Suncatcher ont envoyé une commande en orbite, démarré la puce TPU, lancé un prompt et récupéré au sol une première réponse complète. La réponse en question : un haïku.
La vidéo jointe à la publication montre la consigne envoyée depuis le sol : écrire un haïku du point de vue d’une TPU en orbite, avec « le monde merveilleux qui tourne sous toi ». Et la réponse de Gemma, le modèle ouvert de Google, qui tournait sur la puce est la suivante : « Blue marble below, Data streams in silent grace, Starlight feeds my core. ✨ » (« Bille bleue en bas, / les données ruissellent, grâce muette, / la lumière des étoiles nourrit mon cœur. »)
Cinq, sept, cinq syllabes : la métrique est respectée.
C’est quoi Suncatcher ?
Le satellite a décollé le 1er octobre 2026 à bord de Transporter-18, une mission de covoiturage spatial de SpaceX partie de la base de Vandenberg, en Californie. Surnommé MVP (pour Minimum Viable Product), il a été conçu avec Planet, l’opérateur de satellites d’observation de la Terre. De la taille d’un réfrigérateur, il embarque quatre TPU de génération Trillium, les puces que Google dessine pour l’IA et installe dans ses data centers, alimentées par environ un kilowatt de panneaux solaires.
Google présentait lui-même ce vol comme un test minimal : vérifier que des puces pensées pour des salles climatisées encaissent les vibrations du lancement (de 50 à 100 g pour certains composants), le vide, les écarts thermiques et les radiations. Le haïku confirme qu’à ce stade, elles tiennent.
L’idée de Suncatcher, dévoilée en novembre 2025, part d’un constat que nous avions creusé dans notre vidéo sur l’eau des data centers : l’IA bute désormais moins sur les puces que sur l’électricité, le refroidissement et le foncier.
Sur une orbite héliosynchrone dite « aube-crépuscule », vers 650 km d’altitude, un satellite longe en permanence la frontière entre le jour et la nuit. Selon Google, des panneaux solaires y produisent jusqu’à huit fois plus d’énergie qu’au sol. Le papier de recherche publié en 2025 imagine des grappes de 81 satellites volant à quelques centaines de mètres les uns des autres, reliés par laser. Au banc d’essai, ces liaisons optiques ont atteint 1,6 térabit par seconde. Bombardées de protons dans un accélérateur, les TPU Trillium n’ont montré aucune panne franche jusqu’à 15 krad, bien au-delà de la dose attendue pour une mission de cinq ans.
Interrogé par Fox News en décembre dernier, Sundar Pichai estimait que d’ici une dizaine d’années, construire des data centers dans l’espace paraîtrait « plus normal ».
Google n’est d’ailleurs même pas le premier à faire parler une IA en orbite. En décembre 2025, la start-up Starcloud, soutenue par Nvidia, faisait tourner sur un GPU H100 embarqué Gemma, le modèle ouvert de Google, qui saluait poliment les Terriens. Elle y avait aussi entraîné le petit nanoGPT d’Andrej Karpathy sur l’œuvre complète de Shakespeare. Le haïku de Suncatcher arrive donc après le pastiche élisabéthain.
Le vrai examen aura lieu en 2027, quand deux satellites devront échanger par laser en volant en formation serrée. Si l’essai réussit, on cessera de parler de haïkus pour parler de gigawatts. S’il échoue, le haïku sera à l’image de cette expérimentation : par définition, un poème très court.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Syrian Hacker Gets Prison Time in US After Over a Decade on the Run
articles.text:
A Syrian man tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA) has received a 42-month prison sentence in the US, more than 12 years after he was first charged.
Ahmad Umar Agha, who used the online handle Th3Pr0, was sentenced on Thursday by a federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia. According to the Justice Department, he evaded US authorities for more than a decade.
Prosecutors say the hacking conspiracy Agha took part in was directed by figures close to Bashar al-Assad, among them the head of Syria’s General Intelligence Directorate. The scheme began as early as August 2011 and continued until January 2024.
The DOJ described Agha as a central figure in the operation. He compromised around 47 targets, a mix of Western news outlets, companies, NGOs, and government bodies in the US and allied countries.
Among the intrusions highlighted by prosecutors was the 2013 takeover of the Associated Press’s Twitter account. Agha used it to publish a fabricated report claiming that President Barack Obama had been hurt in two blasts at the White House. The fake post triggered a flash crash that briefly wiped $136 billion off the combined value of the Dow Jones Industrial Average’s component stocks.
Agha also gained access to the company hosting the Marine Corps’ recruiting website and sent its traffic to an image calling on Marines to defy their orders.
He twice went after the White House’s social media presence by targeting the email credentials of White House employees. In one case he obtained them, but his attempt to use that access to dupe other staffers into handing over the accounts did not work.
The intrusions left many victims with large bills for cleanup and security overhauls. A firm providing online publishers with content, advertising, and outbound links lost around $35,000 per day for about six months. A global NGO spent roughly $250,000 on new network monitoring tools, retrained more than 800 employees, and upgraded its security, with total losses of $480,000.
Agha and his alleged accomplice, Firas Dardar, were first charged by criminal complaint in June 2014. The case was unsealed in March 2016, when the FBI put both men on its Cyber’s Most Wanted list and offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to Agha’s arrest.
A grand jury indicted the pair in May 2018. Dardar has yet to be caught.
Agha’s appearance in a federal courtroom in November 2025 was first reported by legal news outlet Court Watch. The DOJ’s announcement does not explain how or where he was taken into custody.

articles.title: Welche deutschen Unternehmen Bewerber transparent über den KI-Einsatz informieren – und welche nicht
articles.text:
KI im Recruiting: So findest du heraus, ob deine Bewerbung zuerst von einem Bot aussortiert wird
Zahlreiche Personaler:innen kämpfen mit einer Flut an Bewerbungen. Sie sind auf die Nutzung von KI zurückzuführen, die Anschreiben und Lebensläufe innerhalb kürzester Zeit ausspucken können und so die Hürde der Bewerbung minimieren. Um diesem Ansturm entgegenzuwirken, greifen viele Personalabteilungen mittlerweile selbst auf KI zurück. Wie jetzt eine Untersuchung des HR-Softwareanbieters Lucca zeigt, gehen aber gerade deutsche Unternehmen nicht flächendeckend transparent damit um.
Bewerbungen im KI-Zeitalter: Welche Unternehmen sind transparent?
Insgesamt wurden für den KI-Transparenz-Index 25 deutsche Unternehmen genauer unter die Lupe genommen. Es handelt sich dabei um die größten deutschen Arbeitgeber, gemessen an der Anzahl der Mitarbeiter:innen. Dabei untersuchte Lucca vier Bereiche genauer: die rechtliche Transparenz in Datenschutzhinweisen für Bewerber:innen, die Transparenz zum KI-Einsatz während des Bewerbungsablaufs sowie über die eingesetzte Recruiting-Software und die „unternehmensweite KI-Steuerung mitsamt Richtlinien, Ethik-Kodizes und Geschäfts-, Nachhaltigkeits- und Menschenrechtsberichten“.
Dabei konnten die deutschen Unternehmen insgesamt 30 Punkte sammeln. Je mehr Punkte, desto transparenter der Umgang mit KI. Die Allianz erreichte dabei mit einem Score von 26 die höchste Punktzahl. Auf den zweiten und dritten Platz kommen die Deutsche Telekom und SAP mit jeweils 20 Punkten. Auf dem letzten Platz liegt hingegen laut Lucca Aldi Nord mit nur einem Punkt. Siemens Energy landet mit fünf Punkten auf dem vorletzten Platz.
Laut Lucca nutzen 21 der untersuchten Unternehmen ihre Bewerbungen über eine Software, die zumindest theoretisch auch KI-Funktionen unterstützt. Lediglich vier Unternehmen kommunizieren diese KI-Funktionen auch offen. Dazu zählen Bayer, SAP, Allianz und Siemens. Bei anderen Unternehmen haben Bewerber:innen meist nur die Chance, über die Datenschutzhinweise etwas über die KI-Nutzung zu erfahren.
Marek Kraus, Country Manager Germany bei Lucca, sagt dazu: „Unsere Untersuchung zeigt: KI ist in den Systemen vieler Unternehmen angekommen, wird für Bewerber:innen aber oft erst im Datenschutztext sichtbar. Mittelfristig sollte der KI-Einsatz transparent dort offengelegt werden, wo Bewerber:innen sich tatsächlich informieren.“
Für Bewerber:innen empfiehlt Lucca deshalb, immer einen Blick auf die Datenschutzhinweise zu werfen. Darin wird dargelegt, welche personenbezogenen Daten während der Bewerbung verarbeitet werden. Anhand von KI-zugehörigen Begriffen wie „automatisierte Verarbeitung“ oder unscheinbaren Formulierungen wie „Vorauswahl“ lässt sich die KI-Nutzung erkennen.
Wer die KI-Nutzung frühzeitig sieht, kann sie auch für sich nutzen. Dabei sollten gezielt Schlagworte und Anforderungen aus der Stellenausschreibung im Lebenslauf und dem Anschreiben integriert und hervorgehoben werden, damit KI-Systeme sie schneller erkennen. Natürlich ist das nur dann empfehlenswert, wenn Bewerber:innen die nötigen Qualifikationen auch wirklich mitbringen.

articles.title: Adieu les écrans géants et les gadgets inutiles ? La Chine durcit le ton face à la démesure automobile
articles.text:
Leurs vaisseaux ont certainement impressionné les visiteurs du dernier Mondial de l’Auto. Présentes en nombre, les marques chinoises ont en effet marqué la 91ème édition du salon avec des technologies plus étonnantes les unes que les autres. Sauf que le bluff pourrait bientôt prendre fin, puisque l’Empire du Milieu resserrera prochainement les boulons autour de ces modèles au nom de la sécurité. Enfin une bonne nouvelle ?
L’idée fait en tout cas son chemin, car le ministère chinois de l’Industrie et des Technologies de l’Information vient de lancer une consultation publique sur un projet de loi visant à contrôler davantage les technologies embarquées. Une attention particulière est notamment portée sur la taille des écrans tactiles, l’inclinaison des sièges zéro gravité, les feux personnalisables et les poignées de portes affleurantes. Voyons cela en détail.
Écrans tactiles géants : l’overdose qui met en danger les conducteurs
Les dalles XXL, d’abord, posent un réel problème d’ergonomie. Comment rester insensible au fait de devoir farfouiller dans d’innombrables sous-menus pour régler simplement la température intérieure ? Le ministère demande ainsi aux constructeurs d’évaluer l’impact de ces afficheurs sur la distraction des automobilistes. Leur fiabilité et leur sécurité en cas d’accident seront pareillement analysées.
De cela découlerait des mesures concrètes, comme l’interdiction pure et simple des écrans pliables et flexibles. Signature des modèles haut de gamme, les sièges zéro gravité sont aussi dans le collimateur des autorités. Des tests de collision, d’anti-pincement et de fiabilité plus exigeants sont ainsi suggérés pour améliorer leur sécurité. Le ministère conseille même de limiter l’usage de ces assises, voire de l’interdire en fonction des situations.
À lire aussi : « Les écrans tactiles pires que l’alcool au volant » – cette étude choc pointe du doigt les véhicules modernes
Messages et dessins sur les feux : la censure s’invite sur la route
Les feux personnalisables permettant d’écrire des messages coquins ou de dessiner des motifs amusants pourraient aussi être sous strict contrôle. Certains hauts responsables du ministère craignent que du contenu non autorisé soit affiché sur les routes. Les constructeurs sont vivement invités à modérer activement tout ce qui sera affiché dans ces feux. Toute inscription considérée comme sensible pourrait donc être bannie. Mais la fonctionnalité subsistera.
Le dernier point est déjà connu. Il s’agit des poignées affleurantes qui ont causé dans le passé des accidents gravissimes. Raison pour laquelle le ministère a déjà publié plusieurs modèles de poignées de portes qu’il juge sûrs. Une poignée de paramètres comme leur prise en main, leur emplacement ou leur mécanisme ont été pris en compte. Une ouverture de secours manuelle sera également imposée pour permettre une utilisation même après un accident.

articles.title: Chainalysis discloses data breach from "offensive agentic techniques"
articles.text:
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis has disclosed a security incident after attackers used what it describes as "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its internal systems and tools.
The company says some customer information was accessed, including names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels, but claims there is no evidence that sensitive investigation data or authentication credentials were exposed.
Chainalysis says attackers accessed internal systems and tools
Chainalysis provides blockchain analytics tools used by law enforcement, government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, and financial institutions to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering.
On Friday, roughly 5:14 PM ET, Chainalysis published a security incident disclosure along with the full text of the email sent to affected customers.
The disclosure says the company detected an external actor using "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools earlier this month, and has since been patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems.
The accessed data includes user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels for users provisioned on the platform.
Chainalysis is still determining which records were accessed for each organization and will provide a detailed breakdown once that analysis is complete.
A Chainalysis spokesperson confirmed the incident to BleepingComputer and said the company is working with external cybersecurity experts. It is also using large language models (LLMs) to support a broader security review of its platform.
"Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens," the company said, adding that the incident is unrelated to the recent Binance theft.
Customers are advised to enable two-factor authentication (2FA) and watch for unexpected password reset requests, authentication prompts, and scammers impersonating Chainalysis, particularly those offering fund recovery or recruiting services.
What are "offensive agentic techniques"?
Chainalysis has not shared technical details about the intrusion, including which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were accessed, or how long the attackers had access.
It is unclear whether the attackers used existing agentic offensive security frameworks, such as ARTEX, or custom-built AI agents capable of autonomously identifying vulnerabilities, exploiting them, and chaining together subsequent actions.
ARTEX has recently been used by threat actors, including in the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, according to Microsoft.
The term "agentic" generally describes AI systems capable of executing multi-step tasks with limited human intervention, potentially allowing attackers to automate portions of the intrusion process rather than relying on traditional hands-on exploitation.
A relentless week of security incidents
The Chainalysis disclosure comes amid a relentless week of security incidents affecting the cryptocurrency and technology industries.
On Friday, Binance linked the roughly $6.3 billion theft, now the largest crypto heist on record and attributed to North Korean state-backed hackers, to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.
Separately, hardware wallet maker Trezor warned of a suspected cryptocurrency-stealing implant reported in a Trezor Safe 5 device sold by a Southeast Asian reseller. The implant can reportedly read the recovery phrase shown on the device's screen and transmit it over a mobile network.
Meanwhile, a malicious version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through the Cursor extension marketplace, planting persistent SSH backdoors on developers' machines.
Chainalysis says it will share further updates with affected customers as its investigation progresses.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: When Electric Cars Were the Clean, Quiet Choice for Women
articles.text:
At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.
For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.
Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.
Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.
In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science
A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.
Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier?
Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images
Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.
The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.
A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric Cars
I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.
This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens
According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.
Thomas Edison Designed a Bad Battery
Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.
While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).
Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens
Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.
When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.
Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science
Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)
Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.
Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.
Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.
An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.
References
For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.
Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

articles.title: Sechs Wege zum ewigen Ich: Was Forscher mit Gehirnen anstellen, damit wir nie ganz verschwinden
articles.text:
Kopf ab, Gehirn rein, Geist hochladen: 6 waghalsige Experimente für ein Leben ohne Körper
Habt ihr schon einmal darüber nachgedacht, was euch zu dem macht, was ihr seid? Die Wissenschaft versichert uns, dass dies ausschließlich mit dem drei Pfund schweren Organ zwischen unseren Ohren zu tun hat – mit seinen Milliarden von Neuronen und Billionen feiner Verbindungen. Viel schwieriger ist es jedoch zu erklären, warum wir ein Selbstbewusstsein haben, oder genau zu bestimmen, wo diese erste Erinnerung an Mama tatsächlich gespeichert ist. Wenn wir älter werden, vergessen wir das meiste, was wir erlebt haben, und doch gibt es eine unbestreitbare Kontinuität: Mit 30, 50 oder 70 wirst du immer noch du selbst sein.
Um diese schwer fassbare Kontinuität des Selbst zu bewahren, arbeiten einige weitsichtige Technologen an Möglichkeiten, dein Gehirn am Laufen zu halten – sogar über den Tod hinaus. Nennen wir sie die „Mind Saver“. Sie erforschen alles, vom Einfrieren von Gehirnen in flüssigem Stickstoff über die Verbesserung lebender Gehirne bis hin zum Hochladen unserer Erinnerungen in die Cloud. Hier betrachten wir sechs mögliche und teilweise auch verrückte Wege, um euren Geist am Leben zu erhalten. Wir ordnen ein, wie realisierbar sie wären und welche Vorteile die heutige Forschung mit sich bringen könnte – selbst wenn die kognitive Unsterblichkeit nicht gelingen sollte.
